# The long read — normalization is a claim about the future

Codd's normal forms are usually taught as a hygiene ritual: apply the
rules, arrive at 3NF, feel professional. That framing survives contact
with exactly no production system, because it leaves out what the rules
are *for*. A normalized schema is a claim about which states of the world
are possible. Every table you split off is a sentence: "a carrier has one
name". Every foreign key is a sentence: "a leg cannot reference a carrier
that does not exist". The value of the exercise is not tidiness. It is
that a whole category of bug — the database disagreeing with itself —
stops being representable, and therefore stops needing to be tested for,
monitored, or apologised for.

## What redundancy actually costs

The classic argument is storage, and the classic argument is wrong. Disk
is cheap and text compresses. The real costs are three.

The first is **write amplification of meaning**. A single business event
("this carrier rebranded") maps to one row in a normalized schema and
40,000 rows in the feed. Not because the update is slow — it is, but that
is the small part — but because a 40,000-row update is a *transaction that
can fail halfway*, and in a system where the same fact lives in 40,000
places, a partial failure produces a state that no constraint can detect
as wrong. Normalization converts a class of consistency bug into a class
of referential-integrity error, and referential-integrity errors are
loud.

The second is **the drift you cannot see**. By the time `shipment_feed`
reaches you, three spellings of one carrier already coexist. No query
errored. No alert fired. Reports have been quietly splitting one carrier
into three for years, and the number in the board deck has been wrong in a
way that is invisible unless someone thinks to check. This is the failure
mode that makes normalization worth arguing for: not that it prevents
corruption, but that it prevents *silent* corruption.

The third is **schema ambiguity**. In a wide table, nothing says whether
`carrier_name` is authoritative or a cached copy. A new engineer has to
guess, and half of them guess "authoritative" and write to it. A
normalized schema answers the question structurally.

## How Postgres actually helps

Postgres gives you three mechanisms that make derived data safe, and they
sit on a spectrum of ownership.

**Generated columns** (PG12+) are the strongest. `GENERATED ALWAYS AS
(expr) STORED` computes on insert and update, rejects direct writes with
an error, and stores the result in the heap tuple, so reads cost nothing
extra. The expression must be immutable and may reference only columns of
the same row — which rules out "count of children", and rules it out for
a good reason: a value that depends on other rows cannot be maintained by
a per-row computation without locking those rows. Postgres 16 has no
virtual (non-stored) generated columns; `STORED` is your only option, and
the table is rewritten when you add one.

**Triggers** are the general case and the weakest guarantee. A `FOR EACH
ROW` trigger can maintain anything, including cross-row aggregates, and
that generality is exactly why it is fragile: `ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE
TRIGGER` is a single statement, `session_replication_role = 'replica'`
silently disables user triggers for the whole session (this is how many
restore and migration tools work), and `COPY` paths in some tools bypass
them by design. Every trigger-maintained cache is therefore a cache with
an *operational* failure mode, not just a logical one. This is why the
reconciliation query is not optional; it is half of the design.

**Materialized views** are the coarse-grained option. One writer
(`REFRESH`), a known staleness, no possibility of a second write path.
`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` requires a unique index on the
view because it implements the refresh as a `FULL OUTER JOIN` diff against
a freshly computed temporary copy and applies the differences — it needs a
key to match old rows to new ones. Without the unique index, refresh takes
an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock and the view is unreadable for the duration,
which for a reporting table read by a dashboard is an outage.

## The history the rules came from

Codd published the relational model in 1970 and 1NF-3NF in the years
after; Boyce-Codd normal form arrived in 1974 to close a case 3NF permits
— a determinant that is not a superkey, in a table with overlapping
candidate keys. Fagin's 4NF (1977) and 5NF (1979) handle multivalued and
join dependencies. The practical distribution is steeply skewed: you will
apply 3NF constantly, recognise a BCNF violation a few times, and meet a
genuine 4NF violation approximately never — though when you do, it is
usually a junction table with two independent multivalued facts crammed
into it, and the fix is obvious once named.

What is worth carrying from the theory is not the ladder but the idea of
**dependency preservation**. A decomposition can be lossless (you can
rejoin without inventing rows) and still lose the ability to enforce a
functional dependency with a single constraint. BCNF decompositions are
lossless but not always dependency-preserving; 3NF decompositions can
always be made both. That is the real reason 3NF is the practical
stopping point: it is where you can still enforce everything you know.

## Performance, honestly

Normalized schemas are not slower in the way people assume. A hash join
between a 40,000-row fact table and a 60-row carrier table costs almost
nothing; the lookup table fits in a single page and stays in shared
buffers forever. What actually costs is join *fan-out* in analytic
queries, star-schema-shaped queries touching six dimensions at high row
counts, and — the honest one — latency in chatty ORMs that fetch parents
one row at a time. Note that two of those three are query problems, not
schema problems.

When measurement does show the joins are the cost, the response is
ordered: index the join columns; try a covering index for an index-only
scan; try a materialized view for the specific report; and only then
consider a maintained denormalized column. Skipping to the last step is
how schemas acquire columns nobody can explain.

## When not to normalize

**Event and log tables.** An `events` table records what a request looked
like at the moment it happened, including the user's name and plan at that
instant. Those are snapshots, not copies, and joining them to current
dimension tables at read time would answer a different question than the
one being asked.

**Analytical stores.** Star and wide-table designs exist because
analytical engines scan columns and hate joins, and because the data is
append-only and derived from an authoritative normalized source. The
warehouse being denormalized is fine precisely because the OLTP database
is not.

**Genuinely single-valued attribute bags.** A `settings jsonb` column
holding preferences nothing joins against or constrains is not a 1NF
violation worth fixing. The moment you want "all users with feature X
enabled, where X must exist", you have rediscovered why join tables exist
— and that moment is the signal to normalize, not the day you created the
column.

**Small, stable, embedded value objects.** An address that is only ever
read with its owner, never searched, never shared, and never independently
updated can live as columns on the parent. Extracting it buys a join and
sells nothing.

The rule underneath all four exceptions is the same: normalize what can
change independently, and embed what cannot. When you get that judgement
wrong in the embedding direction, you get the update anomaly. When you get
it wrong in the extracting direction, you get a schema with forty tables
where twelve would do, which is a smaller problem — but still a problem,
and one worth naming so that nobody mistakes normal forms for a score.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — find the drift before you design for it

`setup.sql` loads `shipment_feed`, 40,000 rows, one per shipment leg:

```sql
shipment_feed(shipment_id int, leg_no int, carrier_code text,
              carrier_name text, carrier_scac text,
              origin_code text, origin_city text, origin_country text,
              dest_code text, dest_city text, dest_country text,
              customer_ref text, customer_name text,
              customer_billing_country text,
              service_level text, service_transit_days int,
              weight_kg numeric(10,2), rate_per_kg numeric(10,4),
              leg_cost numeric(12,2), booked_at timestamptz,
              PRIMARY KEY (shipment_id, leg_no))
```

You are about to extract `sf_carriers` keyed on `carrier_code`. Before you
write a line of DDL, prove whether the feed can supply one name per code.

Return every `carrier_code` that appears with **more than one distinct**
`carrier_name`. Columns `carrier_code`, `name_count` (bigint), `variants`
(a `text[]` of the distinct names, ascending).

Example row: `('MAEU', 2, {'Maersk','Maersk Line A/S'})`.

**Ordered by `carrier_code` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e01_normalization_practice ex1`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You are not looking for duplicate rows. You are looking for a key that
fails to determine a column it is supposed to determine — one code, more
than one name. That is a per-group question, so it is a `GROUP BY` with a
`HAVING`.

## Hint 2

The shape, on a different column:

```sql
SELECT origin_code, count(DISTINCT origin_city) AS n
FROM shipment_feed
GROUP BY origin_code
HAVING count(DISTINCT origin_city) > 1;
```

`count(DISTINCT ...)` inside `HAVING` is legal and is the point of the
query.

## Hint 3

Group by `carrier_code`, keep groups where the distinct name count exceeds
one, and collect the names with `array_agg`. The collection needs its own
ordering to be deterministic — an aggregate can take `ORDER BY` inside its
parentheses, and whether you also need `DISTINCT` in there is the decision
left to you.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the failure you are trying to avoid. Write the migration insert
first, in your head: `INSERT INTO sf_carriers SELECT DISTINCT carrier_code,
carrier_name FROM shipment_feed`. What error does it raise, and on which
rows? This exercise returns exactly those rows.

## Hint 2

A useful debugging move is to look at the raw pairs before summarising
them:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT carrier_code, carrier_name
FROM shipment_feed
ORDER BY carrier_code, carrier_name;
```

Scroll it. Codes with two adjacent lines are your answer set; now express
"has two adjacent lines" as an aggregate.

## Hint 3

If you prefer the window-function route: `count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY
carrier_code)` over that distinct-pairs subquery flags the offenders, and
then you still have to collapse to one row per code — which is the moment
you notice `GROUP BY` was the shorter road. Either way, the `array_agg`
must be ordered or the gate's comparison is a coin flip.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e01_normalization_practice/ex1 — carrier codes whose name has drifted
SELECT carrier_code,
       count(DISTINCT carrier_name)                        AS name_count,
       array_agg(DISTINCT carrier_name ORDER BY carrier_name) AS variants
FROM shipment_feed
GROUP BY carrier_code
HAVING count(DISTINCT carrier_name) > 1
ORDER BY carrier_code;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3e01_normalization_practice/ex1 — same answer, staged from distinct pairs
WITH pairs AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT carrier_code, carrier_name
  FROM shipment_feed
)
SELECT carrier_code,
       count(*)                                     AS name_count,
       array_agg(carrier_name ORDER BY carrier_name) AS variants
FROM pairs
GROUP BY carrier_code
HAVING count(*) > 1
ORDER BY carrier_code;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — the reference tables

Three lookup entities hide in `shipment_feed`: carriers, locations and
service levels. Create them, with these exact names, columns and keys:

```sql
sf_carriers (carrier_code text PRIMARY KEY,
             carrier_name text NOT NULL,
             carrier_scac text NOT NULL)

sf_locations (location_code text PRIMARY KEY,
              city    text NOT NULL,
              country text NOT NULL)

sf_services (service_level text PRIMARY KEY,
             transit_days  int  NOT NULL)
```

Two design notes the gate checks. `sf_locations` is **one** table, not
`sf_origins` and `sf_destinations`: origin and destination are two *roles*
played by the same entity, and a port is a port whichever end of the leg
it is on. And `sf_services.transit_days` gets a `CHECK (transit_days > 0)`
constraint named `sf_services_transit_positive` — a service level with
zero transit days is not a thing the business can sell, so say so in the
schema.

Create nothing else. The tables stay empty until ex4.

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e01_normalization_practice ex2`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three `CREATE TABLE` statements and one named `CHECK`. The only judgement
call was made for you in the prompt: origin and destination share a table
because they share an identity.

## Hint 2

A named check constraint, spelled out rather than inline-anonymous:

```sql
CREATE TABLE demo (
  n int NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT demo_n_positive CHECK (n > 0)
);
```

The name matters because your application will one day match on it in an
error handler.

## Hint 3

Write the three tables in dependency order even though none of them
reference each other yet — it is a habit that pays in ex3. Whether you
declare the `CHECK` as a table constraint or as a column constraint with
`CONSTRAINT <name> CHECK (...)` is up to you; both produce the same
`pg_constraint` row, which is what the gate reads.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it as an interface, not a schema. Somebody reading only these
three `CREATE TABLE` statements should be able to recite the business
rules: a carrier code identifies exactly one carrier, a location code
exactly one place, a service level exactly one promise. If a reader could
not deduce that, a key is missing.

## Hint 2

Check your work through the catalog rather than by rereading your file:

```sql
SELECT conname, contype, pg_get_constraintdef(oid)
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE conrelid = 'sf_services'::regclass;
```

You should see the primary key and your named check, and nothing else.

## Hint 3

The trap in this exercise is over-building. No foreign keys yet, no
indexes yet, no `sf_customers` yet — those arrive in ex3, and adding them
early means ex3's gate finds the objects already present and your later
script fails on a duplicate name. Build exactly the three tables asked
for.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — the fact tables, and one entity in two roles

Your ex2 tables are created automatically first. Now the rest of the
decomposition:

```sql
sf_customers (customer_ref     text PRIMARY KEY,
              customer_name    text NOT NULL,
              billing_country  text NOT NULL)

sf_shipments (shipment_id   int PRIMARY KEY,
              customer_ref  text NOT NULL REFERENCES sf_customers,
              service_level text NOT NULL REFERENCES sf_services,
              booked_at     timestamptz NOT NULL)

sf_legs (shipment_id  int  NOT NULL REFERENCES sf_shipments,
         leg_no       int  NOT NULL,
         carrier_code text NOT NULL REFERENCES sf_carriers,
         origin_code  text NOT NULL,
         dest_code    text NOT NULL,
         weight_kg    numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
         rate_per_kg  numeric(10,4) NOT NULL,
         PRIMARY KEY (shipment_id, leg_no))
```

`origin_code` and `dest_code` both reference `sf_locations(location_code)`
— **two separate foreign keys to the same parent table**, which must be
named `sf_legs_origin_fk` and `sf_legs_dest_fk`. Postgres will not invent
two usable default names for you here, and your error handlers need to
tell "unknown origin" from "unknown destination".

Also add `CONSTRAINT sf_legs_weight_positive CHECK (weight_kg > 0)`.

The gate probes both foreign keys with a ghost location code and checks
that each one raises, by name.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e01_normalization_practice ex3`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The only new idea here is that a table may reference the same parent
twice. Nothing about a foreign key says the parent must be a different
table from the other foreign key's parent — it only says the referenced
columns must be unique.

## Hint 2

Named, table-level foreign keys:

```sql
CREATE TABLE flight (
  from_airport text NOT NULL,
  to_airport   text NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT flight_from_fk FOREIGN KEY (from_airport)
    REFERENCES airports(code),
  CONSTRAINT flight_to_fk   FOREIGN KEY (to_airport)
    REFERENCES airports(code)
);
```

## Hint 3

Create the tables in the order a foreign key would demand: customers
before shipments, shipments before legs. The composite primary key on
`sf_legs` is `(shipment_id, leg_no)` in that order — and thinking for a
moment about *why* that order rather than the reverse is worth more than
the exercise itself.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the failing query you want. `SELECT ... FROM sf_legs JOIN
sf_locations o ON o.location_code = l.origin_code JOIN sf_locations d ON
d.location_code = l.dest_code` — two aliases of one table. The schema has
to permit that join to be trustworthy, which means two constraints, not
one.

## Hint 2

If you let Postgres generate the constraint names, you get
`sf_legs_origin_code_fkey` and `sf_legs_dest_code_fkey`, which are
serviceable but not what the gate wants. Check what you actually created:

```sql
SELECT conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid)
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE conrelid = 'sf_legs'::regclass AND contype = 'f';
```

## Hint 3

A foreign key creates no index on the child side. You are not asked to add
one here, but note the consequence now: with 40,000 legs and no index on
`origin_code`, deleting a location will sequentially scan `sf_legs` to
check the constraint. V3·E3 makes that failure concrete.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e01_normalization_practice/ex3 — shipment tables, two FKs to one parent
CREATE TABLE sf_customers (
  customer_ref    text PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_name   text NOT NULL,
  billing_country text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE sf_shipments (
  shipment_id   int  PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_ref  text NOT NULL REFERENCES sf_customers(customer_ref),
  service_level text NOT NULL REFERENCES sf_services(service_level),
  booked_at     timestamptz NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE sf_legs (
  shipment_id  int  NOT NULL REFERENCES sf_shipments(shipment_id),
  leg_no       int  NOT NULL,
  carrier_code text NOT NULL REFERENCES sf_carriers(carrier_code),
  origin_code  text NOT NULL,
  dest_code    text NOT NULL,
  weight_kg    numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
  rate_per_kg  numeric(10,4) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (shipment_id, leg_no),
  CONSTRAINT sf_legs_weight_positive CHECK (weight_kg > 0),
  CONSTRAINT sf_legs_origin_fk FOREIGN KEY (origin_code)
    REFERENCES sf_locations(location_code),
  CONSTRAINT sf_legs_dest_fk   FOREIGN KEY (dest_code)
    REFERENCES sf_locations(location_code)
);

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — migrate the parents

Your ex2 and ex3 DDL runs automatically first. Fill four tables from
`shipment_feed`, parents before children:

1. `sf_locations` — every distinct code that appears as an **origin or a
   destination**, with its city and country. A port that only ever appears
   as a destination must still be present.
2. `sf_services` — distinct `(service_level, service_transit_days)`.
3. `sf_customers` — distinct `(customer_ref, customer_name,
   customer_billing_country)`.
4. `sf_shipments` — one row per `shipment_id`, carrying `customer_ref`,
   `service_level` and `booked_at`.

These four are the clean ones: the feed happens to be internally
consistent for them, so plain deduplication works and the primary keys
will accept the result. `sf_carriers` is *not* clean, which is why it
waits for ex5.

`sf_shipments` needs one row per shipment while the feed has one row per
leg. Both `DISTINCT` on the shipment-level columns and `GROUP BY
shipment_id` with an aggregate reach the same place; pick one and be able
to say why it is safe.

Expected counts after your script: `sf_locations` 48, `sf_services` 3,
`sf_customers` 120, `sf_shipments` 9,000.

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e01_normalization_practice ex4`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four `INSERT ... SELECT` statements. The only one with a twist is
locations, where a single output table is fed by two input columns — that
is a set union, and the deduplicating kind.

## Hint 2

Two roles, one table:

```sql
INSERT INTO airports (code, city)
SELECT from_code, from_city FROM flights
UNION
SELECT to_code,   to_city   FROM flights;
```

`UNION` (not `UNION ALL`) deduplicates for you, which is exactly the
behaviour the primary key demands.

## Hint 3

Order matters: locations, services and customers can go in any order among
themselves, but `sf_shipments` must come after `sf_customers` and
`sf_services` or the foreign keys will stop you. Being stopped is the
constraint doing its job during your own migration — a small preview of
what it will do for you at 3am.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what could go wrong with each insert and what would catch it. Locations:
a code with two cities would break the key — the prompt promises it does
not, but the promise is checkable with the ex1 query pointed at
`origin_code`. Run it. Trusting a prompt is a habit you do not want.

## Hint 2

For the shipment-level rows, the deduplication is over a *subset* of
columns, and `SELECT DISTINCT` over exactly the columns you insert is only
safe if those columns are functionally determined by `shipment_id`. Verify
before you rely on it:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM (
  SELECT DISTINCT shipment_id, customer_ref, service_level, booked_at
  FROM shipment_feed) d;   -- must equal count(DISTINCT shipment_id)
```

## Hint 3

If that check fails in some future feed, the fix is not `DISTINCT ON` — it
is asking the vendor which value is right. Silently picking one with
`min(booked_at)` buries a data-quality bug inside a migration where nobody
will find it. Here the check passes, so plain `DISTINCT` is honest.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — deduplicate with a stated rule, then load the legs

Your ex2-ex4 scripts run automatically first, so the four clean parents
are already populated. Two statements left.

**Carriers.** ex1 proved that some codes carry more than one spelling of
the name. `INSERT ... SELECT DISTINCT carrier_code, carrier_name,
carrier_scac` would raise a unique violation. You must choose a winner,
and the rule is:

> For each `carrier_code`, keep the `(carrier_name, carrier_scac)` pair
> that appears on the **most feed rows**; break ties on `carrier_name`
> ascending, then `carrier_scac` ascending.

Write the rule as an `ORDER BY` rather than as hand-picked values, so that
a reviewer can disagree with the policy instead of with your typing.

**Legs.** Then load `sf_legs` from the feed: `shipment_id`, `leg_no`,
`carrier_code`, `origin_code`, `dest_code`, `weight_kg`, `rate_per_kg`.
One feed row becomes one leg row; no deduplication needed. Do not load
`leg_cost` — the column does not exist yet, and ex7 explains why.

Expected counts: `sf_carriers` 12, `sf_legs` 40,000.

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e01_normalization_practice ex5`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

"Most feed rows" is a count, and the count is over `(carrier_code,
carrier_name, carrier_scac)` triples. So you need two stages: count the
triples, then pick one triple per code.

## Hint 2

`DISTINCT ON` picks the first row per key under an explicit ordering:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT ON (dept) dept, title, headcount
FROM staffing
ORDER BY dept, headcount DESC, title;
```

The `ORDER BY` must start with the `DISTINCT ON` columns; everything after
that is the policy.

## Hint 3

Stage the counts in a CTE, then `DISTINCT ON (carrier_code)` with `ORDER
BY carrier_code, uses DESC, carrier_name, carrier_scac`. `row_number()`
filtered to 1 is the same query wearing different clothes — either is
fine, but only one of them puts the policy on a single readable line.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Run the insert you know is wrong first, and read the error:

```sql
INSERT INTO sf_carriers
SELECT DISTINCT carrier_code, carrier_name, carrier_scac FROM shipment_feed;
-- ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "sf_carriers_pkey"
```

The constraint is telling you that the feed does not contain the fact you
claimed it did. Everything after this is you deciding what to do about
that, which is a business decision, not a SQL one.

## Hint 2

Inspect the competing spellings and their weights before choosing, so you
know what your rule is actually deciding:

```sql
SELECT carrier_code, carrier_name, carrier_scac, count(*) AS uses
FROM shipment_feed
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY carrier_code, uses DESC;
```

For at least one code you will see a lopsided split — thousands of rows
against a handful — which is what makes "most used wins" defensible here
and would not make it defensible if the split were even.

## Hint 3

Load the legs last and let the foreign keys audit your carrier table for
you: if any leg references a code your dedup dropped, `sf_legs_carrier_...`
raises. It will not — you kept every code, only collapsed the names — but
the fact that the database would have caught the mistake is the reason to
run the two statements in this order rather than the other.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e01_normalization_practice/ex5 — dedup carriers by a stated policy, load legs
WITH spellings AS (
  SELECT carrier_code, carrier_name, carrier_scac, count(*) AS uses
  FROM shipment_feed
  GROUP BY carrier_code, carrier_name, carrier_scac
)
INSERT INTO sf_carriers (carrier_code, carrier_name, carrier_scac)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (carrier_code) carrier_code, carrier_name, carrier_scac
FROM spellings
ORDER BY carrier_code, uses DESC, carrier_name, carrier_scac;

INSERT INTO sf_legs (shipment_id, leg_no, carrier_code,
                     origin_code, dest_code, weight_kg, rate_per_kg)
SELECT shipment_id, leg_no, carrier_code,
       origin_code, dest_code, weight_kg, rate_per_kg
FROM shipment_feed;

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — prove the decomposition is lossless

Your ex2-ex5 scripts run automatically first, so the six normalized tables
are populated. A decomposition is only correct if joining the pieces back
reproduces the original **exactly** — same rows, same multiplicities. Normal
forms are the design; this is the test.

Return **one row**, two `bigint` columns:

- `missing` — feed rows the rejoined schema fails to produce
- `extra` — rejoined rows that are not in the feed

Compare these columns, in this order:
`shipment_id, leg_no, carrier_code, carrier_name, carrier_scac,
origin_code, origin_city, origin_country, dest_code, dest_city,
dest_country, customer_ref, customer_name, customer_billing_country,
service_level, service_transit_days, weight_kg, rate_per_kg, booked_at`.

Note what is absent: `leg_cost`, because you deliberately did not migrate
it.

Both numbers must be counted with **`EXCEPT ALL`**, not `EXCEPT`. Plain
`EXCEPT` deduplicates both sides, which hides exactly the bug this test
exists to catch — a join that silently doubled some rows.

Expected result: `(0, 0)`. If you get anything else, the ex5 dedup changed
a name, which is the honest cost of the drift ex1 found — and the gate
allows for it, but you should be able to say which rows and why.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e01_normalization_practice ex6`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You need the rejoined feed twice — once on each side of a set difference —
so define it once in a CTE and reference it twice. That CTE is a six-table
join: legs to shipments to customers and services, legs to carriers, legs
to locations twice.

## Hint 2

Two aliases of one parent, and the count of a difference:

```sql
WITH rebuilt AS (
  SELECT l.id, o.city AS from_city, d.city AS to_city
  FROM legs l
  JOIN places o ON o.code = l.origin_code
  JOIN places d ON d.code = l.dest_code)
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT ... EXCEPT ALL SELECT ... ) x) AS missing;
```

## Hint 3

Column order and types must match across a set operation — `numeric(10,2)`
against `numeric(10,2)`, not against `numeric`. Select the feed columns
explicitly in the listed order rather than `SELECT *`, because `SELECT *`
on `shipment_feed` includes `leg_cost` and the two sides will not line up.
The two scalar subqueries can share the CTE; whether you write them as two
subselects or as a `CROSS JOIN` of two one-row queries is your call.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what each failure mode would look like, then build the test
that distinguishes them. A missing foreign-key row shows up as `missing`.
A join on a non-unique column shows up as `extra` — and would also inflate
`missing` if it displaced rows. A dedup that changed a spelling shows up
as *both*, one of each, per affected row. The two-column answer is
diagnostic, not decorative.

## Hint 2

Sanity-check the join before you diff, because a row-count mismatch is
easier to read than a set difference:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM sf_legs l
JOIN sf_shipments s USING (shipment_id)
JOIN sf_customers c USING (customer_ref)
JOIN sf_services  sv USING (service_level)
JOIN sf_carriers  ca USING (carrier_code)
JOIN sf_locations o ON o.location_code = l.origin_code
JOIN sf_locations d ON d.location_code = l.dest_code;
-- must be exactly 40000
```

If it is more than 40,000 you have a fan-out; if less, an inner join is
dropping rows a foreign key should have made impossible.

## Hint 3

`USING (customer_ref)` works here because the column is named identically
on both sides, and it also merges the column, which is convenient until
the day two tables share a name you did not intend to join on. Some teams
ban `USING` for that reason. Use whichever you can defend; the gate reads
only the two numbers.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e01_normalization_practice/ex6 — lossless-join proof, both directions
WITH rebuilt AS (
  SELECT l.shipment_id, l.leg_no, ca.carrier_code, ca.carrier_name,
         ca.carrier_scac,
         o.location_code AS origin_code, o.city AS origin_city,
         o.country AS origin_country,
         d.location_code AS dest_code, d.city AS dest_city,
         d.country AS dest_country,
         c.customer_ref, c.customer_name,
         c.billing_country AS customer_billing_country,
         sv.service_level, sv.transit_days AS service_transit_days,
         l.weight_kg, l.rate_per_kg, s.booked_at
  FROM sf_legs l
  JOIN sf_shipments s  ON s.shipment_id   = l.shipment_id
  JOIN sf_customers c  ON c.customer_ref  = s.customer_ref
  JOIN sf_services  sv ON sv.service_level = s.service_level
  JOIN sf_carriers  ca ON ca.carrier_code = l.carrier_code
  JOIN sf_locations o  ON o.location_code = l.origin_code
  JOIN sf_locations d  ON d.location_code = l.dest_code
), feed AS (
  SELECT shipment_id, leg_no, carrier_code, carrier_name, carrier_scac,
         origin_code, origin_city, origin_country,
         dest_code, dest_city, dest_country,
         customer_ref, customer_name, customer_billing_country,
         service_level, service_transit_days,
         weight_kg, rate_per_kg, booked_at
  FROM shipment_feed
)
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT * FROM feed
                              EXCEPT ALL
                              SELECT * FROM rebuilt) a) AS missing,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT * FROM rebuilt
                              EXCEPT ALL
                              SELECT * FROM feed) b) AS extra;

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — put the derived column back, owned by the database

Your ex2-ex5 scripts run automatically first.

`shipment_feed.leg_cost` was `round(weight_kg * rate_per_kg, 2)` on every
row — the vendor computed it and shipped it. You left it out of `sf_legs`,
which is correct as far as it goes, but the reporting team needs the column
and does not want to type the multiplication.

Add it back as a column that **cannot drift**:

```sql
sf_legs.leg_cost numeric(12,2)
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (round(weight_kg * rate_per_kg, 2)) STORED
```

Then prove the point: the gate will attempt

```sql
UPDATE sf_legs SET leg_cost = 0 WHERE shipment_id = 1;
```

and expects it to **raise** — a generated column rejects direct writes.
It also checks that every row's `leg_cost` equals the feed's, so the
`round(...)` and the `numeric(12,2)` type both matter.

One `ALTER TABLE`. Note for later: this statement rewrites all 40,000 rows
and holds `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` for the duration. On this table that is
milliseconds; V3·E6 is about the version of this statement that is not.

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e01_normalization_practice ex7`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is one `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN`, with the generation clause in the
column definition. The interesting part is not the syntax; it is that you
are choosing the database as the owner of a derived value instead of your
application or a trigger.

## Hint 2

```sql
ALTER TABLE boxes
  ADD COLUMN volume numeric
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (w * h * d) STORED;
```

The expression may reference only columns of the same row, and must be
immutable — no `now()`, no subqueries, no other tables.

## Hint 3

Type the column `numeric(12,2)` to match the feed rather than leaving it
bare `numeric`; the `round(...)` and the declared scale do different jobs
and ex6-style comparisons notice when only one of them is present. Whether
you also want a `CHECK (leg_cost >= 0)` is a real question — the generated
expression already guarantees it given the `weight_kg > 0` check from ex3,
so adding one is redundant documentation rather than protection.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Argue the alternative first, so you know what you are buying. Write the
trigger version in your head: a `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE` function setting
`NEW.leg_cost`. Now list the ways it can be bypassed —
`session_replication_role = 'replica'`, `ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER
ALL`, a restore that recreates the table without it. A generated column has
none of those failure modes because it is not a hook, it is part of the
column's definition.

## Hint 2

After you run it, read what the catalog now says about the column:

```sql
SELECT attname, attgenerated, pg_get_expr(adbin, adrelid) AS expr
FROM pg_attribute a
LEFT JOIN pg_attrdef d ON d.adrelid = a.attrelid AND d.adnum = a.attnum
WHERE a.attrelid = 'sf_legs'::regclass AND a.attname = 'leg_cost';
```

`attgenerated = 's'` is Postgres telling you the column is stored-generated
— documentation that no comment can fall out of sync with.

## Hint 3

If the gate reports value mismatches rather than a syntax error, the
suspect is rounding. `weight_kg * rate_per_kg` is `numeric(10,2) *
numeric(10,4)`, which is exact and can have six decimal places; assigning
it to `numeric(12,2)` rounds half-up, and so does `round()`, so the two
agree here. They do not agree for `double precision`, which is one more
reason money never lives in a float.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e01_normalization_practice/ex7 — leg_cost as a stored generated column
ALTER TABLE sf_legs
  ADD COLUMN leg_cost numeric(12,2)
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (round(weight_kg * rate_per_kg, 2)) STORED;

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the one table 3NF does not save

`setup.sql` also loads a small, separate table:

```sql
CREATE TABLE terminal_assignment (
  shipment_id   int  NOT NULL,
  service_level text NOT NULL,
  gate_code     text NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (shipment_id, service_level)
);
```

Two business rules hold:

- a shipment uses one gate per service level:
  `(shipment_id, service_level) → gate_code`
- **each gate handles exactly one service level**: `gate_code →
  service_level`

The table is in 3NF — `service_level` is prime, so the transitive
dependency is forgiven — and it is not in BCNF, because `gate_code` is a
determinant that is not a superkey. The anomaly is concrete: nothing stops
`(1, 'express', 'G7')` and `(2, 'deferred', 'G7')` coexisting, and then G7
handles two service levels.

Decompose it. Create exactly:

```sql
ta_gates (gate_code text PRIMARY KEY,
          service_level text NOT NULL REFERENCES sf_services(service_level))

ta_shipment_gate (shipment_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES sf_shipments(shipment_id),
                  gate_code   text NOT NULL REFERENCES ta_gates(gate_code),
                  PRIMARY KEY (shipment_id, gate_code))
```

and migrate every row. `ta_gates` gets one row per gate; the service level
comes from the assignment rows, which are consistent (verify that, do not
assume it). `ta_shipment_gate` gets one row per original row, minus the
column that is now derivable.

Your ex2-ex5 scripts run first, so `sf_services` and `sf_shipments` exist.

The gate then inserts `('G7', 'deferred')`-shaped conflicts and expects
them to be impossible.

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e01_normalization_practice ex8`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The illegal state is "one gate, two service levels". Make it
unrepresentable by giving each gate exactly one row in a table keyed on
`gate_code`. Once that table exists, the service level is no longer
something `ta_shipment_gate` needs to store.

## Hint 2

The migration is two inserts, parent first:

```sql
INSERT INTO ta_gates (gate_code, service_level)
SELECT DISTINCT gate_code, service_level FROM terminal_assignment;
```

If that raises a unique violation, the *data* already contains the anomaly
and you have a cleaning problem before you have a schema problem — which
is exactly the ex1 lesson, met again in a smaller table.

## Hint 3

Run the ex1-shaped drift check on `gate_code → service_level` before
inserting, so that you know rather than hope. Then load
`ta_shipment_gate` with just the two columns. What you should notice
afterwards: you can no longer write a single constraint saying "one gate
per shipment per service level" — the two columns live in different tables
now. That loss is real, and naming it is part of the answer.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the query side. After the split, "what service level is
shipment 42 on gate G7?" is a join, and "which gate does shipment 42 use
for express?" is also a join. Nothing you could ask before is unanswerable
— that is losslessness. What changed is only which *illegal writes* the
schema refuses.

## Hint 2

Verify the anomaly is absent from the current data first:

```sql
SELECT gate_code, count(DISTINCT service_level)
FROM terminal_assignment
GROUP BY gate_code
HAVING count(DISTINCT service_level) > 1;
```

Zero rows means the business rule has held so far by luck and discipline.
The decomposition replaces luck with structure.

## Hint 3

The dependency you lose is `(shipment_id, service_level) → gate_code`. If
a stakeholder insists it must still be enforced, the honest options are: a
trigger, a materialized `service_level` column on `ta_shipment_gate` with a
composite foreign key back to `ta_gates(gate_code, service_level)` plus a
unique index on `(shipment_id, service_level)`, or accepting the risk.
The middle option is the interesting one — write it out and notice that it
reintroduces the redundancy under an owner, which is the second half of
this whole sector.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a counter cache, and the query that keeps it honest

Your ex2-ex5 scripts run automatically first.

The shipment list page shows "N legs" next to every shipment. Measured:
`count(*)` over `sf_legs` per shipment, for a page of 50 shipments, is the
dominant cost of the page. This is the situation in which a counter cache
is legitimate — so build one properly, which means three deliverables in
one script.

**1. The column.** `sf_shipments.leg_count int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`, then
backfilled from `sf_legs` so that it is correct for the 9,000 existing
shipments. A shipment with no legs must end at 0, not NULL.

**2. The owner.** A `plpgsql` trigger function `sf_leg_count_sync()` and an
`AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE FOR EACH ROW` trigger named
`sf_legs_count_trg` on `sf_legs`, keeping the column correct. It must
handle all three operations, and specifically the case the gate hammers:
an `UPDATE` that moves a leg from one shipment to another must decrement
the old parent and increment the new one. An `UPDATE` that touches only
`weight_kg` must leave both counts unchanged.

**3. The reconciliation.** End the script with a **view** named
`sf_leg_count_drift` returning the shipments where the cache disagrees
with reality, columns `shipment_id`, `cached` (the column), `actual` (the
count). It must return zero rows immediately after your backfill, and it
is what you would schedule, because triggers get disabled during restores
and nobody tells you.

The gate: checks the backfill, then inserts, reparents and deletes legs and
re-checks the view is empty after each; then it disables the trigger, moves
a leg, and asserts the view is **non-empty** — proving the reconciliation
actually detects drift rather than being a decorative query.

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e01_normalization_practice challenge`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three parts, and the middle one is where the thinking is. Write the
trigger body as two independent statements — "if there was an old parent,
decrement it" and "if there is a new parent, increment it" — rather than
as three branches per operation. The two-statement form is correct for
`INSERT`, `DELETE` and both flavours of `UPDATE` without special cases.

## Hint 2

The skeleton, with the branch structure that generalises:

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION t() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF TG_OP IN ('DELETE','UPDATE') THEN
    UPDATE parent SET n = n - 1 WHERE id = OLD.parent_id;
  END IF;
  IF TG_OP IN ('INSERT','UPDATE') THEN
    UPDATE parent SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = NEW.parent_id;
  END IF;
  RETURN NULL;   -- AFTER triggers ignore the return value
END $$;
```

For an `UPDATE` that does not move the row, this decrements and increments
the same shipment — net zero, correct, no branch needed.

## Hint 3

The backfill wants a correlated update or a join to a grouped subquery;
either works, but only one of them leaves legless shipments at 0 without
help — check which, and reach for `coalesce` if you need it. For the view,
a `LEFT JOIN` to the grouped counts plus `IS DISTINCT FROM` handles the
NULL side cleanly, and `IS DISTINCT FROM` rather than `<>` is the detail
that makes it work at all.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Design the reconciliation view first and let it tell you whether the rest
is right. If you can write "cached disagrees with actual" as a query, you
can run it after every experiment you make by hand, and you will find the
`UPDATE`-reparent bug in thirty seconds instead of in production.

## Hint 2

Reproduce the bug deliberately before you fix it. Write a naive trigger
that only handles `INSERT` and `DELETE`, then:

```sql
UPDATE sf_legs SET shipment_id = 2 WHERE shipment_id = 1 AND leg_no = 1;
SELECT * FROM sf_leg_count_drift;
```

Two rows: shipment 1 too high, shipment 2 too low. That is the shape of
every counter-cache incident you will ever be paged for.

## Hint 3

Two subtleties worth knowing even though the gate does not force them.
An `AFTER ... FOR EACH ROW` trigger fires once per row, so a 10,000-row
insert issues 10,000 `UPDATE`s against the parent — for bulk loads you
disable the trigger and rerun the backfill, which is precisely how the
cache gets left drifted. And concurrent inserts against the same shipment
serialise on the parent row lock; that is correctness, but it is also a
hot spot, and it is the reason counter caches on a single global row are a
classic outage.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — the duplication that is not duplication

Your ex2-ex5 scripts run automatically first.

Operations is changing the `express` promise from 3 transit days to 2,
effective now. Somebody proposes `UPDATE sf_services SET transit_days = 2
WHERE service_level = 'express'` and closing the ticket.

That update is wrong on its own, and the reason is the distinction this
sector turns on: **"the transit days for this service" and "the transit
days promised on this shipment" are two different facts.** Every shipment
already booked was promised 3. A lookup table stores the current promise;
it cannot store the historical one.

Do it properly, in one script:

1. Add `sf_shipments.promised_transit_days int` — nullable at first,
   because you cannot add a `NOT NULL` column to a populated table without
   a value for every row.
2. Backfill it from `sf_services` as it stands *now* — that is what each
   existing shipment was in fact promised.
3. `ALTER` it to `NOT NULL`, now that every row has a value.
4. Apply the change: `express` becomes 2 transit days in `sf_services`.
   Existing shipments keep their 3.
5. Finish with a **view** named `sf_promise_divergence` listing shipments
   whose promise differs from their service's current promise, columns
   `shipment_id`, `service_level`, `promised` (the snapshot), `current_days`
   (the lookup). Ordered by `shipment_id`.

After your script the view must be non-empty — every pre-existing express
shipment appears — and that is the correct state, not a bug. It is the
history the naive `UPDATE` would have destroyed.

Edit `review1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e01_normalization_practice review1`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Order is everything: add nullable, backfill, constrain, *then* change the
lookup. Change the lookup first and your backfill copies the new promise
onto old shipments — silently, with no error, and unrecoverably.

## Hint 2

The add-backfill-constrain shape:

```sql
ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c int;
UPDATE t SET c = ... ;
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET NOT NULL;
```

Three statements, in that order, every time you add a required column to a
populated table.

## Hint 3

The backfill is an `UPDATE ... FROM` joining `sf_shipments` to
`sf_services` on `service_level`. The view is the same join with an
inequality in the `WHERE`. What you decide for yourself: whether
`promised_transit_days` should also carry a foreign key or check tying it
to a real service — and the answer is no, because a snapshot must survive
the service being changed or removed, which is the whole point of it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Argue against the column before you build it. "This duplicates
`sf_services`; V3·E1 spent six exercises removing duplication." The
counter-argument has to be a sentence you can say to a reviewer: it is not
a copy of the service's transit days, it is *this shipment's promise*,
which happened to equal the service's value on the day it was booked and
will not tomorrow. If you cannot say that sentence, you cannot tell
snapshots from denormalization, and you will delete history one day.

## Hint 2

Check the state at each step rather than at the end:

```sql
SELECT service_level, count(*), min(promised_transit_days),
       max(promised_transit_days)
FROM sf_shipments GROUP BY service_level;
```

Run it after the backfill — every service should show min = max, because
nothing has diverged yet. Run it after step 4 — unchanged, because you
touched only the lookup. If step 4 changed these numbers, your backfill
ran in the wrong order or you updated the wrong table.

## Hint 3

Extend the thought: the same argument applies to `rate_per_kg` on
`sf_legs`, which you migrated from the feed without comment in ex5. It is
a snapshot too — the rate agreed for that leg — and the fact that no
`sf_rates` lookup table exists in this schema is why nobody was tempted to
normalize it away. Snapshots are safest when the thing they snapshot has
no table, and most endangered when it does.

lessons.title: V3·E2 — Keys: natural, surrogate, and identity columns
lessons.summary: A forum keyed on email address, migrated to the shape production converges on: bigint identity primary key, unique constraint on the natural key, UUID for the outside world. Along the way, OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE, resyncing a sequence, serial-to-identity, and why gapless numbering costs a lock.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·E2 — Keys: natural, surrogate, and identity columns

V3·E1 ended with a schema whose primary keys were all natural:
`carrier_code`, `location_code`, `customer_ref`. That was deliberate, and
it was also a loan you now have to repay. Natural keys are meaningful,
readable in raw data, and free of an extra join when you only need the
code — and they are *mutable*, because the meaning belongs to the outside
world and the outside world changes its mind.

This sector is about what to key a table on, and it ends where almost every
production schema ends: a surrogate primary key, a unique constraint on the
natural key, and a third identifier for anything outside the database.
Getting there means meeting the machinery — identity columns, sequences,
the `serial` pseudo-type Postgres now regrets, and UUIDs — and meeting the
migration hazards nobody warns you about until the sequence collides.

## The schema

`setup.sql` builds a small forum, keyed the way a 2011 codebase keys
things:

```sql
CREATE TABLE legacy_members (
  email        text PRIMARY KEY,
  display_name text NOT NULL,
  handle       text NOT NULL,
  joined_on    date NOT NULL,
  plan         text NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE legacy_posts (
  post_id     int  PRIMARY KEY,
  author_email text NOT NULL
    REFERENCES legacy_members(email) ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  title       text NOT NULL,
  body        text NOT NULL,
  posted_at   timestamptz NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE legacy_reactions (
  post_id      int  NOT NULL REFERENCES legacy_posts(post_id),
  author_email text NOT NULL
    REFERENCES legacy_members(email) ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  kind         text NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (post_id, author_email, kind));

CREATE TABLE legacy_signups (
  signup_id serial PRIMARY KEY,
  email     text NOT NULL,
  source    text NOT NULL);
```

Notice the `ON UPDATE CASCADE`s. They are not decoration: without them,
changing an email would be impossible, because two child tables reference
it. With them, changing one member's email rewrites every post and every
reaction that member ever made. That is the price of a mutable primary
key, and ex5 makes you measure it on real rows rather than assert it.

## Candidate keys, and the one you pick

A **candidate key** is any minimal set of columns that is unique across
every legal state of the table. `legacy_members` has at least three:
`email`, `handle`, and — once you add one — a surrogate integer. The
**primary key** is the candidate key you nominate for other tables to
reference. Nominating one does not demote the others; they still deserve
`UNIQUE` constraints, and ex1 makes you *check* uniqueness in the data
before you assume it, because "handles are unique" is a sentence people
say about columns that are not.

The argument for a surrogate is narrow and decisive: **it never changes**,
so no child table ever has to. Every other argument for surrogates is
weaker than people think, and every argument against them is real. They
carry no meaning, so a table keyed only on a surrogate happily stores the
same member twice; the unique constraint on the natural key is not
optional garnish, it is the thing that was doing the work before you
arrived. They cost a join whenever you already had the natural value in
hand. And they leak: a sequential integer in a URL tells the world how
many members you have and lets anyone walk your data by counting.

## Identity, serial, and the sequence underneath

Postgres has two spellings for "an integer that assigns itself".

```sql
id bigserial PRIMARY KEY                       -- 1995 style
id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY   -- SQL standard
```

`serial` is not a type. It is a macro: create a sequence, make the column
`integer` (or `bigint`) with `DEFAULT nextval('...')`, and mark the
sequence as owned by the column. Everything after that is a default like
any other — you can insert an explicit value, you can drop the default and
the sequence survives, and the type of the column is just `integer`.
`GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` uses the same sequence machinery but the
column *owns* it structurally: explicit inserts are rejected unless you say
`OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`, the sequence is dropped with the column, and
`\d` tells you the truth. Use identity. Reach for `serial` only when
matching an existing schema.

Two rules that cost people days:

- **`bigint` from the start.** `int` runs out at 2,147,483,647, and the
  table that will "never" have two billion rows is the one that gets a
  retry loop. Widening a live primary key from `int` to `bigint` rewrites
  the table and every referencing table and index — a V3·E6-shaped
  problem you can avoid entirely with eight extra bytes per row.
- **Gaps are not a bug.** `nextval()` is deliberately non-transactional:
  it does not roll back, because a sequence that rolled back would have to
  serialise every transaction that touched it. A failed insert, a
  cancelled request, `CACHE 32` on a busy connection — all leave holes.
  If your invoice numbering must be gapless, you cannot use a sequence,
  and the challenge makes you build what you must use instead and feel
  what it costs.

## UUIDs, and where they belong

`gen_random_uuid()` is built in since Postgres 13, no extension required.
A v4 UUID is 128 random bits, which makes it unguessable and makes it a
poor *primary* key at scale: every insert lands in a random leaf of the
B-tree, so the index has no locality, cache hit rates collapse, and full-page
writes amplify the WAL. Time-ordered variants — UUIDv7, ULID — fix the
locality by putting a millisecond timestamp in the high bits, at the price
of leaking approximate creation time. Postgres 16 has no built-in v7
generator, so you either generate them in the application or write the
`overlay()` expression yourself.

The shape that survives contact with production, and the one ex2 asks you
to build:

```sql
person_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,  -- joins
public_id uuid NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() UNIQUE,   -- URLs
email     text NOT NULL UNIQUE                              -- identity
```

Three identifiers, three jobs, and none of them doing another's.

## What the exercises do

ex1 tests candidate keys against the data instead of trusting the schema.
ex2 and ex3 build the new tables and migrate, and ex3 is where you meet
`OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE` — because preserving the old `post_id` values
means inserting into a column that has sworn to generate them itself. ex4
is the step everyone forgets afterwards: the sequence is still at 1, so
the next real insert collides with row 1, and you have to resync it. ex5
measures the cascade cost of the mutable key you are leaving behind. ex6
converts `legacy_signups.signup_id` from `serial` to identity, sequence
and all. ex7 adds the public UUID. ex8 is the junction table and the
column-order decision that lesson 33 taught you to care about. The
challenge builds gapless numbering and shows you the lock. review1 asks
what your keys tell a stranger.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate

Keys are the one design decision that is expensive to revisit, because
every other table has copied it.

## Notes

**Candidate key, primary key, unique constraint.** A candidate key is a
minimal unique column set. A primary key is the candidate you nominated,
plus an implied `NOT NULL`. A unique constraint is how you keep the other
candidates honest. The common failure is not choosing wrong — it is
choosing a surrogate and then *forgetting the unique constraint on the
natural key*, which turns "we have duplicate customers" into a quarterly
data-cleaning ritual.

**Uniqueness is a property of the data, not of your intention.** Before
declaring `handle` unique, count it. `count(*)` versus `count(DISTINCT
handle)` takes two seconds and is the difference between a migration that
runs and a migration that half-runs.

**`serial` is a macro; identity is a feature.** `serial` expands to a
sequence plus a column default. Consequences: `INSERT ... (id) VALUES (7)`
is allowed and silently desynchronises the sequence; `pg_get_serial_
sequence('t','id')` is how you find the sequence; granting `INSERT` on the
table is not enough, the role also needs `USAGE` on the sequence, which is
a permission bug that only appears for non-owner roles. Identity columns
fix all three: writes are rejected without `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`, the
sequence is an internal dependency, and no separate grant is needed.

**`GENERATED ALWAYS` versus `BY DEFAULT`.** `ALWAYS` rejects your value
unless you explicitly override; `BY DEFAULT` accepts it silently. `BY
DEFAULT` looks friendlier and is the worse default, because "silently
accepts explicit ids" is precisely the behaviour that desynchronises
sequences during migrations and data loads. Use `ALWAYS`, and let
`OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE` be the loud, greppable marker of the few places
that legitimately supply ids.

**After any id-preserving load, resync the sequence.** This is the single
most common migration bug in this area, and it produces a duplicate-key
error on the *next* insert, minutes or days later, far from the cause.
Two spellings:

```sql
SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('mem_posts','post_id'),
              (SELECT max(post_id) FROM mem_posts));
ALTER TABLE mem_posts ALTER COLUMN post_id RESTART WITH 5001;
```

`setval` works for both serial and identity because both are backed by a
sequence; `ALTER TABLE ... RESTART` is identity-specific and reads better.

**Sequences do not roll back, and that is the design.** `nextval()` takes
a lightweight lock, increments, releases — outside your transaction's
visibility rules — precisely so concurrent inserters do not queue. A
gapless counter is the opposite trade: one row, one lock, every
transaction serialised behind it. That is not a Postgres limitation; it is
what "gapless" means. Build it only when a regulator demands it.

**UUID keys are an index-locality decision.** Random v4 keys scatter
inserts across the whole B-tree; sequential keys append to one hot leaf.
The scattered version costs cache misses, more full-page writes in the
WAL, and a bigger index (128 bits versus 64, plus worse fill). None of
that matters at ten thousand rows and all of it matters at a hundred
million. Keep the bigint for joins and let the UUID be the public handle.

**Composite keys in junction tables have a column order, and it matters.**
`PRIMARY KEY (post_id, tag_id)` creates one index whose left prefix is
`post_id`; "tags of this post" is fast and "posts with this tag" is a
scan. The fix is the second index `(tag_id, post_id)`, which is also
covering. Deciding you only need one direction is fine — deciding it by
accident is not.

## ex1

Counting before trusting. Note that `count(DISTINCT x)` and `count(x)`
differ from `count(*)` in the presence of NULLs, which is why a nullable
column can be "unique" and still be a terrible key.

## ex2

The three-identifier shape. `GENERATED ALWAYS`, not `BY DEFAULT`, and the
unique constraint on `email` doing the job the old primary key used to do.

## ex3

`OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`. The error you get without it —
`cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column "post_id"` — is Postgres
correctly refusing to let a migration pretend to be an application.

## ex4

The resync. Test it the way the gate does: insert one row with no id and
check it does not collide.

## ex5

The cascade cost, in rows. `ON UPDATE CASCADE` makes the natural key
usable; it does not make it cheap. Every cascaded row is a new tuple
version, more WAL, and index churn on tables you were not thinking about.

## ex6

`serial` to identity, in four statements, and the one that surprises
people is `DROP DEFAULT` before `ADD GENERATED` — the column cannot have
both.

## ex7

The public UUID, added to a populated table. Note that the `DEFAULT` alone
does not fill existing rows in the way you might hope: it does, because
adding a column with a volatile default rewrites the table, which is worth
knowing before you run it on a hundred million rows.

## ex8

The junction table, its composite key, and the reverse index. Also the FK
actions: `ON DELETE CASCADE` from a junction row to its post is correct,
and would be wrong on `legacy_posts` itself.

## challenge

Gapless numbering. The `UPDATE ... RETURNING` on a single counter row is
the whole mechanism, and the row lock it takes is the whole cost.

## review1

What a key tells a stranger. Sequential ids are a side channel, and the
answer is not "encrypt the id" but "publish a different one".

## Further reading

- [`CREATE TABLE` — identity columns](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createtable.html) — `GENERATED ALWAYS`/`BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` and `OVERRIDING`.
- [Serial Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-numeric.html#DATATYPE-SERIAL) — the macro spelled out, including the deprecation note.
- [Sequence Manipulation Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-sequence.html) — `nextval`, `setval`, and why gaps happen.
- [UUID Type](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-uuid.html) and [`gen_random_uuid()`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-uuid.html) — built in since PG13.
- [Constraints — Unique](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html#DDL-CONSTRAINTS-UNIQUE-CONSTRAINTS) — the constraint that keeps a surrogate-keyed table honest.

# V3·E2 — Keys (archive)

Everything about choosing an identifier, plus the migration mechanics that
turn a good choice into a working schema.

## The decision, compressed

```sql
CREATE TABLE people (
  person_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  public_id uuid   NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email     text   NOT NULL,
  handle    text   NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT people_email_key  UNIQUE (email),
  CONSTRAINT people_handle_key UNIQUE (handle),
  CONSTRAINT people_public_key UNIQUE (public_id)
);
```

- `person_id` is what other tables reference. Narrow, immutable, ordered,
  cheap to index, never shown to a user.
- `public_id` is what URLs and APIs use. Unguessable, so it leaks neither
  row counts nor growth rate.
- `email` and `handle` are the natural keys. They are unique because the
  business says so, and the constraints are what make that true rather
  than aspirational.

Three columns is not redundancy. Each answers a different question: *what
do we join on*, *what do we publish*, *what does the user recognise*.

## Identity mechanics you will need

**Insert an explicit value into `GENERATED ALWAYS`:**

```sql
INSERT INTO mem_posts (post_id, author_id, title)
OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE
SELECT post_id, ..., title FROM legacy_posts;
```

`OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE` goes between the column list and the source. It
is deliberately ugly; the ugliness is the point.

**Resync afterwards, always:**

```sql
SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('mem_posts', 'post_id'),
              (SELECT max(post_id) FROM mem_posts));
```

`setval(seq, n)` sets the sequence so the *next* `nextval` returns `n+1`.
The three-argument form `setval(seq, n, false)` makes the next value `n`
itself, which is what you want when loading into an empty table where the
first id must be 1.

**Convert `serial` to identity:**

```sql
ALTER TABLE legacy_signups ALTER COLUMN signup_id DROP DEFAULT;
DROP SEQUENCE IF EXISTS legacy_signups_signup_id_seq CASCADE;  -- optional
ALTER TABLE legacy_signups
  ALTER COLUMN signup_id ADD GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY;
SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('legacy_signups','signup_id'),
              (SELECT max(signup_id) FROM legacy_signups));
```

`DROP DEFAULT` first: a column may not have both a default and an
identity. Dropping the old sequence is optional but tidy — if you leave
it, it is now an orphan that nothing advances.

**Gapless numbering, when a regulator insists:**

```sql
UPDATE inv_counter SET next_no = next_no + 1
WHERE year = 2026
RETURNING next_no - 1;
```

One statement, inside your transaction, so the number rolls back with
everything else. The row lock it takes is held to commit, which serialises
every concurrent claimant — that block is not a defect to tune away, it is
the definition of gaplessness. Key the counter per series (year, document
type) so the queue is short, and claim the number as late in the
transaction as you can.

**Find the sequence for any column, whatever its provenance:**

```sql
SELECT pg_get_serial_sequence('t', 'c');
SELECT last_value, log_cnt, is_called FROM t_c_seq;
```

## Composite keys and column order

A junction table needs no surrogate. `PRIMARY KEY (post_id, tag_id)` is
minimal, immutable and already unique, and adding an `id bigserial`
alongside it does nothing except permit duplicate pairs until you add back
a unique constraint on the two columns you declined to key on.

What the composite key *does* decide is which query is fast. The primary
key creates one B-tree ordered by `post_id` then `tag_id`, so:

```sql
SELECT tag_id  FROM mem_post_tags WHERE post_id = 42;  -- index-only scan
SELECT post_id FROM mem_post_tags WHERE tag_id  = 7;   -- full scan
```

The second query wants a leading `tag_id`, which no left prefix of the
primary key provides. Hence the companion index:

```sql
CREATE INDEX mem_post_tags_tag_post_idx ON mem_post_tags (tag_id, post_id);
```

Two narrow indexes, both covering, one per direction. Deciding you only
need one direction is a legitimate choice; discovering under load that you
needed two is not.

The delete actions carry meaning too. `ON DELETE CASCADE` toward the post
says "a link has no life without its post". `ON DELETE RESTRICT` toward
the tag says "a tag still in use is not deleted by accident". `SET NULL`
is unavailable on either side, because both columns are part of the
primary key and therefore `NOT NULL` — a small check that you understand
what you keyed on.

## Common mistakes

- **Surrogate key, no unique constraint on the natural key.** The table
  now permits two rows for one person, and it will contain them within a
  quarter.
- **Forgetting the sequence resync after an id-preserving migration.** The
  failure is a duplicate-key violation on a later insert, far from the
  cause.
- **`int` instead of `bigint`.** Widening a live key is one of the most
  expensive migrations there is, because every foreign key column must
  widen too.
- **Treating a sequence gap as data loss.** Gaps mean the sequence did its
  job without serialising your writes.
- **Random UUID as the clustered-ish primary key of a huge table.** Index
  locality collapses. Measure before you commit; keep the bigint for
  joins.
- **Exposing the bigint in URLs.** `/orders/10432` publishes your order
  count and invites enumeration.
- **`GENERATED BY DEFAULT` everywhere.** It silently accepts explicit ids,
  which is how sequences fall behind in the first place.
- **A composite junction key with only one usable direction.** `PRIMARY
  KEY (post_id, tag_id)` and no `(tag_id, post_id)` index means "posts
  with this tag" scans.

## Interview answer

*"Natural or surrogate keys?"*

Answer with the shape, not with a side. Surrogate primary key, unique
constraint on the natural key, and a separate public identifier if the key
is ever exposed. Then give the reason the surrogate wins, which is
narrower than most candidates think: **a primary key is copied into every
child table, so its cost of change is multiplied by the schema**. Natural
keys change — people change email addresses, countries change ISO codes,
ISBNs get reissued — and `ON UPDATE CASCADE` makes that survivable, not
free.

Then say what a surrogate does *not* buy you: it does not make rows
unique in any way a human cares about. Without the unique constraint on
`email`, your surrogate-keyed table is a duplicate factory. Candidates who
volunteer that have actually run the migration.

If asked about UUIDs: distinguish the identifier's *job* from its *type*.
Unguessability is a security property you need in URLs; index locality is
a performance property you need in the primary key; those are different
columns unless the table is small.

## Check yourself

1. Name three candidate keys of `legacy_members` and say which you would
   nominate as primary and why.
2. What exactly does `serial` expand to? Name all three objects or
   properties it creates.
3. Which error does `INSERT INTO t (id) VALUES (1)` raise when `id` is
   `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`, and what clause suppresses it?
4. After loading 5,000 rows with explicit ids into an identity column,
   what is the next `nextval` and why is that a problem?
5. Write the resync in both spellings, `setval` and `ALTER TABLE`.
6. Why does `GRANT INSERT ON t` fail for a `serial` column but not for an
   identity column?
7. Give two mechanisms that create gaps in a sequence, neither of them a
   bug.
8. Why is a gapless counter necessarily a serialisation point?
9. Explain the index-locality argument against random UUID primary keys in
   two sentences, and name the WAL effect.
10. What does UUIDv7 trade away to buy locality?
11. `PRIMARY KEY (post_id, tag_id)`: which of the two obvious queries is
    fast, and what index fixes the other?
12. Why is widening a primary key from `int` to `bigint` more expensive
    than widening an ordinary column?
13. What does `/members/10432` tell an attacker who has never seen your
    database?
14. When is a natural primary key the right call? Give a concrete example.

# The long read — an identifier is a promise about change

Every primary key is a bet on what will stay still. Key a table on an
email address and you have bet that email addresses do not change; key it
on a generated integer and you have bet only that you can generate
integers. The second bet is easier to win, which is why the industry
converged on it — but the convergence hid the reason, and a generation of
schemas now carries surrogate keys with no unique constraint on anything
meaningful, which is strictly worse than the natural keys they replaced.

## What a sequence actually is

A Postgres sequence is a one-row table with special handling. `nextval()`
takes a short lock on the sequence's page, increments the counter, writes
a WAL record every `SEQ_LOG_VALS` (32) increments rather than every time,
and releases. Three consequences follow, and all three surprise people.

**It ignores your transaction.** Sequences are explicitly outside MVCC. If
they were not, two concurrent inserters would have to serialise, because
each would need to know whether the other's increment committed. The
non-transactional design is what makes concurrent inserts scale, and gaps
are the visible residue of that choice. A rolled-back transaction does not
give its number back; nobody is coming to collect it.

**It can jump after a crash.** Because WAL is written only every 32
increments, recovery may restart the sequence above the last value
actually handed out. Values are never *reused*, which is the guarantee
that matters, but they are not dense.

**`CACHE n` multiplies the gaps per session.** With `CACHE 50`, a session
grabs fifty values at once and keeps them in backend memory. It is faster
and the unused tail is lost when the session ends. Sequences are also
per-session-cached in a way that means two concurrent sessions can hand
out interleaved, non-monotonic values — so "id order equals insert order"
is approximately true and not guaranteed.

`serial` arrived in the mid-1990s as a convenience macro over this
machinery. `GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY` arrived in Postgres 10 as the SQL:2003
standard spelling, and it is better in ways that are all about ownership:
the sequence is an internal dependency of the column rather than a
separate object you can accidentally drop; `ALWAYS` closes the hole where
an explicit insert desynchronises everything; the privilege model no
longer requires a separate `USAGE` grant, which removes a whole category
of "works for me, fails for the app role" bug. The Postgres wiki lists
`serial` under *Don't Do This*. There is no controversy left here.

## The int4 cliff

`integer` tops out at 2,147,483,647. This sounds enormous until you
remember that ids are consumed by *attempts*, not by rows: failed inserts,
rolled-back transactions, and `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` upserts all burn
numbers. A high-churn table can exhaust a 32-bit sequence with a few
hundred million surviving rows.

Widening it afterwards is genuinely painful. `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN
id TYPE bigint` rewrites the entire table under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, and it
must be done for every referencing foreign-key column too, each with its
own rewrite and index rebuild. The online version is an expand/contract
migration spanning weeks — add a new bigint column, dual-write, backfill in
batches, add a unique index concurrently, swap the constraints, drop the
old column — which is exactly the pattern V3·E6 teaches, applied to the
one column every other table depends on. Eight extra bytes per row buys
you out of all of it. Use `bigint`.

## UUIDs, honestly

The case for UUIDs is real: they can be generated client-side without a
round trip, they merge across shards and offline clients without
collision, and they are unguessable. The case against them as *primary*
keys is equally real and is entirely about B-tree behaviour.

A B-tree index on a monotonically increasing key concentrates all inserts
in the rightmost leaf page, which stays in shared buffers permanently. A
random key spreads inserts uniformly across every leaf, so at any table
size beyond memory each insert reads a cold page. Worse, the first write
to a page after a checkpoint emits a *full page image* into the WAL — 8KB
for a handful of bytes of change — so random keys amplify WAL volume, and
WAL volume is replication lag, backup size, and disk throughput. The index
is also bigger: 16 bytes per entry against 8, with poorer fill because
random inserts split pages at 50% rather than filling them.

Time-ordered UUIDs (v7, or ULID) restore locality by putting a 48-bit
millisecond timestamp in the high bits. Postgres 16 does not generate them
natively; you produce them in the application or assemble one with
`overlay()` over `gen_random_uuid()`. The trade you accept is that the
identifier now leaks creation time, which is usually fine and occasionally
is exactly the thing you were hiding.

The synthesis most teams land on is the one this sector builds: bigint
identity for the primary key and all foreign keys, random UUID for the
public identifier, unique-constrained but never joined on in hot paths.
You pay one extra column and one extra index, and you get locality and
unguessability instead of choosing.

## Gapless numbering

Invoice numbers in several jurisdictions must be consecutive with no
holes. A sequence cannot do this, by construction. What can:

```sql
UPDATE inv_counter SET next_no = next_no + 1
WHERE year = 2026
RETURNING next_no - 1;
```

One row, updated inside your transaction. If you roll back, the number is
returned. If two transactions try at once, the second blocks on the row
lock until the first commits or aborts. That block is not a defect to
optimise away — it is the only way to guarantee density, and any scheme
that claims gaplessness without serialisation is either wrong or has moved
the serialisation somewhere you have not looked. Partition the counter by
year, or by document type, so the contention is per-series rather than
global, and accept that your invoice throughput has a ceiling set by
transaction duration.

## When not to use a surrogate key

**Pure junction tables.** `post_tags(post_id, tag_id)` needs no `id`
column. The composite key is natural, immutable, and already the index you
want. Adding a surrogate here is cargo cult: it permits duplicate pairs
unless you also add the unique constraint you were trying to avoid.

**Small, immutable reference data.** Currency codes, ISO country codes,
US state abbreviations. `USD` will not be renamed, the code is what
everyone means, and the join saved is real. `sf_carriers` in V3·E1 is the
borderline case: carrier codes are stable, but carriers merge.

**Range-partitioned tables where the key must include the partition
key.** V3·E7 covers this: a partitioned table's primary key must contain
the partition column, so a pure surrogate primary key is not available and
`(tenant_id, id)` or `(day, id)` is what you get.

**Tables that already have a legally authoritative identifier.** If the
regulator says the record is identified by its filing number, arguing for
a surrogate is a conversation you will lose, and rightly.

Everywhere else: bigint identity, unique on the natural key, UUID for the
door. The reason is one sentence — a primary key is copied into every
child, so it must be the column least likely to ever change — and if you
can say that sentence, you can defend the schema in any review you will
sit in.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — count before you trust

`setup.sql` loads `legacy_members` (4,000 rows):

```sql
legacy_members(email text PRIMARY KEY, display_name text NOT NULL,
               handle text NOT NULL, joined_on date NOT NULL,
               plan text NOT NULL)
```

Somebody is about to declare `handle` unique and key a new table on it.
Before anyone writes DDL, establish which columns are actually candidate
keys **in the data as it stands**.

Return **one row**, five `bigint` columns:

`rows` = `count(*)`, `d_email`, `d_display_name`, `d_handle`, and
`d_email_handle` = the number of distinct `(email, handle)` pairs.

A column is a candidate key here exactly when its distinct count equals
`rows`. You should find that `email` qualifies, `handle` does not, and
`display_name` is not close — and that `(email, handle)` also equals
`rows`, which makes it unique but **not minimal**, so not a candidate key.
Minimality is half the definition and the half people drop.

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate ex1`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One row out, five aggregates in, no `GROUP BY`. Every column is a count
over the whole table.

## Hint 2

`count(DISTINCT ...)` takes a single expression, so a pair needs a
composite value:

```sql
SELECT count(DISTINCT (a, b)) FROM t;
```

The row constructor `(a, b)` is one value of a composite type, and
`DISTINCT` compares it field by field.

## Hint 3

Watch the NULL rule: `count(x)` and `count(DISTINCT x)` both skip NULLs,
so a half-empty column can report a distinct count far below `rows` and a
fully-NULL column reports zero. None of these columns are nullable, so it
does not bite here — but it is the reason a `UNIQUE` constraint on a
nullable column does not mean what you think, which ex7 of V3·E3 makes
concrete.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Reframe it as a falsification test. You are not proving `handle` unique —
you cannot, from data — you are trying to *disprove* it, and one duplicate
is enough. The aggregate query is just the cheapest way to look for that
one duplicate across every candidate at once.

## Hint 2

If you want to see the offenders rather than the count, the drift query
from V3·E1 works unchanged:

```sql
SELECT handle, count(*) FROM legacy_members
GROUP BY handle HAVING count(*) > 1
ORDER BY count(*) DESC;
```

Run it. Looking at the actual duplicate handles tells you something the
