number does not: whether this is a data-quality accident or a rule that
was never true.

## Hint 3

The `(email, handle)` column is in the exercise to make a point about
minimality. Any superset of a key is unique, so uniqueness alone would
make half the column combinations in the table "keys". A candidate key
must be unique *and* have no unique proper subset. When you nominate a
composite primary key later, check that you actually need both columns.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate/ex1 — candidate-key census
SELECT count(*)                             AS rows,
       count(DISTINCT email)                AS d_email,
       count(DISTINCT display_name)         AS d_display_name,
       count(DISTINCT handle)               AS d_handle,
       count(DISTINCT (email, handle))      AS d_email_handle
FROM legacy_members;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate/ex1 — same census via scalar subqueries
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM legacy_members)                     AS rows,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT email
                              FROM legacy_members) a)            AS d_email,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT display_name
                              FROM legacy_members) b)            AS d_display_name,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT handle
                              FROM legacy_members) c)            AS d_handle,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT email, handle
                              FROM legacy_members) d)            AS d_email_handle;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — the shape production converges on

Build the replacement member table. Exact name and columns:

```sql
mem_people (
  person_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  public_id uuid   NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email     text   NOT NULL,
  display_name text NOT NULL,
  handle    text   NOT NULL,
  joined_on date   NOT NULL,
  plan      text   NOT NULL)
```

plus three named constraints:

- `mem_people_email_key`   — `UNIQUE (email)`
- `mem_people_public_key`  — `UNIQUE (public_id)`
- `mem_people_plan_check`  — `CHECK (plan IN ('free','pro','team'))`

Three deliberate decisions the gate verifies:

1. `GENERATED ALWAYS`, not `BY DEFAULT`. The gate inserts a row with an
   explicit `person_id` and expects it to be **rejected**.
2. There is **no** unique constraint on `handle`, because ex1 proved the
   data cannot support one. Declaring a constraint the data violates is
   how migrations fail at 3am.
3. `email` is unique, because ex1 proved it can be — the surrogate key
   does not replace that constraint, it sits beside it.

`gen_random_uuid()` is built in from PG13; no extension needed.

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate ex2`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One `CREATE TABLE`. The only thing to get exactly right is the identity
clause and the constraint names, both of which the gate reads from the
catalog rather than from your file.

## Hint 2

```sql
CREATE TABLE t (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  code text NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT t_code_key UNIQUE (code)
);
```

Table-level `CONSTRAINT <name> ...` is how you control the name; the
inline `UNIQUE` keyword on a column gives you `t_code_key` by convention
but you are not in charge of it.

## Hint 3

`public_id` is `NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()` and unique — three
properties, each doing separate work. Whether `public_id` also deserves to
be the primary key is the question the sector answers with no: it is
random, so as a key it scatters every insert across the index, and every
foreign key in the schema would carry 16 bytes instead of 8.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Read the table as documentation before you write it. Three identifier
columns look redundant until you name their audiences: `person_id` is for
other tables, `public_id` is for the internet, `email` is for the human.
If you can name the audience of each column you add, you rarely add a bad
one.

## Hint 2

Prove decision 1 to yourself rather than taking the prompt's word:

```sql
INSERT INTO mem_people (person_id, email, display_name, handle,
                        joined_on, plan)
VALUES (1, 'a@b.c', 'A', 'a', '2024-01-01', 'free');
-- ERROR: cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column "person_id"
```

That error is the whole argument for `ALWAYS` over `BY DEFAULT`, and you
will meet it again in ex3 where it is the *wrong* answer and you have to
override it.

## Hint 3

Consider what you would lose by making `handle` unique anyway and cleaning
the data first. Nothing, in principle — it is the better end state. The
reason this exercise says no is sequencing: a constraint is a claim about
every row, and you add it *after* the rows comply, not before. V3·E6 gives
you `NOT VALID` for exactly the case where you want the claim to hold for
new rows while you clean the old ones.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate/ex2 — surrogate PK, natural unique, public uuid
CREATE TABLE mem_people (
  person_id    bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  public_id    uuid   NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email        text   NOT NULL,
  display_name text   NOT NULL,
  handle       text   NOT NULL,
  joined_on    date   NOT NULL,
  plan         text   NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT mem_people_email_key  UNIQUE (email),
  CONSTRAINT mem_people_public_key UNIQUE (public_id),
  CONSTRAINT mem_people_plan_check CHECK (plan IN ('free', 'pro', 'team'))
);

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — migrate, and keep the post ids

Your ex2 table is created automatically first. Now migrate both tables.

**Members.** Load `mem_people` from `legacy_members` — `email`,
`display_name`, `handle`, `joined_on`, `plan`. Let `person_id` and
`public_id` generate themselves. Insert in `email` order so the assignment
is deterministic.

**Posts.** Create and fill:

```sql
mem_posts (
  post_id   bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  author_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES mem_people(person_id),
  title     text NOT NULL,
  body      text NOT NULL,
  posted_at timestamptz NOT NULL)
```

The catch: **the existing `legacy_posts.post_id` values must be
preserved.** They are in URLs, in a search index, and in three years of
support tickets. Renumbering them is not on the table.

So you are inserting explicit values into a `GENERATED ALWAYS` column,
which Postgres refuses — `cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column
"post_id"` — unless you say so out loud with `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`.

`author_id` comes from joining `legacy_posts.author_email` to
`mem_people.email`. This join is the entire point of the surrogate
migration: the email stops being the reference and becomes just an
attribute.

Expected counts: `mem_people` 4,000, `mem_posts` 12,000, and
`max(mem_posts.post_id)` must equal `max(legacy_posts.post_id)`.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate ex3`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two inserts and one `CREATE TABLE`, in an order the foreign key will
accept. The only unfamiliar token is the clause that lets you write to a
`GENERATED ALWAYS` column.

## Hint 2

Where the clause goes:

```sql
INSERT INTO t (id, name)
OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE
SELECT old_id, name FROM legacy;
```

After the column list, before `VALUES` or `SELECT`. The alternative,
`OVERRIDING USER VALUE`, does the opposite — it ignores the value you
supplied — and is almost never what you want.

## Hint 3

For the posts, join `legacy_posts` to `mem_people` on
`author_email = email`. Use an inner join and let it prove the referential
integrity for you: if the count comes out below 12,000, some post has an
author who is not a member, which the old `REFERENCES` was supposed to
prevent. Whether you would rather find that out with a `LEFT JOIN ... IS
NULL` check first is your call, and the more careful habit.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what the identity column is *for* on a table whose ids you are
importing. It is for the rows you insert from tomorrow onwards. Today's
load bypasses it entirely, and the whole hazard of this exercise is the
gap between those two facts — which ex4 exists to close.

## Hint 2

Watch what the sequence does while you work:

```sql
SELECT last_value, is_called
FROM pg_sequences
WHERE sequencename LIKE 'mem_posts%';
```

Before your insert: 1, false. After inserting 12,000 rows with explicit
ids: still 1, false. The sequence has no idea anything happened, because
you never called it. That is not a bug in your script; it is the
consequence of overriding, and it is why the next unqualified insert would
try to use id 1.

## Hint 3

An alternative design worth considering and rejecting: keep the legacy
`post_id` as a plain `bigint` column with no identity, and add a separate
identity `id` for new posts. It avoids the resync entirely and it gives
you two id columns forever, which every future reader has to disambiguate.
Preserving the numbering in one identity column and resyncing once is the
smaller ongoing cost.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate/ex3 — migrate members, preserve post ids
INSERT INTO mem_people (email, display_name, handle, joined_on, plan)
SELECT email, display_name, handle, joined_on, plan
FROM legacy_members
ORDER BY email;

CREATE TABLE mem_posts (
  post_id   bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  author_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES mem_people(person_id),
  title     text NOT NULL,
  body      text NOT NULL,
  posted_at timestamptz NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO mem_posts (post_id, author_id, title, body, posted_at)
OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE
SELECT p.post_id, m.person_id, p.title, p.body, p.posted_at
FROM legacy_posts p
JOIN mem_people m ON m.email = p.author_email;

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the step everyone forgets

Your ex2 and ex3 scripts run automatically first, so `mem_posts` holds
12,000 rows with ids 1..12000 — and its identity sequence has never been
called. The next application insert asks for id 1 and collides with a
row from 2019.

This is the most common migration bug in this whole area, and it fails
*later*, in production, far from the script that caused it.

Fix it, and prove the fix, in one script:

1. Resync the identity sequence for `mem_posts.post_id` so that the next
   generated value is `max(post_id) + 1`. Do not hard-code 12001 — read
   the maximum from the table, because a script with a literal in it is a
   script that breaks on the next environment.
2. Then insert one new post to prove it: author = the `person_id` whose
   email is `'ada@example.com'`, title `'resynced'`, body `'ok'`,
   `posted_at` = `'2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'`, letting `post_id` generate.

After your script, `mem_posts` has 12,001 rows and the new row's
`post_id` is `12001`.

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate ex4`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Identity columns are backed by an ordinary sequence, so an ordinary
sequence function fixes them. You need the sequence's name, and there is a
function that derives it from the table and column rather than making you
guess the naming convention.

## Hint 2

Both spellings do the job:

```sql
SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('t','id'), (SELECT max(id) FROM t));
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN id RESTART WITH 5001;
```

The first reads the maximum at runtime. The second is clearer but takes a
literal, which the prompt rules out — unless you generate the statement
dynamically, which is more machinery than this needs.

## Hint 3

`setval(seq, n)` makes the *next* `nextval` return `n + 1`. The
three-argument form `setval(seq, n, false)` makes the next value `n`
itself — the form you want when seeding an empty table where the first id
must be exactly `n`. Getting this backwards produces an off-by-one that
looks like a mysterious skipped id.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Before fixing it, produce the failure. Insert a post without an id and
read the error: `duplicate key value violates unique constraint
"mem_posts_pkey"`, `Key (post_id)=(1) already exists`. Now you have seen
what your future on-call self would see, with no context, three weeks
after a migration nobody remembers.

## Hint 2

Check the sequence's state directly rather than inferring it:

```sql
SELECT sequencename, last_value, is_called FROM pg_sequences
WHERE schemaname = current_schema();
```

`last_value = 1, is_called = false` means "nobody has drawn a number yet;
the next one is 1". After your resync it should read `12000, true`.

## Hint 3

Generalise the habit: after **any** load that supplies explicit values for
a generated column — a restore, a `COPY`, a data fix, a fixture loader —
resync. A one-line check makes a good post-migration assertion:

```sql
SELECT max(post_id) < (SELECT last_value FROM mem_posts_post_id_seq)
FROM mem_posts;
```

If that ever returns false, you have a time bomb with a fuse of length
"one insert".

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate/ex4 — resync the identity sequence, then prove it
SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('mem_posts', 'post_id'),
              (SELECT max(post_id) FROM mem_posts));

INSERT INTO mem_posts (author_id, title, body, posted_at)
SELECT person_id, 'resynced', 'ok', timestamptz '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00'
FROM mem_people
WHERE email = 'ada@example.com';

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — what the mutable key costs, in rows

The legacy schema is still there, and it still keys members on `email`
with `ON UPDATE CASCADE` down to `legacy_posts` and `legacy_reactions`.
Support gets a few dozen "I changed my email" requests a month, and
somebody claims that is cheap because it is one `UPDATE`.

Measure it. For the **five members whose email change would rewrite the
most rows**, return `email`, `posts` (their rows in `legacy_posts`),
`reactions` (their rows in `legacy_reactions`), and `cascade_rows` =
`1 + posts + reactions` — the member row plus every child row the cascade
must touch.

Members with no posts and no reactions must still be countable, so count
them as zero rather than dropping them — even though none of the top five
will be one of those, the query should be correct for a member who is.

**Ordered by `cascade_rows` descending, then `email` ascending. Five
rows.**

Example row: `('ada@example.com', 87, 412, 500)`.

The number to take away is not the total. It is that a single logical fact
— one person's new address — becomes hundreds of new tuple versions, each
one WAL, each one index churn, in tables the requester has never heard of.

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate ex5`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two child tables at two different grains. Count each on its own and join
the summaries to the member — the mistake this exercise is built around
is joining both children to the parent at once, which multiplies posts by
reactions.

## Hint 2

Aggregate first, join after:

```sql
WITH p AS (SELECT author_email, count(*) AS n FROM legacy_posts
           GROUP BY author_email),
     r AS (SELECT author_email, count(*) AS n FROM legacy_reactions
           GROUP BY author_email)
SELECT m.email, coalesce(p.n,0), coalesce(r.n,0)
FROM legacy_members m
LEFT JOIN p ON p.author_email = m.email
LEFT JOIN r ON r.author_email = m.email;
```

## Hint 3

`LEFT JOIN` plus `coalesce` is what keeps the zero-child members correct;
an inner join silently answers a different question. Alternatively two
correlated scalar subqueries in the `SELECT` list read very cleanly here
and cost nothing extra at this size — pick whichever you would rather find
in a code review, and be able to say why.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Frame the output as an argument, not a report. You are producing the
number that ends the "it is just one UPDATE" conversation. That means the
column that matters is `cascade_rows`, and the ordering is descending
because the worst case is the one that decides architecture.

## Hint 2

Watch the cascade actually happen, in a transaction you throw away:

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE legacy_members SET email = 'new@example.com'
WHERE email = 'ada@example.com';
SELECT count(*) FROM legacy_posts WHERE author_email = 'new@example.com';
ROLLBACK;
```

The posts followed. Now imagine the same statement without the
`ON UPDATE CASCADE`: it fails on a foreign-key violation, and the member
simply cannot change their email at all. Both outcomes are consequences of
the key choice.

## Hint 3

Extend the thought past row counts. Each cascaded update is a new row
version, so every index on those tables gets a new entry too, and the dead
tuples wait for VACUUM (lesson 44). A cascade of 500 rows across two
tables with four indexes is a couple of thousand index writes — for a
change of address. In the `mem_people` schema the same request updates
exactly one row and zero children, because nothing references the email.
That difference is the entire argument for surrogate keys, expressed as a
number you just computed.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate/ex5 — cascade cost of a mutable natural key
WITH p AS (
  SELECT author_email, count(*) AS n FROM legacy_posts GROUP BY author_email
), r AS (
  SELECT author_email, count(*) AS n FROM legacy_reactions GROUP BY author_email
)
SELECT m.email,
       coalesce(p.n, 0)                     AS posts,
       coalesce(r.n, 0)                     AS reactions,
       1 + coalesce(p.n, 0) + coalesce(r.n, 0) AS cascade_rows
FROM legacy_members m
LEFT JOIN p ON p.author_email = m.email
LEFT JOIN r ON r.author_email = m.email
ORDER BY cascade_rows DESC, m.email
LIMIT 5;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate/ex5 — same numbers via correlated subqueries
SELECT m.email,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM legacy_posts p
        WHERE p.author_email = m.email)      AS posts,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM legacy_reactions x
        WHERE x.author_email = m.email)      AS reactions,
       1 + (SELECT count(*) FROM legacy_posts p
            WHERE p.author_email = m.email)
         + (SELECT count(*) FROM legacy_reactions x
            WHERE x.author_email = m.email)  AS cascade_rows
FROM legacy_members m
ORDER BY cascade_rows DESC, m.email
LIMIT 5;

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — retire a `serial`

```sql
legacy_signups (signup_id serial PRIMARY KEY,
                email text NOT NULL,
                source text NOT NULL)   -- 3,000 rows
```

`serial` is not a type. That column is an `integer` with `DEFAULT
nextval('legacy_signups_signup_id_seq'::regclass)`, plus a sequence marked
as owned by it. Everything problematic about it follows from being an
ordinary default: an explicit insert is accepted and desynchronises the
sequence, and a role with `INSERT` on the table still needs `USAGE` on the
sequence or the insert fails.

Convert it to an identity column, in place, preserving every existing
`signup_id`:

1. `DROP DEFAULT` on the column — a column may not have both a default and
   an identity, and the error if you skip this says exactly that.
2. `ADD GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` on the column. **`BY DEFAULT`,
   not `ALWAYS`**, this once: an existing application is inserting
   explicit ids in places you have not audited, and `ALWAYS` would break
   it on deploy. Tightening to `ALWAYS` is a separate, later change with
   its own rollout.
3. Resync the new identity sequence to `max(signup_id)`.

The gate checks `pg_attribute.attidentity = 'd'` for the column, that no
default remains, that the row count and every id are unchanged, and that
an insert with no id lands at 3001.

Note the sequence: after `ADD GENERATED`, `pg_get_serial_sequence` points
at a **new** sequence starting at 1, which is why step 3 is not optional.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate ex6`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three `ALTER`/`SELECT` statements, in the order the prompt lists them.
Each one fails informatively if you run it in the wrong order, so if you
are unsure, try it and read the message.

## Hint 2

```sql
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN id DROP DEFAULT;
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN id ADD GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY;
```

Note `ADD GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY` is a column-level `ALTER`, unlike
`SET GENERATED` which changes an existing identity's flavour.

## Hint 3

Step 3 is ex4's `setval` with a different table name — which is the point:
the resync is not a migration-specific trick, it is what you do any time a
sequence and its column have drifted. Whether you also drop the now-orphan
`legacy_signups_signup_id_seq` is a judgement call; nothing advances it any
more, but dropping objects in the same transaction as a conversion is how
rollbacks get complicated.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Look at what you are converting before you convert it, so the change means
something:

```sql
SELECT column_default, is_identity, identity_generation
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'legacy_signups' AND column_name = 'signup_id';
```

`column_default` full, `is_identity = NO`. Afterwards it should be the
mirror image. That flip is the entire deliverable.

## Hint 2

The failure mode if you skip step 1:

```
ERROR:  column "signup_id" of relation "legacy_signups" already has a default
```

Postgres will not silently discard your default, because a default and an
identity are two different answers to "what value goes here" and it
refuses to guess which you meant.

## Hint 3

The `BY DEFAULT` choice in step 2 is the interesting decision, and it is a
deployment decision rather than a modelling one. `ALWAYS` is the better end
state; going straight there breaks any code path that supplies an id, and
you cannot know from inside the database whether such a path exists. The
professional sequence is: convert with `BY DEFAULT`, add monitoring or a
trigger that logs explicit-id inserts, wait, then
`ALTER COLUMN signup_id SET GENERATED ALWAYS`. That last statement is one
line and belongs to a different ticket.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — a public identifier for an existing table

Your ex2-ex4 scripts run automatically first, so `mem_posts` holds 12,001
rows keyed on a sequential `bigint`.

Post URLs currently read `/posts/12001`. That number publishes your
content volume, your growth rate (two requests, a week apart, give the
slope), and an invitation to walk the whole table by counting. The fix is
not to obscure the key; it is to publish a different identifier.

In one script:

1. Add `mem_posts.public_id uuid` with `DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()`. Adding
   a column with a volatile default rewrites the table and fills every
   existing row with its own fresh value — which is what you want here,
   and is worth knowing before you run it on a table of a hundred million
   rows under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`.
2. Make it `NOT NULL`.
3. Add `CONSTRAINT mem_posts_public_key UNIQUE (public_id)`.
4. Create a view `mem_public_posts` exposing only `public_id`, `title`,
   `posted_at`, and the author's `public_id` as `author_public_id` — no
   `bigint` ids anywhere in the output. This is what the API layer should
   be selecting from.

The gate checks that all 12,001 rows have distinct non-null `public_id`s,
that the unique constraint exists, and that `mem_public_posts` returns
exactly those four columns.

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate ex7`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three `ALTER TABLE` statements and a `CREATE VIEW`. The subtlety is that
step 1 already fills the existing rows, so no separate backfill `UPDATE`
is needed — but check that assumption rather than trusting it.

## Hint 2

```sql
ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN u uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid();
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN u SET NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE t ADD CONSTRAINT t_u_key UNIQUE (u);
```

The order is forced: you cannot declare `NOT NULL` before the values
exist, and a unique constraint on a column full of NULLs would succeed
misleadingly.

## Hint 3

The view joins `mem_posts` to `mem_people` on `author_id = person_id` and
selects only the public columns. What to decide for yourself: whether the
view should also be the *write* surface. It cannot be, as written — a view
over a join is not automatically updatable — and that limitation is a
feature here, because the public identifier is for reading. If you want the write path too, that is
`INSTEAD OF` triggers, and a larger commitment than this exercise wants.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Quantify the leak before you patch it. `/posts/12001` today and
`/posts/12240` next Monday tells an observer you publish about 34 posts a
day. Sequential identifiers are a side channel, and the general fix is
always the same: publish an identifier that carries no information.

## Hint 2

Confirm what step 1 actually did, because "adding a column with a default
does not rewrite the table" is a rule people half-remember from PG11:

```sql
SELECT count(*), count(public_id), count(DISTINCT public_id)
FROM mem_posts;
```

All three equal. The PG11 optimisation applies to *constant* defaults,
which are stored once in the catalog; a volatile default like
`gen_random_uuid()` must produce a different value per row, so the table
is rewritten. This distinction is exactly V3·E6's subject.

## Hint 3

Consider and reject two alternatives. Hashing the bigint (`md5(id)`) is
reversible by anyone who can hash the numbers 1..N — it hides nothing.
Encrypting it with a shared secret works but ties every URL to key
management forever. A random UUID has neither problem and costs one
column. If you later need time-ordering in the public id, that is UUIDv7,
which you generate in the application because PG16 has no built-in.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — a junction table, and the column order that decides two queries

Your ex2-ex4 scripts run automatically first.

Posts get tags. Build the two tables:

```sql
mem_tags (
  tag_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  slug   text NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT mem_tags_slug_key UNIQUE (slug))

mem_post_tags (
  post_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES mem_posts(post_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  tag_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES mem_tags(tag_id)   ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  PRIMARY KEY (post_id, tag_id))
```

Three decisions worth defending:

- **No surrogate key on the junction table.** `(post_id, tag_id)` is
  already unique, minimal and immutable. An `id bigserial` here buys
  nothing and permits duplicate pairs unless you add back a unique
  constraint on exactly the columns you just declined to key on.
- **`ON DELETE CASCADE` toward the post, `ON DELETE RESTRICT` toward the
  tag.** Deleting a post should remove its tag links; deleting a tag that
  is still in use should be refused, because it is almost always a
  mistake.
- **The primary key index has a left prefix.** `(post_id, tag_id)` serves
  "tags of this post" and cannot serve "posts with this tag", which is the
  query the tag page runs. So also create index
  `mem_post_tags_tag_post_idx` on `(tag_id, post_id)` — the reverse pair,
  which is covering for that direction.

Then seed it: insert the tags `'sql'`, `'design'`, `'ops'` (in that
order), and tag every post whose `title` contains the word `index`
(case-insensitive) with `'sql'`.

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate ex8`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two `CREATE TABLE`s, one `CREATE INDEX`, two inserts. The idea being
tested is that a composite index is ordered, so it answers questions that
start with its first column and not questions that start with its second.

## Hint 2

The seeding insert is a select over the posts:

```sql
INSERT INTO mem_post_tags (post_id, tag_id)
SELECT p.post_id, t.tag_id
FROM mem_posts p, mem_tags t
WHERE t.slug = 'sql' AND p.title ILIKE '%index%';
```

A cross join filtered to one tag row is a perfectly honest way to attach a
constant.

## Hint 3

`ILIKE '%index%'` matches the substring, which will also match
"reindexing" — the prompt says "contains the word index" loosely on
purpose, and the gate uses the same predicate. If you wanted true word
matching you would reach for `~* '\yindex\y'`, and knowing that the two
differ is worth more than which one this gate wants.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with the two queries the tables exist to serve, and let them dictate
the indexes:

```sql
SELECT tag_id FROM mem_post_tags WHERE post_id = 42;   -- post page
SELECT post_id FROM mem_post_tags WHERE tag_id = 7;    -- tag page
```

One index cannot serve both efficiently. That is not a limitation to work
around; it is the reason junction tables usually carry two indexes and
why people who skip the second one discover it under load.

## Hint 2

Check the plans once the data is in:

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT post_id FROM mem_post_tags WHERE tag_id = 1;
```

With only the primary key present you get a sequential scan or a full
index scan; with `mem_post_tags_tag_post_idx` you get an index-only scan,
because the index contains both columns and the query wants nothing else.
Lesson 34's payoff, arriving for free out of the key design.

## Hint 3

Push on the delete actions. `ON DELETE RESTRICT` toward the tag means an
attempt to delete a used tag raises immediately; `NO ACTION` — the default
— behaves the same except that it is deferrable, so the check can be
postponed to commit. `SET NULL` is impossible here because the column is
part of the primary key. Being able to say why `SET NULL` is unavailable
tells you that you have understood what the key is.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — gapless numbering, and what it costs

Your ex2-ex4 scripts run automatically first.

Finance needs invoice numbers that are **consecutive within a year with no
gaps** — a legal requirement in several jurisdictions. A sequence cannot
do this: `nextval()` is deliberately non-transactional, so a rolled-back
insert leaves a hole and nobody is coming back for it. You have to build
the thing sequences exist to avoid.

Deliver three objects:

1. **`inv_counter (year int PRIMARY KEY, next_no int NOT NULL)`**, seeded
   with `(2026, 1)`.

2. **`inv_invoices`**:

```sql
inv_invoices (
  invoice_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  year       int NOT NULL,
  invoice_no int NOT NULL,
  person_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES mem_people(person_id),
  amount     numeric(12,2) NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT inv_invoices_no_key UNIQUE (year, invoice_no),
  CONSTRAINT inv_invoices_no_positive CHECK (invoice_no > 0))
```

Note the two keys doing different jobs: `invoice_id` is the surrogate the
rest of the schema joins on and is allowed to have gaps; `(year,
invoice_no)` is the gapless business key, unique-constrained because the
numbering scheme is a promise to a regulator.

3. **`next_invoice_no(p_year int) RETURNS int`**, `plpgsql` or `sql`,
   which atomically claims and returns the next number for that year. It
   must be a single `UPDATE ... RETURNING` against `inv_counter` — that
   statement takes a row lock held until your transaction ends, which is
   precisely what makes the numbering gapless and precisely what makes it
   a serialisation point. Do not write it as `SELECT` then `UPDATE`; two
   concurrent sessions would read the same value.

Then use it: insert three invoices for the member `'ada@example.com'` with
amounts `100.00`, `250.00`, `75.00`, each taking its number from the
function.

The gate: checks the three invoices are numbered 1, 2, 3; opens a
transaction, calls the function, rolls back, then calls it again and
asserts the next number is **4, not 5** — proving the counter rolls back
where a sequence would not. It also asserts that `inv_invoices.invoice_id`
*does* skip after a rolled-back insert, so you can see both behaviours in
one schema.

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate challenge`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The whole mechanism is one statement. `UPDATE` the counter row,
incrementing it, and return the value it had *before* the increment — all
inside the caller's transaction, so the row lock and the rollback
semantics come for free.

## Hint 2

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION next_no(p int) RETURNS int LANGUAGE sql AS $$
  UPDATE counter SET n = n + 1 WHERE k = p RETURNING n - 1;
$$;
```

`RETURNING n - 1` returns the pre-increment value because `RETURNING` sees
the *new* row. Returning `n` instead gives you the next number and starts
your invoices at 2 — an off-by-one that a gate catches and a regulator
does not.

## Hint 3

For the inserts, call the function once per row. Whether you write three
`INSERT ... VALUES` statements or one insert over a `VALUES` list is your
choice, but be careful with the second: the order in which the function is
evaluated across rows of a multi-row insert is not something to rely on
for a numbering scheme where order matters. Three statements are boring
and defensible.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build the wrong version first and understand why it is wrong. `SELECT
next_no FROM inv_counter WHERE year = 2026;` then `UPDATE ... SET next_no
= next_no + 1;` looks equivalent. Two sessions running it concurrently
both read 1, both write 2, and both issue invoice number 1 — a unique
violation if you are lucky and a duplicate invoice if you are not. The
single `UPDATE ... RETURNING` is atomic because the row lock is taken
before the read that matters.

## Hint 2

See the serialisation with your own hands. In one session:

```sql
BEGIN; SELECT next_invoice_no(2026);   -- do not commit
```

In another session, run the same thing. It hangs. Look at why:

```sql
SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, query
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state <> 'idle';
```

The second session is waiting on a transaction lock. Every invoice in your
system now queues behind whichever transaction is currently open, for as
long as it stays open. That is the price of gaplessness, and it is why the
counter is keyed by year rather than being a single global row.

## Hint 3

Two refinements worth knowing and not building here. Keying the counter by
`(year, document_type)` narrows contention to one series. And issuing the
number as late as possible in the transaction — after all the slow work —
shortens the window the lock is held, which is the single most effective
tuning available. Neither changes the fundamental shape: gapless means
serialised, and any design that claims otherwise has hidden the queue
rather than removed it.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — what your keys tell a stranger

Your ex2-ex4 and ex7 scripts run automatically first, so `mem_people` and
`mem_posts` both carry a sequential `bigint` key and a random `uuid`.

A security review asks a simple question: *given only what a logged-out
visitor can see, what can they infer?* Answer it with SQL rather than with
opinion.

Produce **one row**, four columns:

- `max_post_id` — `max(post_id)` from `mem_posts`. On a site with
  sequential URLs, this number is public: it is the id in the newest
  post's link. It is also, to within the number of deletions, the total
  number of posts ever made.
- `real_posts` — `count(*)` from `mem_posts`, the true figure.
- `leak_ratio` — `round(max_post_id::numeric / real_posts, 4)`. A ratio
  near 1 means the sequential id is an accurate census; the further from
  1, the more the gaps and deletions obscure it. On this data it is very
  close to 1, which is the uncomfortable finding.
- `public_ids_distinct` — `count(DISTINCT public_id)`, which must equal
  `real_posts`, showing the replacement identifier is a working substitute
  before you recommend switching to it.

Then, in the same script, create a view `mem_id_exposure` with one row per
member, columns `person_id`, `public_id`, `posts` — the count of that
member's posts — restricted to members with at least one post, ordered by
`person_id`. The point of the view is what an auditor does next: it makes
it trivial to check whether any query in the codebase selects `person_id`
where it should select `public_id`.

**Expected shape:** one row from the query, plus the view existing.

Edit `review1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate review1`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The query is four aggregates over one table and no `GROUP BY`. The view is
a grouped join. The thinking is in what the numbers mean, not in how to
compute them.

## Hint 2

Guard the division:

```sql
round(max(id)::numeric / nullif(count(*), 0), 4)
```

`nullif` turns the empty-table case into NULL instead of a division error.
The gate's table is not empty, but a metric query that dies on an empty
table is a metric query that dies exactly when something is already wrong.

## Hint 3

For the view, aggregate the posts per author and join to the member, or
join and group — either is fine at this size. What you must not do is
expose `author_id` in the output when the view's entire purpose is to make
`public_id` the visible identifier; the `person_id` column is there for
the auditor, not for the API.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Do the attack by hand first. Open the newest post, read its id, wait, read
it again. You now have volume and growth rate. Then fetch ids 1..N and you
have the archive, including anything that was quietly unpublished but not
deleted. Every step of that is possible because the identifier is dense and
ordered — the two properties that make it a good primary key.

## Hint 2

Verify the substitute before recommending it:

```sql
SELECT count(*), count(public_id), count(DISTINCT public_id) FROM mem_posts;
```

Three equal numbers means the UUID is total and unique, so it can carry
every URL the bigint carried. If they are not equal, ex7's `NOT NULL` or
`UNIQUE` did not take, and you would be recommending a broken migration.

## Hint 3

Be precise about what UUIDs do and do not fix. They stop enumeration and
volume leakage. They do **not** provide authorisation — a random URL is
still a URL, and "unguessable" is not "permitted". Anyone relying on
`public_id` secrecy as access control has built a capability system by
accident, with no revocation. That is V3·E8's subject, and the honest
summary is that the UUID closes the side channel and row-level security
closes the door.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e02_keys_natural_surrogate/review1 — what sequential ids disclose
SELECT max(post_id)                                          AS max_post_id,
       count(*)                                              AS real_posts,
       round(max(post_id)::numeric / nullif(count(*), 0), 4) AS leak_ratio,
       count(DISTINCT public_id)                             AS public_ids_distinct
FROM mem_posts;

CREATE VIEW mem_id_exposure AS
SELECT m.person_id,
       m.public_id,
       count(p.post_id) AS posts
FROM mem_people m
JOIN mem_posts p ON p.author_id = m.person_id
GROUP BY m.person_id, m.public_id
ORDER BY m.person_id;

lessons.title: V3·E3 — Constraints as documentation
lessons.summary: A clinic booking schema, written so the rules live in the database rather than in a wiki nobody reads. Named CHECKs, NOT VALID for dirty history, partial unique indexes, NULLS NOT DISTINCT, the four foreign-key actions, MATCH FULL, exclusion constraints, and deferred constraints for the swap.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·E3 — Constraints as documentation

Lesson 25 taught you what constraints are. This sector is about what they
are *for*, which is a different question with a more opinionated answer:
a constraint is the only documentation that cannot go out of date.

Every business rule in a system lives in one of four places. In a wiki,
where it is wrong within a quarter. In application code, where it is right
for the one code path that was updated and absent from the batch job. In a
code review comment, where it is not enforced at all. Or in the schema,
where it is checked on every write by every writer, forever, including the
psql session somebody opens at 2am to "just fix one row". Constraints are
the fourth place, and the reason to prefer them is not correctness in the
abstract — it is that they are the only mechanism that survives staff
turnover.

## The schema

`setup.sql` builds a clinic booking system, deliberately underconstrained:

```sql
CREATE TABLE clinics (
  clinic_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name      text NOT NULL,
  timezone  text NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE rooms (
  room_id   bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  clinic_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES clinics(clinic_id),
  code      text NOT NULL,          -- 'A1', 'A2' — unique per clinic
  capacity  int  NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE practitioners (
  prac_id   bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  clinic_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES clinics(clinic_id),
  full_name text NOT NULL,
  licence_no text);                 -- nullable: trainees have none yet

CREATE TABLE bookings (
  booking_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  room_id    bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES rooms(room_id),
  prac_id    bigint REFERENCES practitioners(prac_id),
  patient_ref text NOT NULL,
  starts_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  ends_at    timestamptz NOT NULL,
  status     text NOT NULL,          -- 'held','confirmed','cancelled'
  price      numeric(10,2) NOT NULL);
```

Read it as a stranger would and list what it fails to say. Nothing stops
`ends_at` preceding `starts_at`. Nothing stops a negative price. Nothing
stops `status = 'banana'`. Nothing stops two confirmed bookings in the
same room at the same time, which is the rule the entire business exists
to honour. Nothing stops a room in clinic 1 being booked by a practitioner
from clinic 2. All of those rules exist; none of them are written down
here; all of them are enforced, partially, somewhere in a Rails
controller.

## The five mechanisms, and when each one is right

**`CHECK`** states a rule about a single row. Cheap, always enforced, and
the right home for anything you can express without looking at another
row: `price >= 0`, `ends_at > starts_at`, `status IN (...)`. Its limit is
strict — a `CHECK` may not query another table, may not use a volatile
function, and is assumed immutable, so `CHECK (starts_at > now())` is not
merely a bad idea, it silently breaks restores.

**`UNIQUE`** states that a fact is single-valued, and its most useful form
is the one that is not a constraint at all: a **partial unique index**.
"One held booking per patient at a time" is not `UNIQUE (patient_ref)` —
it is unique *among the rows where `status = 'held'`*, which only an index
with a `WHERE` clause can express. Most real uniqueness rules in
applications are conditional like this, and most schemas express them with
an application-level check that races.

**Foreign keys** state that a reference is meaningful, and their `ON
DELETE`/`ON UPDATE` clauses state what should happen to the child when the
parent moves. Those four actions — `CASCADE`, `RESTRICT`, `SET NULL`, `SET
DEFAULT` — are a design decision per relationship, and picking `CASCADE`
everywhere because it makes tests pass is how audit tables get deleted.

**Exclusion constraints** state that no two rows may *conflict* under an
operator of your choosing. With `&&` on a range, that is "no overlap",
which is the double-booking rule expressed exactly. This is the mechanism
people do not know exists, and it replaces a page of trigger code with one
line.

**Deferrable constraints** state a rule that must hold at the end of the
transaction rather than after each statement. They exist for the two cases
where correct intermediate states are impossible: swapping two values that
are unique, and inserting two rows that reference each other.

## Naming is not cosmetic

```sql
CONSTRAINT bookings_time_order CHECK (ends_at > starts_at)
```

That name reaches your application in the error's `constraint_name` field,
and mature code matches on it to produce a message a human can act on.
Anonymous constraints get names like `bookings_check1`, which are stable
enough to match on and meaningless enough that nobody does, so the
application shows "database error" and a support ticket is filed. Name
every constraint, `<table>_<rule>`, and treat a rename as a breaking API
change — because it is.

## What the exercises do

ex1 writes the row-level rules as named `CHECK`s. ex2 meets the hard case:
history that already violates the rule you want to add, and `NOT VALID`
plus a later `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` as the way through. ex3 is the
conditional uniqueness rule and the partial index that expresses it. ex4
is the NULL trap — a unique constraint that permits unlimited duplicates
because the column is nullable — and `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`, new in PG15.
ex5 walks all four foreign-key actions with four child tables and makes
each one raise or cascade. ex6 is a composite foreign key and the
difference between `MATCH SIMPLE` and `MATCH FULL`, which is entirely
about partially-NULL keys. ex7 is the exclusion constraint that ends
double-booking. ex8 is the swap that only a deferred unique constraint can
perform. The challenge builds a genuinely circular reference. review1 asks
the schema to describe itself, and adds the index a foreign key does not
create for you.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - v3e03_constraints_as_documentation

The rules a schema states are the rules that stay true. Everything else is
a convention, and conventions decay.

## Notes

**`CHECK` is per-row and must be immutable.** It cannot reference other
tables, cannot use `now()` or `random()`, cannot use a subquery. Postgres
does not fully police this — you can smuggle a non-immutable function in
via a wrapper marked `IMMUTABLE` — and if you do, `pg_dump`/restore will
re-check every row against a function whose answer has changed, and the
restore fails. The constraint is a statement about the row, forever, not
about the row today.

**`NOT VALID` is how you add a rule to a table with a past.** `ALTER TABLE
... ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (...) NOT VALID` enforces the rule for every
new or updated row while leaving existing rows unexamined. It takes a
brief `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock; the subsequent `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` scans
the table under a much weaker `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE`, which does not
block reads or writes. Two statements, one of them cheap and one of them
long but non-blocking — this is the online pattern, and V3·E6 generalises
it. The same trick works for foreign keys.

**Partial unique indexes express conditional rules.** `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX
... ON t (a) WHERE status = 'held'` is the mechanism for "at most one
active X". Note it is an *index*, not a constraint: it does not appear in
`pg_constraint`, cannot be deferred, and cannot be referenced by a foreign
key. Those limits are real but rarely binding, and the alternative — a
trigger that counts — races unless it locks.

**A `UNIQUE` constraint on a nullable column is weaker than it looks.**
By default NULLs are distinct from each other, so `UNIQUE (licence_no)`
permits any number of NULL licences, which is usually what you want and
occasionally a serious bug. PG15 added `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT`, which
treats NULLs as equal and so permits exactly one. Know which one you
declared, because "we have 4,000 rows with a NULL external id and the
unique constraint did nothing" is a real incident class.

**The four FK actions are four different sentences.** `CASCADE`: the child
has no meaning without the parent. `RESTRICT`: deleting the parent while
children exist is an error the user must resolve. `SET NULL`: the link was
optional and its absence is meaningful. `SET DEFAULT`: the child moves to a
fallback parent, which must exist or you get a foreign-key violation from
inside the cascade. `NO ACTION`, the default, behaves like `RESTRICT`
except that its check is deferrable.

**Foreign keys index the parent, never the child.** The parent side must
be unique, so an index is already there. The child side gets nothing, and
without one, deleting a parent row sequentially scans the child to check
the constraint — every time. This is one of the most common causes of
mysterious `DELETE` latency, and review1 makes you feel it.

**`MATCH SIMPLE` versus `MATCH FULL` is only about partial NULLs.** With a
two-column foreign key, `MATCH SIMPLE` — the default — skips the check
entirely if *any* column is NULL. `MATCH FULL` requires all columns NULL
or none. If your composite reference is optional, `MATCH FULL` is almost
always what you meant.

**Exclusion constraints generalise `UNIQUE`.** `UNIQUE` says no two rows
are equal on these columns; `EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during
WITH &&)` says no two rows are equal on `room_id` *and* overlapping on
`during`. Mixing `=` on a scalar with `&&` on a range needs the
`btree_gist` extension, because a plain GiST index does not know how to
handle `bigint` equality.

**Deferrable constraints buy you an invalid moment.** `DEFERRABLE
INITIALLY IMMEDIATE` is checkable per statement but can be deferred with
`SET CONSTRAINTS ... DEFERRED`; `INITIALLY DEFERRED` defers by default.
Deferring is not free: violations surface at `COMMIT` with no statement to
blame, and the deferred-trigger queue holds every pending check in memory.
Defer the specific constraints that need it, not everything.

## ex1

Row rules, named. Note `status IN (...)` as a check versus an enum type —
the check is easier to change, which V3·E4 argues about at length.

## ex2

`NOT VALID`, then `VALIDATE`. The point is that "we cannot add this
constraint because of old data" is a solved problem, not a reason to leave
the rule undocumented.

## ex3

Partial unique index. The rule is conditional, so the index is
conditional; anything else is either wrong or a trigger.

## ex4

NULLs in unique constraints. The default is right for licence numbers and
wrong for external ids, and the difference is one keyword.

## ex5

The four actions, side by side, each proved by an attempted delete. Seeing
`SET DEFAULT` fail because the default parent does not exist is worth the
exercise on its own.

## ex6

`MATCH FULL`. The half-NULL composite reference is the entire subject.

## ex7

The exclusion constraint. One line replaces the trigger you were about to
write, and unlike the trigger it is correct under concurrency because the
index does the locking.

## ex8

The swap. Two rows exchanging unique values must pass through a state
where they collide, and deferral is the only way to permit it without a
temporary sentinel value.

## challenge

Circular references. Both foreign keys deferred, both rows inserted, one
commit.

## review1

The schema describing itself out of `pg_constraint`, plus the index that
makes a foreign key cheap to delete against.

## Further reading

- [Constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html) — checks, uniqueness, foreign keys, exclusion, in one page.
- [`ALTER TABLE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-altertable.html) — `NOT VALID`, `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`, and each form's lock level.
- [`CREATE INDEX`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — partial and unique indexes, and `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`.
- [`SET CONSTRAINTS`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-set-constraints.html) — deferring checks to commit time.
- [btree_gist](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/btree-gist.html) — the extension that lets `=` and `&&` share an exclusion constraint.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·E3 — Constraints as documentation (archive)

The reference version: every mechanism, the syntax, the lock it takes, and
the sentence it lets your schema say.

## The catalogue

```sql
-- a rule about one row
CONSTRAINT bookings_time_order CHECK (ends_at > starts_at)
CONSTRAINT bookings_price_nonneg CHECK (price >= 0)
CONSTRAINT bookings_status_known
  CHECK (status IN ('held','confirmed','cancelled'))

-- a fact is single-valued
CONSTRAINT rooms_clinic_code_key UNIQUE (clinic_id, code)

-- ... but only among some rows
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX bookings_one_hold_per_patient
  ON bookings (patient_ref) WHERE status = 'held';

-- ... and NULLs are distinct unless you say otherwise
CONSTRAINT prac_licence_key UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (licence_no)

-- a reference is meaningful, and here is what happens when it moves
prac_id bigint REFERENCES practitioners(prac_id) ON DELETE SET NULL

-- no two rows may conflict
CONSTRAINT bookings_no_overlap
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)
  WHERE (status <> 'cancelled')

-- ... checked at commit, not per statement
CONSTRAINT sections_order_key UNIQUE (doc_id, position)
  DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE
```

## Adding a rule to a table with a past

The problem: 40,000 historical bookings have `price = -1` as a sentinel,
and you want `price >= 0` from now on. The wrong answers are "clean the
data first, in one transaction" (a long `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock) and
"enforce it in the application" (it will not be).

```sql
ALTER TABLE bookings
  ADD CONSTRAINT bookings_price_nonneg CHECK (price >= 0) NOT VALID;
-- new and updated rows are checked from this moment.
-- ... clean the history at your leisure, in batches ...
ALTER TABLE bookings VALIDATE CONSTRAINT bookings_price_nonneg;
```

The first statement takes `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` but does no scan, so it is
instantaneous. The second takes `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE`, scans the table,
and blocks neither readers nor writers. The same two-step works for
foreign keys, which is how you add referential integrity to a large table
without an outage.

Until validated, the constraint exists with `convalidated = false`, and
the planner will not use it for constraint exclusion. That is the only
functional cost of leaving it half-done — but leaving it half-done for two
years is how schemas end up with rules nobody trusts.

## Uniqueness that is conditional

Almost every real uniqueness rule has a qualifier:

- one *active* subscription per customer
- one *primary* address per account
- one *undeleted* row per slug
- one *open* shift per employee

None of these are `UNIQUE (customer_id)`. All of them are partial unique
indexes, and the qualifier goes in the `WHERE`:

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX subs_one_active
  ON subscriptions (customer_id) WHERE status = 'active';
```

The temptation is a trigger that counts existing active rows. It races:
two concurrent transactions each see zero and each insert one. The unique
index does not race, because index insertion takes the lock for you.

## The four actions, decided per relationship

| action | the sentence it states |
| --- | --- |
| `CASCADE` | the child cannot exist without the parent |
| `RESTRICT` | deleting the parent is a mistake the user must fix |
| `SET NULL` | the link was optional; losing it is meaningful |
| `SET DEFAULT` | the child falls back to a designated parent |

`SET DEFAULT` has a sharp edge: the default value must itself satisfy the
foreign key, or the cascade fails at the moment of deletion with an error
that names the child table and confuses everyone. Point it at a real
"unassigned" row that you created deliberately.

`ON UPDATE CASCADE` matters only for mutable keys — V3·E2's whole subject.
With surrogate keys it is dead code, and writing it anyway is a small
signal that nobody thought about it.

## MATCH FULL

```sql
FOREIGN KEY (clinic_id, room_code)
  REFERENCES rooms (clinic_id, code) MATCH FULL
```

With `MATCH SIMPLE` (the default), a row with `clinic_id = 3, room_code =
NULL` passes the check without any lookup — one NULL disables the whole
constraint. With `MATCH FULL`, that row is rejected: either both columns
are NULL or neither is. If the reference is mandatory, `NOT NULL` on both
columns makes the distinction moot; if it is optional, `MATCH FULL` is
what you meant.

## Exclusion constraints

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

ALTER TABLE bookings ADD COLUMN during tstzrange
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (tstzrange(starts_at, ends_at, '[)')) STORED;

ALTER TABLE bookings ADD CONSTRAINT bookings_no_overlap
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)
  WHERE (status <> 'cancelled');
```

Read it as a sentence: no two non-cancelled bookings may have the same
room and overlapping times. The `'[)'` bound is doing real work — a
booking ending at 10:00 and one starting at 10:00 do not overlap, which is
what a half-open interval means and what a scheduler wants. Use `'[]'` and
back-to-back appointments become illegal.

`btree_gist` is required because GiST natively indexes ranges and
geometry, not `bigint` equality; the extension supplies the missing
operator class.

## Common mistakes

- **Anonymous constraints.** `bookings_check1` in an error message helps
  nobody. Name every one.
- **`CHECK` with a non-immutable function.** Works today, fails during
  restore, which is the worst possible time to discover it.
- **Plain `UNIQUE` for a conditional rule.** Either it rejects legitimate
  rows or it is enforced nowhere.
- **Forgetting NULLs are distinct.** A `UNIQUE` on a nullable column
  permits unlimited NULLs.
- **`CASCADE` by reflex.** Cascading deletes into an audit or ledger table
  destroys the record you were legally required to keep.
- **No index on the child side of a foreign key.** Every parent delete
  scans the child.
- **`MATCH SIMPLE` on an optional composite reference.** Half-filled keys
  slip through unchecked.
- **`SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED` as a habit.** Violations then appear at
  commit with no statement to blame, and debugging is miserable.
- **A trigger where an exclusion constraint would do.** The trigger races;
  the constraint does not.

## Interview answer

*"Where should business rules live?"*

In the database when they are invariants, in the application when they are
workflow. The test is whether a rule must be true of *every row in every
state of the system*, regardless of which code path wrote it — "an
appointment cannot end before it starts", "a room cannot be double-booked",
"a price is not negative". Those are invariants, and putting them anywhere
other than the schema means they are enforced by whichever writer
remembered.

Workflow rules are different: "a booking can only be confirmed by a
practitioner with an active licence during business hours" involves other
tables, time, and permissions. `CHECK` cannot express it, a trigger can but
becomes unreadable, and the application is the honest home.

Then say the operational half: name constraints so error handlers can
match them, and use `NOT VALID`/`VALIDATE` so that "old data violates it"
never becomes a reason to leave a rule unwritten.

## Check yourself

1. Name three things a `CHECK` constraint may not reference, and say what
   breaks if you smuggle one in.
2. What lock does `ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID` take, and what lock does
   `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` take?
3. Express "one open shift per employee" as a schema object.
4. How many NULLs does `UNIQUE (licence_no)` permit? How do you change
   that, and since which version?
5. Give a relationship where `ON DELETE CASCADE` is the correct choice and
   one where it is a data-loss incident.
6. What must be true for `ON DELETE SET DEFAULT` to work at all?
7. A two-column foreign key with one NULL: what happens under `MATCH
   SIMPLE`, and under `MATCH FULL`?
8. Why does `EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)` need an
   extension?
9. Why does `'[)'` matter in `tstzrange(starts_at, ends_at, '[)')`?
10. Describe the intermediate state that makes swapping two unique values
    impossible without deferral.
11. What is the practical downside of `INITIALLY DEFERRED`?
12. Which side of a foreign key gets an index automatically, and what is
    the symptom when the other side lacks one?
13. Why is a counting trigger not equivalent to a partial unique index?
14. Where does a constraint's name show up in your application, and why is
    renaming one a breaking change?
lessons.fullReading:
# The long read — the rules that outlive the code

There is a particular kind of production incident that only happens to
systems whose rules live in application code. The API validates a booking,
the mobile client validates it slightly differently, the CSV importer
written in 2019 validates nothing, and the support tool bypasses all three
because it was built to fix the cases the API refused. Four writers, four
opinions, one table. The rule was never wrong; it was just never in one
place.

A constraint is the answer to that, and the reason is structural rather
than moral. There is exactly one code path into a Postgres table — the
storage engine — and a constraint sits on it. Every writer is checked,
including the ones written after you leave, including the ones written by
people who never read your wiki, including you at 2am with `psql` open.

## What each mechanism actually costs

**`CHECK`** is evaluated per row on insert and on update, and only when
the update touches a column the expression mentions. It is close to free —
an expression evaluation against a tuple already in memory. The cost is
entirely at `ALTER TABLE` time, where adding one scans the table under
`ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` unless you say `NOT VALID`.

**`UNIQUE`** is an index, so it costs what an index costs: space, an entry
per insert, and page splits. The check itself is not extra work — it is
the index insertion discovering a duplicate. This is also why unique
constraints are concurrency-safe without any locking of your own: the
B-tree insertion protocol serialises conflicting inserters, blocking the
second until the first commits or aborts. A `SELECT`-then-`INSERT` in
application code cannot replicate this without an explicit lock, and
almost nobody takes one.

**Foreign keys** are implemented as system triggers — you can see them in
`pg_trigger`. An insert into the child fires a trigger that runs `SELECT 1
FROM parent WHERE key = $1 FOR KEY SHARE`. That lock is why concurrent
inserts into a child table can contend on a hot parent row, and why
`FOR KEY SHARE` exists at all: it blocks key changes without blocking
ordinary updates to the parent. Deleting from the parent fires the
matching trigger on the child, and *that* one has no index to use unless
you built one.

**Exclusion constraints** are GiST index scans. Each insert probes for a
conflicting row and takes a lock, so they are more expensive than a unique
constraint but of the same shape. They are also the only general-purpose
mechanism in this list — `EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH
&&)` is one instance of a family that includes non-overlapping IP ranges,
non-intersecting polygons, and mutually-exclusive feature flags.

**Deferred constraints** move work to commit. Postgres queues an
after-trigger event per deferred check; the queue lives in memory (spilling
to disk when large), and a transaction that updates a million rows against
a deferred foreign key queues a million events. That is the real cost, and
it is why `SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED` as a blanket habit is a
performance problem waiting for a bulk load.

## The constraint name is part of your API

There is a habit that separates schemas people enjoy working with from
schemas people fear, and it is smaller than it sounds: naming every
constraint, deliberately, in a scheme.

When a write fails, Postgres returns SQLSTATE `23505` (unique violation),
`23503` (foreign key), `23514` (check) and — critically — the constraint's
name in the error's `constraint_name` field. Every mature driver exposes
it. Application code that matches on it can turn a database error into
"that email address is already registered" or "this room is already
booked at that time", which is the difference between a form a user can
complete and a support ticket.

Anonymous constraints defeat this. `bookings_check1` is stable enough to
match on and opaque enough that nobody will, so the handler falls back to
a generic 500 and the rule you carefully encoded becomes invisible to the
person it exists to protect. Worse, the generated numbering shifts if
constraints are added in a different order in a rebuilt environment, so
even a team that did match on it finds the match failing in staging only.

Two practical consequences. First, name constraints `<table>_<rule>` —
`bookings_time_order`, not `bookings_check`. Second, treat renaming one as
a breaking change with a deprecation period, because somewhere a
`catch (e) { if (e.constraint === 'bookings_time_order') ... }` depends on
it. Schema names are an interface even when nobody wrote them down as
one, and this is the case where the interface is consumed by code rather
than by humans.

## A short history

Check constraints and foreign keys arrived with SQL-92 and are universal.
Postgres has had deferrable constraints since the 1990s, and its
implementation — constraints as system triggers — is why deferral works
uniformly for foreign keys and unique constraints alike, where some other
engines defer only some kinds.

Exclusion constraints are a Postgres invention, added in 9.0 (2010) by
Jeff Davis, generalising `UNIQUE` from "equal" to "any operator with an
index-supported search". Range types arrived alongside them in 9.2, and
the combination is still one of the strongest arguments for Postgres over
its competitors: the double-booking problem is solved by a schema line
rather than by a distributed lock.

`NULLS NOT DISTINCT` arrived in Postgres 15, closing a thirty-year gap
between what people write and what they mean. The standard's default —
NULLs are distinct in unique constraints — is defensible (NULL means
unknown, and two unknowns may differ) and is not what anyone expects the
first time.

`NOT VALID` for check constraints came in 9.1 and for foreign keys in 9.2.
Its importance is out of proportion to its size: it converts "we cannot
add this rule to a live table" into a two-step operation, and it is the
single most useful thing to know about constraints in an operational
context.

## When not to put the rule in the schema

**When it involves other tables and changes over time.** "A practitioner
may not be booked outside their contracted hours" spans three tables and a
calendar. A trigger can do it; a trigger doing it will be four hundred
lines and will be the reason someone proposes moving off Postgres. Keep
invariants in the schema and workflow in the application.

**When the rule is a policy, not an invariant.** "Bookings must be at
least 24 hours in advance" is a policy: marketing will want to change it
for one clinic, then for one weekend. A constraint makes that a migration.
A configuration row makes it a form field.

**When violation must be recorded rather than rejected.** An import
pipeline that must accept dirty vendor data and quarantine it cannot have
the constraint on the landing table. Constrain the clean table and let the
staging table be permissive — the boundary between them is where
validation belongs, and that boundary should be explicit.

**When the check is expensive and the write path is hot.** An exclusion
constraint on a table taking ten thousand inserts a second is a
measurement, not a certainty — but it is a real consideration, and the
answer is sometimes to partition the constraint (per room, per day) rather
than to abandon it.

**When you are still learning the domain.** A constraint that turns out to
be wrong is a migration, sometimes a painful one. Early in a project,
`NOT VALID` and a monitoring query — "how many rows would violate this
rule?" — is a better first step than the constraint itself. Add the rule
when the count has been zero for a month.

The failure this list is guarding against is not "too few constraints",
which is the common disease, but its rarer opposite: a schema so tightly
specified that every product change requires a migration, and the team
learns to route around the database. The target is invariants in the
schema, policy in the application, and a clear answer for every rule about
which one it is.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — write the row rules down

`setup.sql` creates the clinic schema from the briefing. `bookings` is
underconstrained:

```sql
bookings(booking_id bigint PK, room_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES rooms,
         prac_id bigint REFERENCES practitioners,
         patient_ref text NOT NULL,
         starts_at timestamptz NOT NULL, ends_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
         status text NOT NULL, price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL)
```

Add three named constraints stating rules that are currently only in
somebody's head:

- `bookings_time_order` — `ends_at` must be strictly after `starts_at`. A
  zero-length appointment is not a thing.
- `bookings_status_known` — `status` is one of `'held'`, `'confirmed'`,
  `'cancelled'`.
- `bookings_cancelled_free` — a cancelled booking has `price = 0`;
  anything else has `price > 0`. This one spans two columns, which is what
  `CHECK` is for and what a column-level constraint cannot express.

Also add to `rooms`:

- `rooms_clinic_code_key` — `UNIQUE (clinic_id, code)`. Room codes repeat
  across clinics; `A1` exists in every building. Uniqueness is per clinic,
  and the column order matters for the index it creates.

The seeded data already satisfies all four, so plain `ADD CONSTRAINT`
works. The gate inserts a deliberately illegal row for each rule and
expects the failure to name **your** constraint.

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e03_constraints_as_documentation ex1`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT` statements. The only one that needs
thought is the third, where the rule is conditional: *if* cancelled *then*
zero, *otherwise* positive.

## Hint 2

A conditional rule in a `CHECK` is boolean logic, not an `IF`:

```sql
CHECK ((kind = 'refund' AND amount <= 0)
    OR (kind <> 'refund' AND amount > 0))
```

The `CASE` spelling works too and reads better to some eyes:
`CHECK (CASE WHEN kind = 'refund' THEN amount <= 0 ELSE amount > 0 END)`.

## Hint 3

Remember `CHECK` treats NULL as "not violated": a row where `status` is
NULL passes `bookings_status_known` silently. Here `status` is already
`NOT NULL`, so it does not bite — but the interaction between three-valued
logic and constraints is worth holding in mind, because it is the reason
a `CHECK` is never a substitute for `NOT NULL`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write each constraint as an English sentence first, then translate. "An
appointment ends after it starts." "A status is one of three words." "A
cancelled booking is free; a live one is not." If the sentence needs the
word "usually" or "unless the importer", it is not an invariant and does
not belong in a `CHECK`.

## Hint 2

Test each rule the way the gate will, before you trust it:

```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO bookings (room_id, patient_ref, starts_at, ends_at,
                      status, price)
VALUES (1, 'P-1', '2026-03-01 10:00Z', '2026-03-01 10:00Z',
        'confirmed', 50);
ROLLBACK;
```

The error should say `bookings_time_order`, not `bookings_check`. If it
says the latter, you let Postgres name it.

## Hint 3

The composite unique on `rooms` is a design decision hiding as a
constraint. `UNIQUE (clinic_id, code)` builds an index whose left prefix is
`clinic_id`, so "all rooms in clinic 7" is fast and "every room called A1"
is a scan. Reversing to `(code, clinic_id)` would enforce exactly the same
rule with the opposite performance profile. The rule does not choose; you
do, based on which query exists.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — a rule the history violates

`setup.sql` also loads `booking_archive`, 60,000 rows imported from the
system this one replaced:

```sql
booking_archive(archive_id bigint PK, room_code text NOT NULL,
                patient_ref text NOT NULL,
                starts_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
                ends_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
                price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL)
```

About 1,400 of those rows have `price = -1`, which the old system used as
"unknown". You want `price >= 0` enforced from now on. Cleaning 1,400 rows
first is possible but the wrong sequencing: while you clean, new rows keep
arriving unchecked, and if the clean-up takes a week the rule is unwritten
for a week.

Do it in the order that keeps the rule true from the first second:

1. `ADD CONSTRAINT archive_price_nonneg CHECK (price >= 0) NOT VALID` —
   new and updated rows are checked immediately; the 60,000 existing rows
   are not scanned, so the statement returns at once.
2. Repair the history: set `price = 0` where `price = -1`.
3. `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT archive_price_nonneg` — now scan, under a lock
   that blocks neither readers nor writers, and mark the constraint fully
   valid.

The gate checks `pg_constraint.convalidated` is true at the end, that no
negative prices remain, and — between your steps, by re-running a probe —
that an insert of `price = -5` was already rejected *before* validation.
That last check is the whole point: `NOT VALID` means "not yet verified
against history", not "not enforced".

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e03_constraints_as_documentation ex2`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three statements, in the order the prompt lists. The middle one is an
ordinary `UPDATE`; the outer two are the pattern worth memorising.

## Hint 2

```sql
ALTER TABLE t ADD CONSTRAINT t_rule CHECK (x >= 0) NOT VALID;
-- ... fix data ...
ALTER TABLE t VALIDATE CONSTRAINT t_rule;
```

`NOT VALID` goes at the end of the `ADD CONSTRAINT` clause. `VALIDATE
CONSTRAINT` is its own `ALTER TABLE` form and takes only the name.

## Hint 3

The repair is `UPDATE booking_archive SET price = 0 WHERE price = -1`.
Whether `0` is the right replacement for "unknown" is a question the
prompt answers for you and would not answer for you at work — the honest
alternative is a nullable column plus `CHECK (price IS NULL OR price >=
0)`, which distinguishes "free" from "we do not know". Notice that the
constraint you are writing forecloses that distinction.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason this exercise exists is a sentence you will hear in code
review: "we can't add that constraint, the old data doesn't comply."
That sentence is almost always false, and `NOT VALID` is why. Rules get
left out of schemas for years on the strength of it.

## Hint 2

Watch the constraint's own state change as you go:

```sql
SELECT conname, convalidated
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE conrelid = 'booking_archive'::regclass;
```

`false` after step 1, `true` after step 3. Between them, the rule is
enforced for writes and unverified for history — a state the catalog
records honestly, which is more than most systems manage.

## Hint 3

Know the lock levels, because they are the reason this works at scale.
`ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID` takes `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` but performs no
scan, so it holds the lock for microseconds. `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` takes
`SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE`, which permits concurrent `SELECT`, `INSERT`,
`UPDATE` and `DELETE` and conflicts only with other schema changes and
`VACUUM FULL`. On a 500-million-row table that scan runs for an hour and
nobody notices. V3·E6 is a whole sector of this shape.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — uniqueness with a qualifier

The booking flow puts a temporary hold on a slot while the patient enters
payment details. The rule is:

> A patient may have **at most one** booking in status `'held'` at a
> time. They may have any number of `'confirmed'` and `'cancelled'`
> bookings.

`UNIQUE (patient_ref)` is wrong — it would forbid a second confirmed
booking, which is the normal case. A trigger that counts held rows races:
two concurrent requests each see zero holds and each insert one.

Create a **partial unique index** named `bookings_one_hold_per_patient` on
`bookings (patient_ref) WHERE status = 'held'`.

Then, in the same script, demonstrate the operation the index makes safe:
confirm the existing held booking for patient `'P-0042'` by setting its
status to `'confirmed'` — after which that patient may take a new hold,
because the row has left the index.

The gate: inserts a second `'held'` booking for a patient who already has
one and expects a unique violation naming your index; inserts a second
`'confirmed'` booking for the same patient and expects it to succeed; and
checks `'P-0042'` ends `'confirmed'`.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e03_constraints_as_documentation ex3`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The rule has an "among the rows where..." in it. That phrase translates
directly into a `WHERE` clause on an index — and only an index, because
`ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT UNIQUE` has nowhere to put a predicate.

## Hint 2

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_primary_per_account
  ON addresses (account_id) WHERE is_primary;
```

Rows failing the predicate are simply absent from the index, so they
cannot collide with anything.

## Hint 3

Think about what happens at the moment of the `UPDATE` in step two. The
row's status changes from `'held'` to `'confirmed'`, so it leaves the
partial index — Postgres handles that as a delete from the index, not as
an error. The freed slot is available immediately to a concurrent
inserter. Whether that is the behaviour your product wants is a real
question; here it is exactly right.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Try to write the trigger version and find the race yourself. `IF (SELECT
count(*) FROM bookings WHERE patient_ref = NEW.patient_ref AND status =
'held') > 0 THEN RAISE ...` — now imagine two transactions running it
simultaneously. Neither sees the other's uncommitted row, both pass, both
commit. The only fix is an explicit lock on something, which is what the
index does for free.

## Hint 2

Confirm the index is partial and not accidentally total:

```sql
SELECT indexname, indexdef FROM pg_indexes
WHERE tablename = 'bookings';
```

The definition should end in `WHERE (status = 'held'::text)`. If the
`WHERE` is missing you have forbidden repeat customers, and the gate's
second probe will tell you so.

## Hint 3

Note what you *cannot* do with a partial unique index, so the trade is
conscious: it is not in `pg_constraint`, so tools that enumerate
constraints will not see it; it cannot be deferred; and no foreign key can
reference it, because `REFERENCES` requires a real unique constraint. When
a child table needs to point at "the active row", that last limitation is
the one that bites, and the answer is usually to reference the real
primary key instead.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e03_constraints_as_documentation/ex3 — one hold per patient, and only holds
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX bookings_one_hold_per_patient
  ON bookings (patient_ref)
  WHERE status = 'held';

UPDATE bookings
SET status = 'confirmed'
WHERE patient_ref = 'P-0042' AND status = 'held';

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the NULLs your unique constraint is letting through

```sql
practitioners(prac_id bigint PK, clinic_id bigint NOT NULL,
              full_name text NOT NULL, licence_no text)
```

`licence_no` is nullable because trainees have not been licensed yet.
Somebody adds `UNIQUE (licence_no)` and reports that licence numbers are
now guaranteed unique. They are — and the table also contains 300 rows
with a NULL licence, all of them accepted, because **NULLs are distinct
from each other by default** and a unique index treats every NULL as its
own value.

That default is correct here: unlicensed trainees are not duplicates of
each other.

Now add a second column where the default is wrong. The clinic group is
integrating with a national registry, and each practitioner gets an
optional `registry_id text`. The registry's rule is that a practitioner
either has an id or is not registered — and **at most one row may be
unregistered per clinic**, because that slot represents the clinic's own
locum pool entry.

In one script:
