1. Add `CONSTRAINT prac_licence_key UNIQUE (licence_no)` — the ordinary
   kind, NULLs distinct, many trainees allowed.
2. Add column `registry_id text`.
3. Add `CONSTRAINT prac_registry_key UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT
   (clinic_id, registry_id)` — the PG15 form, which treats NULLs as equal
   so that a second NULL `registry_id` in the same clinic is rejected.

The gate inserts two NULL-licence practitioners (must succeed), then two
NULL-registry practitioners in the same clinic (the second must fail
naming `prac_registry_key`), then two NULL-registry practitioners in
*different* clinics (must succeed, because the constraint is composite).

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e03_constraints_as_documentation ex4`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two unique constraints that differ by one clause. The exercise is really
asking you to notice that "unique" has two meanings when NULLs are
involved, and to pick deliberately each time.

## Hint 2

```sql
ALTER TABLE t ADD CONSTRAINT t_key UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (a, b);
```

The `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` goes between `UNIQUE` and the column list.
Postgres 15 and later; on 14 you would emulate it with a unique index on
`coalesce(b, '')`, with all the type-punning that implies.

## Hint 3

The composite matters. `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (clinic_id,
registry_id)` allows one NULL-registry row *per clinic*, because two rows
with different `clinic_id` differ in the first column and never compare
their NULLs at all. Dropping `clinic_id` from the constraint would allow
one unregistered practitioner in the entire group — a rule nobody asked
for.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the incident report. "We added a unique constraint on
`external_id` and we still have 4,000 duplicate customers." The
duplicates all have NULL `external_id`; the constraint did exactly what
the standard says and nothing anybody expected. Every schema with a
nullable unique column has this question in it, answered by default.

## Hint 2

See the two behaviours side by side in a throwaway transaction:

```sql
BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE a (x int UNIQUE);
INSERT INTO a VALUES (NULL), (NULL);            -- 2 rows, fine
CREATE TEMP TABLE b (x int UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT);
INSERT INTO b VALUES (NULL);
INSERT INTO b VALUES (NULL);                    -- ERROR
ROLLBACK;
```

Thirty seconds, and the rule is yours permanently.

## Hint 3

Ask which one you actually want more often. In practice, "NULL means not
applicable, and several rows can be not-applicable" is the common case, so
the default is right most of the time — which is exactly why the rare case
is dangerous. A good habit: whenever you write `UNIQUE` on a nullable
column, add a comment saying how many NULLs you intend to allow. If you
cannot answer, the column probably should not be nullable.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — the four actions, side by side

A foreign key's `ON DELETE` clause is a sentence about the relationship,
and there are four of them. Build one child table per action so the
differences are visible in one place.

Create, referencing `bookings(booking_id)` unless stated:

```sql
bk_notes (note_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
          booking_id bigint NOT NULL
            REFERENCES bookings(booking_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
          body text NOT NULL)

bk_payments (payment_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
             booking_id bigint NOT NULL
               REFERENCES bookings(booking_id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
             amount numeric(10,2) NOT NULL)

bk_followups (followup_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
              booking_id bigint
                REFERENCES bookings(booking_id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
              due_on date NOT NULL)

bk_assignments (assign_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
                prac_id bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
                  REFERENCES practitioners(prac_id) ON DELETE SET DEFAULT,
                shift date NOT NULL)
```

`bk_followups.booking_id` must be **nullable** — `SET NULL` on a `NOT
NULL` column raises at delete time, not at definition time, which is a
lovely trap. And `SET DEFAULT` needs its default to be a real parent row,
so before creating `bk_assignments`, insert a practitioner with
`prac_id = 0` named `'Unassigned'` in clinic 1, using `OVERRIDING SYSTEM
VALUE` because `prac_id` is an identity column.

Then seed one row in each child, all pointing at booking 1 (and
practitioner 1 for assignments).

The gate deletes booking 1 and checks: the note is gone, the delete is
*refused* while the payment exists, the followup's `booking_id` becomes
NULL, and deleting practitioner 1 moves the assignment to practitioner 0.

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e03_constraints_as_documentation ex5`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four tables, one insert of a sentinel parent, four seed rows. The two
things that can go wrong are both about the column definition rather than
the action: `SET NULL` needs a nullable column, `SET DEFAULT` needs a
default that satisfies the reference.

## Hint 2

The sentinel parent, into an identity column:

```sql
INSERT INTO practitioners (prac_id, clinic_id, full_name)
OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE
VALUES (0, 1, 'Unassigned');
```

V3·E2's clause, earning its keep in a different context.

## Hint 3

Order the statements so the sentinel exists before `bk_assignments` is
created — the foreign key does not check defaults at creation time, so it
would succeed either way, but the delete would fail later with a confusing
message about a violation in a table you were not deleting from. Creating
the sentinel first also documents its purpose to the next reader.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

For each of the four, say the sentence out loud before you write the
clause. A note has no meaning without its booking — cascade. A payment is
a financial record and must outlive any deletion attempt — restrict. A
followup can survive its booking being removed, with the link lost — set
null. A shift assignment must always have somebody, so it falls back to
the unassigned pool — set default. If a sentence sounds wrong, the action
is wrong.

## Hint 2

Provoke each behaviour by hand in a transaction you roll back:

```sql
BEGIN;
DELETE FROM bookings WHERE booking_id = 1;
-- ERROR: update or delete on table "bookings" violates foreign key
--        constraint "bk_payments_booking_id_fkey" on table "bk_payments"
ROLLBACK;
```

Then delete the payment first and try again. Watching `RESTRICT` block and
then release is worth more than reading about it.

## Hint 3

Two subtleties. `NO ACTION` is the default and behaves like `RESTRICT`
with one difference: it is deferrable, so the check can be postponed to
commit, which lets a transaction delete a parent and reparent the children
in either order. And `CASCADE` is dangerous in exactly one place — any
table you are legally required to keep. A cascade from `bookings` into an
audit log is not a schema decision, it is a compliance incident, and
V3·E4 will make the audit table refuse to be deleted from at all.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — a composite reference, and the NULL that disables it

Your ex1 script runs automatically first, so `rooms_clinic_code_key` —
`UNIQUE (clinic_id, code)` — exists and can be referenced.

Equipment is loaned between clinics and is sometimes stored in a specific
room, sometimes just "somewhere at clinic 3", sometimes nowhere yet.

Create:

```sql
equipment (
  equip_id  bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  asset_tag text NOT NULL,
  clinic_id bigint,
  room_code text,
  CONSTRAINT equipment_room_fk
    FOREIGN KEY (clinic_id, room_code)
    REFERENCES rooms (clinic_id, code) MATCH FULL)
```

`MATCH FULL` is the whole exercise. With the default `MATCH SIMPLE`, a row
with `clinic_id = 3` and `room_code = NULL` passes the constraint *without
any lookup at all* — one NULL in the key switches the check off. That
permits `(clinic_id = 999, room_code = NULL)`, referencing a clinic that
does not exist, which is exactly the half-correct data a composite
optional reference is prone to.

With `MATCH FULL`, either both columns are NULL (the item is unplaced) or
both are filled and must resolve to a real room.

Seed three rows: `('EQ-1', 1, 'A1')` — a real room; `('EQ-2', NULL,
NULL)` — unplaced; and nothing else.

The gate then attempts `('EQ-3', 3, NULL)` and `('EQ-4', NULL, 'A1')` and
expects both to be **rejected** by `equipment_room_fk`, and attempts
`('EQ-5', 1, 'ZZ')` expecting rejection too.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e03_constraints_as_documentation ex6`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One `CREATE TABLE` with a table-level foreign key, plus two inserts. The
foreign key must be table-level rather than column-level, because it spans
two columns.

## Hint 2

```sql
CONSTRAINT t_parent_fk FOREIGN KEY (a, b)
  REFERENCES parent (a, b) MATCH FULL
```

The referenced column list must be covered by a unique constraint or
unique index on the parent — which is why ex1's `rooms_clinic_code_key`
had to exist before this exercise could.

## Hint 3

Notice the column order in the reference: `(clinic_id, room_code)` maps to
`(clinic_id, code)` positionally, not by name. Swapping them compiles
happily — both are the same pair of types — and produces a constraint that
matches room codes against clinic ids. This is a genuine production bug
class, and the only defence is reading the two lists side by side.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enumerate the four states of a two-column optional reference before
choosing a match type: both NULL, both filled, first filled, second
filled. Decide which of the four are legal. If the answer is "both NULL or
both filled", that is `MATCH FULL` by definition. If the answer is "any of
them", you probably have two independent columns, not a composite
reference.

## Hint 2

Demonstrate the hole `MATCH SIMPLE` leaves, in a temp table you throw
away:

```sql
BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE e2 (clinic_id bigint, room_code text,
  FOREIGN KEY (clinic_id, room_code) REFERENCES rooms (clinic_id, code));
INSERT INTO e2 VALUES (999, NULL);   -- accepted. clinic 999 does not exist.
ROLLBACK;
```

That insert succeeding is the entire argument for `MATCH FULL`.

## Hint 3

There is a third option the standard defines and Postgres does not
implement: `MATCH PARTIAL`, which would check the non-NULL columns and
require at least one match. Nobody misses it, and knowing it is absent
saves you an afternoon reading the standard. Note also that if the
reference is *mandatory*, `NOT NULL` on both columns makes the match type
irrelevant — the simplest fix is often to forbid the ambiguous states
outright.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e03_constraints_as_documentation/ex6 — composite FK with MATCH FULL
CREATE TABLE equipment (
  equip_id  bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  asset_tag text NOT NULL,
  clinic_id bigint,
  room_code text,
  CONSTRAINT equipment_room_fk
    FOREIGN KEY (clinic_id, room_code)
    REFERENCES rooms (clinic_id, code) MATCH FULL
);

INSERT INTO equipment (asset_tag, clinic_id, room_code)
VALUES ('EQ-1', 1, 'A1'),
       ('EQ-2', NULL, NULL);

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — no two bookings in the same room at the same time

This is the rule the business exists to honour, and the schema currently
says nothing about it. Two confirmed bookings can occupy room 4 from 10:00
to 11:00 and nothing objects.

The naive fix is a `BEFORE INSERT` trigger that queries for overlaps. It
races — two concurrent inserts each find no conflict, both commit, both
patients arrive. Making it correct requires locking the room row by hand,
which serialises every booking in the clinic.

Postgres has the right tool. In one script:

1. `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;` — needed because you are
   mixing `=` on a `bigint` with `&&` on a range, and plain GiST has no
   operator class for `bigint` equality.

2. Add a generated range column so the constraint has something to index:

```sql
ALTER TABLE bookings ADD COLUMN during tstzrange
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (tstzrange(starts_at, ends_at, '[)')) STORED;
```

   The `'[)'` bounds are load-bearing: half-open means a booking ending at
   10:00 and one starting at 10:00 do **not** overlap, which is what
   back-to-back appointments require. `'[]'` would make consecutive
   bookings illegal.

3. Add the constraint:

```sql
ALTER TABLE bookings ADD CONSTRAINT bookings_no_overlap
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)
  WHERE (status <> 'cancelled');
```

   Read it as a sentence: no two non-cancelled bookings share a room and
   overlap in time. The `WHERE` clause makes it a partial exclusion
   constraint, so a cancelled booking stops blocking its slot — which is
   the behaviour every scheduler needs and the reason the naive trigger
   version grows a `status` check nobody remembers.

The seeded data contains no overlaps, so the constraint builds cleanly.
The gate inserts an overlapping confirmed booking (must fail naming
`bookings_no_overlap`), a back-to-back booking starting exactly when
another ends (must succeed), and an overlapping *cancelled* booking (must
succeed).

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e03_constraints_as_documentation ex7`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three statements, given almost verbatim in the prompt. Spend your effort
on understanding why each piece is there rather than on typing: the
extension, the range column, the operator pair, the partial predicate.

## Hint 2

The general form is worth recognising away from this example:

```sql
EXCLUDE USING gist (tenant_id WITH =, ip_range WITH &&)
EXCLUDE USING gist (shape WITH &&)
```

`UNIQUE (a, b)` is the special case where every operator is `=`. An
exclusion constraint is `UNIQUE` with the equality generalised.

## Hint 3

Decide for yourself whether `during` should be a generated column or an
ordinary one maintained by the application. Generated is right here: the
range is a function of two columns already present, so a plain column
could disagree with them, and a constraint enforcing a rule over a column
that can lie is not a constraint. The cost is the table rewrite when you
add it — fine at this size, and V3·E6's subject at any other.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the trigger you are replacing, at least in your head, and count its
defects. It must query for overlaps, handle `UPDATE` as well as `INSERT`,
exclude the row being updated from its own check, honour the cancelled
status, and take a lock strong enough to be correct under concurrency.
That is thirty lines and four bugs. The exclusion constraint is one
statement and the locking is the index's problem.

## Hint 2

Inspect what you built, because `EXCLUDE` produces both a constraint and
an index:

```sql
SELECT conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid)
FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'bookings'::regclass
  AND contype = 'x';

SELECT indexname, indexdef FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename = 'bookings';
```

The GiST index is the enforcement mechanism, and it is also usable for
range queries — `WHERE during && tstzrange(...)` can use it, so the
constraint pays for itself twice.

## Hint 3

Probe the boundary case yourself, because it is where scheduling systems
actually fail:

```sql
SELECT tstzrange('2026-03-01 09:00Z','2026-03-01 10:00Z','[)')
    && tstzrange('2026-03-01 10:00Z','2026-03-01 11:00Z','[)');  -- false
SELECT tstzrange('2026-03-01 09:00Z','2026-03-01 10:00Z','[]')
    && tstzrange('2026-03-01 10:00Z','2026-03-01 11:00Z','[]');  -- true
```

One character of bound notation decides whether your clinic can book
consecutive appointments. Half-open intervals are the right default for
every time range you will ever model, and this is the clearest possible
demonstration of why.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the swap that needs an invalid moment

`setup.sql` includes a table for the clinic's intake questionnaire:

```sql
form_sections (section_id bigint PK, form_id bigint NOT NULL,
               title text NOT NULL, position int NOT NULL)
```

Sections are ordered by `position`, and two sections of the same form must
not share a position — an obvious `UNIQUE (form_id, position)`.

Now the product team wants drag-and-drop reordering, and the simplest
operation is swapping two adjacent sections. With an immediate unique
constraint that is impossible in the natural way: whichever `UPDATE` runs
first creates a duplicate position, and the constraint fires at the end of
*that statement*, before the second update repairs it. The usual
workaround is a three-step dance through a sentinel value like `-1`, which
works and leaves your table briefly containing a position that means
nothing.

Do it properly:

1. Add `CONSTRAINT form_sections_pos_key UNIQUE (form_id, position)
   DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE`. Deferrable, but still checked per
   statement by default — so ordinary writers get immediate, precise
   errors.
2. In a single transaction, `SET CONSTRAINTS form_sections_pos_key
   DEFERRED`, then swap positions with two plain `UPDATE` statements, then
   `COMMIT`. Form 1's first two sections are `section_id = 11` (position
   1) and `section_id = 12` (position 2); key both updates on
   `section_id`, never on `position`.

Worth knowing before you start: in Postgres even a *single* `UPDATE`
performing the swap fails against an immediate unique constraint, because
uniqueness is enforced as each index entry is inserted rather than at the
end of the statement. Deferral is not a convenience for multi-statement
code; it is the only way to express this operation at all.

Between the two updates the table genuinely contains two rows at the same
position. That state is invalid and it is also unobservable to anyone
outside your transaction, which is precisely what "deferred" buys.

The gate checks the constraint exists with `condeferrable = true`,
`condeferred = false`, that the two sections have exchanged positions, and
that a plain duplicate insert **outside** a deferring transaction still
fails immediately.

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e03_constraints_as_documentation ex8`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`INITIALLY IMMEDIATE` plus `DEFERRABLE` is the combination worth
defaulting to: normal writes fail fast at the statement that caused them,
and the one transaction that needs an invalid intermediate state can ask
for it explicitly.

## Hint 2

```sql
BEGIN;
SET CONSTRAINTS my_key DEFERRED;
UPDATE t SET pos = 2 WHERE id = 10;
UPDATE t SET pos = 1 WHERE id = 11;
COMMIT;
```

`SET CONSTRAINTS` affects only the current transaction, and takes either a
constraint name list or `ALL`.

## Hint 3

Identify the two rows by something stable — their `section_id` — rather
than by their current position, because after the first `UPDATE` the
positions no longer identify what you thought. `UPDATE ... WHERE position
= 1` followed by `UPDATE ... WHERE position = 2` will happily move the
same row twice, which is a bug the constraint cannot catch because the
final state is perfectly unique.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Try the swap without deferral first and read the failure. It arrives on
the first `UPDATE`, complaining about a constraint your final state would
have satisfied — which is the definition of a constraint checked at the
wrong granularity. Then you understand what deferral is: not weaker
checking, but checking at the transaction boundary instead of the
statement boundary.

## Hint 2

Inspect the flags, because the two are independently meaningful:

```sql
SELECT conname, condeferrable, condeferred
FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname = 'form_sections_pos_key';
```

`condeferrable` says deferral is permitted. `condeferred` says it is the
default. The prompt wants `true, false` — permitted but not by default —
which is the combination that keeps error messages useful for everyone
who did not ask for deferral.

## Hint 3

Know what deferral costs before making it a habit. Each deferred check is
queued as an after-trigger event held until commit; a transaction updating
a million rows against a deferred constraint queues a million events, in
memory first and spilling to disk after. And when a deferred check fails,
the error arrives at `COMMIT` with no statement to blame — you get the
constraint name and nothing else. Both are strong arguments against `SET
CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED` as a default, and no argument at all against
using it for the two statements that need it.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — two tables that need each other

Every clinic has a designated lead practitioner, and every practitioner
belongs to a clinic. Written honestly, that is a cycle:

```sql
clinics.lead_prac_id  -> practitioners.prac_id
practitioners.clinic_id -> clinics.clinic_id
```

With both foreign keys immediate and both columns `NOT NULL`, opening a
new clinic is impossible: the clinic row needs a lead who needs a clinic.
Teams usually escape by making `lead_prac_id` nullable and filling it in a
second statement, which works and silently permits a clinic with no lead
forever.

Build the version that permits no such thing. In one script:

1. `ALTER TABLE clinics ADD COLUMN lead_prac_id bigint` and backfill it
   for the three seeded clinics: each clinic's lead is its
   **lowest-numbered practitioner**.
2. `ALTER TABLE clinics ALTER COLUMN lead_prac_id SET NOT NULL`.
3. Add `CONSTRAINT clinics_lead_fk FOREIGN KEY (lead_prac_id) REFERENCES
   practitioners(prac_id) DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED`. This one is
   `INITIALLY DEFERRED` — unlike ex8's — because *every* insert of a new
   clinic needs the deferral, not just an occasional swap. When the
   invalid intermediate state is the normal case, deferring by default is
   the honest declaration.
4. Add `CONSTRAINT prac_clinic_fk` on `practitioners.clinic_id`
   referencing `clinics(clinic_id)`, also `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED`.
   (`setup.sql` already created an immediate one named
   `practitioners_clinic_id_fkey`; drop it first.)
5. Prove the cycle can be entered: in one transaction, insert clinic 100
   (`'Northgate'`, timezone `'Europe/London'`) with `lead_prac_id = 500`,
   and practitioner 500 (`'Reed Okafor'`) with `clinic_id = 100`, then
   commit. Use `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE` for both ids.

The gate checks both constraints are deferrable-and-deferred, that clinic
100 and practitioner 500 exist and point at each other, and that inserting
a clinic whose lead never materialises **fails at commit**.

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e03_constraints_as_documentation challenge`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two halves. The first is ordinary add-backfill-constrain, in that order,
which V3·E1's review exercise drilled. The second is the cycle, and it
works because a deferred foreign key is not checked until commit — by
which time both rows exist.

## Hint 2

The backfill picks a minimum per group:

```sql
UPDATE clinics c SET lead_prac_id = (
  SELECT min(p.prac_id) FROM practitioners p WHERE p.clinic_id = c.clinic_id);
```

A correlated subquery is the clearest spelling when the update touches one
column per parent row.

## Hint 3

Replacing an existing immediate foreign key means `DROP CONSTRAINT` then
`ADD CONSTRAINT`; there is no `ALTER CONSTRAINT ... SET DEFERRABLE` for
foreign keys that changes the deferrability of an existing one in every
version, and the drop-and-add is clearer anyway. Note that dropping and
re-adding a foreign key on a populated table re-validates it — use `NOT
VALID` if that scan would matter, which here it does not.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Question the cycle before you build it. Circular mandatory references are
often a modelling smell: the alternative here is a separate
`clinic_leads(clinic_id PK, prac_id)` table, which expresses "a clinic has
at most one lead" without either table depending on the other. Build the
deferred version because the exercise asks, but be able to say which you
would choose and why — the join table is usually right, and the deferred
cycle is right when the lead is genuinely an attribute of the clinic that
must always exist.

## Hint 2

Watch the deferred failure, because it looks different from an immediate
one:

```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO clinics (clinic_id, name, timezone, lead_prac_id)
OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE VALUES (200, 'Ghost', 'UTC', 999);
COMMIT;
-- ERROR ... at COMMIT, naming clinics_lead_fk, with no statement to blame
```

The insert appeared to succeed. The transaction failed later. This is the
cost of deferral, and it is why `INITIALLY DEFERRED` is a decision rather
than a default.

## Hint 3

Push on what deferral does *not* give you. It does not make the
intermediate state visible to other sessions — it is invisible either way,
because uncommitted rows are invisible. It does not relax the rule; it
relocates the check. And it does not help with a cycle where one side is
enforced by a partial unique index rather than a constraint, because
indexes cannot be deferred at all. If you ever need "one lead per clinic"
as a partial index *and* deferral, you have to choose, and choosing is the
kind of trade this whole sector is about.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — make the schema describe itself

Your ex1 script runs automatically first.

Every constraint you have written this sector is a sentence, and Postgres
keeps them all in one catalog. A schema that can print its own rules is a
schema whose documentation cannot rot.

Two deliverables.

**1. The self-description.** Create a view `schema_rules` with columns
`table_name` (text), `constraint_name` (text), `kind` (text), and
`definition` (text), covering the tables `clinics`, `rooms`,
`practitioners` and `bookings`. `kind` maps `pg_constraint.contype` to a
readable word: `c` → `'check'`, `f` → `'foreign key'`, `p` → `'primary
key'`, `u` → `'unique'`, `x` → `'exclusion'`, anything else → `'other'`.
`definition` is `pg_get_constraintdef(oid)`. Order by `table_name`, then
`constraint_name`. Use `conrelid::regclass::text` for the table name and
filter with `conrelid = ANY (ARRAY['clinics','rooms','practitioners',
'bookings']::regclass[])`.

**2. The index a foreign key does not create.** `bk_notes` from ex5 is not
present here, but `bookings.room_id` is: it references `rooms(room_id)`,
and the child side has no index. Deleting a room therefore scans all
bookings to check the constraint. Create `bookings_room_id_idx` on
`bookings (room_id)`.

Then return, as the script's final statement, **one row** with two
columns: `constraint_count` = the number of rows in `schema_rules`, and
`unindexed_fks` = the number of foreign-key constraints on those four
tables whose **leading child column** has no index — which, after you
create `bookings_room_id_idx`, should be smaller than it was. Compute it
from `pg_constraint.conkey[1]` against `pg_index.indkey[0]` for indexes on
the same relation.

Edit `review1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e03_constraints_as_documentation review1`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`pg_constraint` has one row per constraint, `conrelid` pointing at the
table and `contype` a single character. Casting `conrelid` through
`regclass` turns an oid into a readable name, which is the trick that
makes catalog queries pleasant.

## Hint 2

The mapping is a `CASE`, and the definition is a function call:

```sql
SELECT conrelid::regclass::text AS table_name,
       conname AS constraint_name,
       CASE contype WHEN 'c' THEN 'check' WHEN 'f' THEN 'foreign key'
                    ELSE 'other' END AS kind,
       pg_get_constraintdef(oid) AS definition
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE conrelid = 'bookings'::regclass;
```

## Hint 3

For the unindexed-foreign-key count, `conkey` is a smallint array of the
child's column numbers and `indkey` is an `int2vector` of the index's
columns; `indkey[0]` is its leading column. A foreign key is "covered" if
some index on the same relation leads with `conkey[1]`. `NOT EXISTS`
against `pg_index` is the natural shape, and whether you also want to
exclude partial indexes is a judgement call worth making explicitly.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach the second deliverable as an operations task rather than a query
puzzle. The question "which of my foreign keys will make deletes slow?" is
one every production database should be able to answer about itself, and
this query is a version of it that people paste into monitoring. Write it
so you would trust the output.

## Hint 2

Feel the cost before fixing it:

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) DELETE FROM rooms WHERE room_id = 9999;
```

An id that matches nothing still runs the referential-integrity check
against `bookings`, and without the index that is a sequential scan. The
plan for the delete itself will not show it — the check runs in a trigger
— so look instead at the time, or set `auto_explain` if you want the
gory detail. Then create the index and rerun.

## Hint 3

Be precise about when the missing index does *not* matter. If the parent
table is never deleted from and its key is never updated, the child-side
index buys nothing for referential integrity, and adding it costs write
throughput on every insert. Reference data — clinics, currencies, statuses
— often falls in this category. The general rule is: index the child side
of every foreign key whose parent rows are ever deleted or re-keyed, and
be able to say which of your foreign keys those are.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e03_constraints_as_documentation/review1 — the schema, described by itself
CREATE VIEW schema_rules AS
SELECT c.conrelid::regclass::text AS table_name,
       c.conname                  AS constraint_name,
       CASE c.contype
         WHEN 'c' THEN 'check'
         WHEN 'f' THEN 'foreign key'
         WHEN 'p' THEN 'primary key'
         WHEN 'u' THEN 'unique'
         WHEN 'x' THEN 'exclusion'
         ELSE 'other'
       END                        AS kind,
       pg_get_constraintdef(c.oid) AS definition
FROM pg_constraint c
WHERE c.conrelid = ANY (ARRAY['clinics', 'rooms',
                              'practitioners', 'bookings']::regclass[])
ORDER BY table_name, constraint_name;

CREATE INDEX bookings_room_id_idx ON bookings (room_id);

SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM schema_rules) AS constraint_count,
       (SELECT count(*)
        FROM pg_constraint c
        WHERE c.contype = 'f'
          AND c.conrelid = ANY (ARRAY['clinics', 'rooms',
                                      'practitioners',
                                      'bookings']::regclass[])
          AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                          FROM pg_index i
                          WHERE i.indrelid = c.conrelid
                            AND i.indkey[0] = c.conkey[1])) AS unindexed_fks;

lessons.title: V3·E4 — Modelling state machines and audit trails
lessons.summary: A support-ticket workflow whose legal transitions are a table with a foreign key rather than a diagram in a slide deck, and whose event log is the truth the status column is derived from. Enum restrictions, jsonb diffing triggers, SET LOCAL for actor identity, and an audit table that refuses to be edited.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·E4 — Modelling state machines and audit trails

Almost every table in a business system has a `status` column, and almost
every one of them is a lie of omission. It records where the row is now.
It says nothing about how it got there, when it got there, who moved it,
or which moves were ever allowed — and every one of those questions gets
asked eventually, usually by someone with a legal interest in the answer.

This sector builds the honest version, in two halves. First, a state
machine whose legal transitions are *data* with a foreign key, so an
illegal move is a constraint violation rather than a missing `if`. Second,
an audit trail that records every change with its actor, cannot be edited
after the fact, and is cheap enough to leave on.

Both halves lean on things you already have. Lesson 23's transactions are
what make a state change atomic with the record of it. Lesson 25's
constraints are what make the rule enforceable rather than advisory.
V3·E3's partial unique index is what enforces "exactly one open row".

## The schema

`setup.sql` builds a support desk, in the state most codebases have it:

```sql
CREATE TABLE tickets (
  ticket_id  bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_ref text NOT NULL,
  subject    text NOT NULL,
  priority   text NOT NULL,          -- 'low','normal','high'
  status     text NOT NULL,          -- free text. anything goes.
  opened_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  closed_at  timestamptz);

CREATE TABLE ticket_events (
  event_id   bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  ticket_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES tickets(ticket_id),
  from_status text,                  -- NULL for the opening event
  to_status  text NOT NULL,
  actor      text NOT NULL,
  at         timestamptz NOT NULL);
```

3,000 tickets, 11,000 events. The events are there — somebody had the
instinct — but nothing connects them to the `status` column, nothing
stops an event recording a transition that the workflow forbids, and
`status` itself accepts any string at all.

The workflow, as described by the team who run it:

```
   open ──▶ triaged ──▶ in_progress ──▶ resolved ──▶ closed
     │          │             │             │
     └──────────┴─────────────┴─────────▶ cancelled
                              ▲
        in_progress ◀── resolved (reopened)
```

That diagram lives in a slide deck. Nothing in the database knows it, so
"a resolved ticket went straight back to open" is a thing that has
happened 40 times and nobody noticed.

## Three ways to constrain a status, and how to choose

**A `CHECK` with a list.** `CHECK (status IN ('open','triaged',...))`.
Simplest, and changing the set is a one-line migration that rewrites
nothing if you use `NOT VALID`. It cannot carry attributes — you cannot
ask "which statuses are terminal?" — and it does not compose into a
transitions table.

**A lookup table plus a foreign key.** `ticket_statuses(status PK,
is_terminal bool, sort_order int)`, referenced by `tickets.status`. Adding
a status is an `INSERT`. Statuses gain attributes, which is what lets you
write "close every ticket in a terminal state" as a join instead of as a
hard-coded list. This is the default choice and what ex1 builds.

**An enum type.** `CREATE TYPE ticket_status AS ENUM (...)`. Compact
storage, ordering for free, and genuine type safety — you cannot compare
it to an unrelated string by accident. The costs are real and
asymmetrical: `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` could not run inside a
transaction block at all before PG12 and still cannot be used in the same
transaction that then uses the new value; you cannot remove a value; and
reordering means recreating the type and every column that uses it. ex3
makes you meet all three, on `priority`, where an enum is a reasonable
choice because the set genuinely never changes.

## Transitions as data

The idea that makes the rest work:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticket_transitions (
  from_status text NOT NULL REFERENCES ticket_statuses(status),
  to_status   text NOT NULL REFERENCES ticket_statuses(status),
  PRIMARY KEY (from_status, to_status));
```

and then a composite foreign key from `ticket_events(from_status,
to_status)` to that table. Now an event recording `resolved → open` fails
with a foreign-key violation, because that pair is not in the table. The
diagram from the slide deck has become fifteen rows and a constraint, and
adding a transition is an `INSERT` a product manager could review.

The `tickets.status` column then stops being authoritative and becomes a
cache of "the `to_status` of the latest event", which ex4 derives and the
challenge maintains. Event-log-as-truth is the design that answers every
question the status column cannot.

## Audit trails that are worth having

An audit table is easy to write and easy to write uselessly. Three
properties separate the two:

- **It records the change, not the state.** `to_jsonb(NEW) - to_jsonb(OLD)`
  is a jsonb object of exactly the columns that changed. Storing whole row
  snapshots also works and costs more; storing "row 42 was updated" is
  worthless.
- **It knows who.** `current_user` is your connection's role, which in a
  pooled application is `app` for every request and tells you nothing.
  The application must pass the human's identity down, and the mechanism
  is `SET LOCAL app.user_id = '...'` read back by `current_setting(
  'app.user_id', true)`. `LOCAL` matters: without it the value survives
  into the next transaction on that pooled connection and attributes one
  user's changes to another.
- **It cannot be rewritten.** An audit table that the application role can
  `UPDATE` is a log, not an audit. Revoking the privilege is step one;
  a trigger that raises on `UPDATE` and `DELETE` is step two, because the
  table owner bypasses privileges.

ex6 through ex8 build exactly that, and the challenge welds the two halves
together: a trigger that consults the transitions table, refuses illegal
moves, writes the event, and handles two agents clicking at once.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - v3e04_state_machines_audit

Status columns forget. Event logs remember. Most of this sector is the
consequences of choosing which one is authoritative.

## Notes

**A status column is a cache of the last transition.** Once you accept
that sentence, the design follows: the events table is the source of
truth, `tickets.status` is a denormalization maintained by a trigger
(V3·E1's counter cache, with a different payload), and the reconciliation
query — does every ticket's status match its latest event? — is something
you can actually run.

**Legal transitions belong in a table, not in code.** The alternative
spellings are a `CASE` in application code (enforced by one writer), a
`CHECK` with a giant boolean expression (enforced always, unreadable, and
a migration to change), and a transitions table with a composite foreign
key (enforced always, readable, and an `INSERT` to change). The last one
also gives you the diagram back: `SELECT * FROM ticket_transitions` is the
state machine.

**Enums are a commitment.** `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` cannot be followed
by a use of the new value in the same transaction — the error is
`unsafe use of new value of enum type` — which means a migration tool that
wraps everything in one transaction cannot add an enum value and backfill
in one step. There is no `DROP VALUE` at all. Renaming is possible
(`ALTER TYPE ... RENAME VALUE`, PG10+); reordering is not, short of
creating a new type and rewriting every column. Choose an enum when the
value set is closed and old — `low/normal/high`, `debit/credit` — and a
lookup table when the business might add one.

**`DISTINCT ON` is the natural shape for "latest per group".** `SELECT
DISTINCT ON (ticket_id) ... ORDER BY ticket_id, at DESC, event_id DESC`.
The second tie-break matters: two events at the same timestamp are
common when a script writes them, and without a deterministic tie the
derived status flickers between runs.

**"Exactly one open row" is a partial unique index.** Assignments, holds,
shifts, tenancies — every one of them has an "and only one at a time"
rule, and every one of them is `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... WHERE released_at
IS NULL`. Writing it as a counting trigger races; writing it as an
application check races harder.

**`to_jsonb(NEW) - to_jsonb(OLD)` is not symmetric, and that is useful.**
The jsonb `-` operator with a jsonb operand removes matching key/value
pairs, so the result is the keys whose value changed *to* the new value.
Columns unchanged vanish. Columns added appear. For the old values you
compute the reverse difference, and storing both is what makes an audit
row answer "what did it used to say?".

**Row triggers see every row; statement triggers see none.** `FOR EACH
ROW` gives you `OLD` and `NEW` and fires once per row — the right choice
for auditing. `FOR EACH STATEMENT` fires once regardless and, since PG10,
can read transition tables (`REFERENCING OLD TABLE AS ...`), which is the
efficient way to audit bulk updates. Start with row-level; reach for
transition tables when a million-row update is spending its time in your
trigger.

**Actor identity travels in a GUC.** `SET LOCAL app.user_id = '...'` sets
a custom setting for the current transaction only; `current_setting(
'app.user_id', true)` reads it, returning NULL rather than erroring when
unset — the `true` is the "missing_ok" flag and forgetting it turns an
unaudited path into a hard failure. In a pooled connection, `SET` without
`LOCAL` is a data-integrity bug waiting for the next request.

**Append-only needs both privileges and a trigger.** `REVOKE UPDATE,
DELETE ON audit FROM app` stops the application. It does not stop the
table's owner, who is exempt from privilege checks on their own tables. A
`BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE ... FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION
raise_immutable()` stops everyone except someone who first drops the
trigger — which is a much louder act, and one that shows up in the audit
of your DDL.

**Concurrent transitions need a lock.** Two agents resolving the same
ticket simultaneously both read `in_progress`, both write `resolved`, and
you get two events for one move. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the ticket row
before deciding serialises them, and the second one then sees the state
its decision depends on. This is the classic lost-update problem, and a
state machine is where it hurts most.

## ex1

The lookup table and the foreign key. Note `is_terminal` — an attribute a
`CHECK` could never carry, and the reason lookup tables win by default.

## ex2

Transitions as rows. The composite foreign key from the event to the
transition pair is the whole idea, and the `NULL` opening event is the
edge case that makes you think about `MATCH SIMPLE` again.

## ex3

Enums, and their three restrictions. The migration is short; the
constraints on it are the lesson.

## ex4

Deriving the truth. `DISTINCT ON` with a deterministic tie-break, and a
reconciliation view that finds the tickets whose cached status lies.

## ex5

One open assignment per ticket, enforced by a partial unique index.

## ex6

The audit trigger and the jsonb diff. Note how little code it is once you
stop trying to enumerate columns.

## ex7

Actor identity through `SET LOCAL`, and the fallback when nobody set it.

## ex8

Append-only, by privilege and by trigger, because either alone is
incomplete.

## challenge

Everything at once: validate the transition against the table, write the
event, update the cache, take the lock.

## review1

Time spent in each state, out of the event log — the question a status
column can never answer.

## Further reading

- [`CREATE TRIGGER`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createtrigger.html) — row versus statement, `REFERENCING` transition tables.
- [Enumerated Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-enum.html) and [`ALTER TYPE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-altertype.html) — including the `ADD VALUE` transaction restriction.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) — `to_jsonb`, the `-` operator, `jsonb_object_keys`.
- [`SET`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-set.html) and [`current_setting`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-admin.html) — custom GUCs and the missing_ok flag.
- [Explicit Locking](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/explicit-locking.html) — `FOR UPDATE` and why a state machine needs it.

# V3·E4 — State machines and audit trails (archive)

The reference build: a workflow the database understands, and a record of
changes that survives the people who made them.

## Statuses: the three encodings

```sql
-- 1. check constraint: simplest, carries no attributes
ALTER TABLE tickets ADD CONSTRAINT tickets_status_known
  CHECK (status IN ('open','triaged','in_progress','resolved',
                    'closed','cancelled'));

-- 2. lookup table: the default. statuses become rows with properties.
CREATE TABLE ticket_statuses (
  status      text PRIMARY KEY,
  is_terminal boolean NOT NULL,
  sort_order  int NOT NULL);
ALTER TABLE tickets
  ADD CONSTRAINT tickets_status_fk
  FOREIGN KEY (status) REFERENCES ticket_statuses(status);

-- 3. enum: compact, ordered, closed
CREATE TYPE ticket_priority AS ENUM ('low','normal','high');
```

Choose the lookup table unless you have a reason. The reason for an enum
is a value set that is genuinely closed and small, where the ordering is
semantic (`low < normal < high` for free) and the storage saving over
`text` matters. The reason for a bare `CHECK` is a table so small and a
set so stable that a lookup table would be ceremony.

The enum restrictions, all three of which bite in practice:

```sql
ALTER TYPE ticket_priority ADD VALUE 'urgent';       -- fine, on its own
BEGIN;
  ALTER TYPE ticket_priority ADD VALUE 'urgent';
  UPDATE tickets SET priority = 'urgent' WHERE ...;  -- ERROR
COMMIT;
```

`unsafe use of new value of enum type` — the value is not usable until the
transaction that added it commits. There is no `DROP VALUE`. Reordering
requires building a new type, `ALTER TABLE ... TYPE ... USING`, and
dropping the old one, which rewrites every table that uses it.

## Transitions as a table

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticket_transitions (
  from_status text NOT NULL REFERENCES ticket_statuses(status),
  to_status   text NOT NULL REFERENCES ticket_statuses(status),
  PRIMARY KEY (from_status, to_status));

ALTER TABLE ticket_events
  ADD CONSTRAINT ticket_events_transition_fk
  FOREIGN KEY (from_status, to_status)
  REFERENCES ticket_transitions (from_status, to_status);
```

The opening event has `from_status IS NULL`, and under the default `MATCH
SIMPLE` a NULL in the key skips the check entirely — which is exactly what
you want here, and is the one time V3·E3's warning inverts. If you would
rather be explicit, add a `'new'` pseudo-status and make every transition
non-NULL; both designs are defensible and the second is easier to explain.

## Deriving state from the log

```sql
CREATE VIEW ticket_derived_status AS
SELECT DISTINCT ON (ticket_id)
       ticket_id, to_status AS status, at AS since, actor
FROM ticket_events
ORDER BY ticket_id, at DESC, event_id DESC;
```

The `event_id DESC` tie-break is not optional: events written by a batch
share a timestamp, and without it the derived status is non-deterministic
between runs — a bug that appears as "the dashboard disagrees with itself
on refresh".

Then the reconciliation, which is the query that proves the cache honest:

```sql
SELECT t.ticket_id, t.status AS cached, d.status AS derived
FROM tickets t JOIN ticket_derived_status d USING (ticket_id)
WHERE t.status IS DISTINCT FROM d.status;
```

## The audit trigger

```sql
CREATE TABLE ticket_audit (
  audit_id  bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  ticket_id bigint NOT NULL,
  op        text   NOT NULL,
  changed   jsonb  NOT NULL,   -- new values of changed columns
  previous  jsonb  NOT NULL,   -- old values of the same columns
  actor     text   NOT NULL,
  at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now());

CREATE FUNCTION ticket_audit_fn() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  who text := coalesce(current_setting('app.user_id', true), session_user);
BEGIN
  IF TG_OP = 'UPDATE' THEN
    INSERT INTO ticket_audit (ticket_id, op, changed, previous, actor)
    VALUES (NEW.ticket_id, 'UPDATE',
            to_jsonb(NEW) - to_jsonb(OLD),
            to_jsonb(OLD) - to_jsonb(NEW),
            who);
  END IF;
  RETURN NULL;
END $$;
```

The diff is the whole trick, and it is worth stating on its own:

```sql
to_jsonb(NEW) - to_jsonb(OLD)   -- new values of changed columns
to_jsonb(OLD) - to_jsonb(NEW)   -- old values of the same columns
```

The `jsonb - jsonb` operator removes pairs present in the right operand,
so unchanged columns disappear from both sides and you are left with
precisely the delta. No column list, no maintenance when the table gains a
column, and a row that is readable a year later.

## Who did it

```sql
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL app.user_id = 'agent:ines';
UPDATE tickets SET status = 'resolved' WHERE ticket_id = 7;
COMMIT;
```

`LOCAL` scopes it to the transaction. Without `LOCAL`, in a pooled
connection, the value persists into whatever request gets that connection
next — and the audit trail then confidently attributes one user's actions
to another, which is worse than no audit trail at all.

`current_setting('app.user_id', true)` returns NULL when unset; the second
argument is `missing_ok` and omitting it raises. Wrap it in `coalesce(...,
session_user)` so an unaudited code path produces a weak attribution
instead of a failed write — or deliberately do not, if you would rather
such a path fail loudly. Both are defensible; choose on purpose.

## Append-only

```sql
REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON ticket_audit FROM PUBLIC, app_role;

CREATE FUNCTION audit_immutable() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  RAISE EXCEPTION 'ticket_audit is append-only (attempted %)', TG_OP;
END $$;

CREATE TRIGGER ticket_audit_immutable
BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE ON ticket_audit
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_immutable();
```

Both are needed. Privileges stop the application role; the trigger stops
the table owner and anyone who inherits its rights, because owners bypass
privilege checks on their own objects. Neither stops a superuser who drops
the trigger, and nothing can — the goal is to make tampering require a
loud, separately-audited act.

## Common mistakes

- **Status column with no constraint at all.** `'Resolved '` with a
  trailing space is a different status forever.
- **Transitions enforced only in application code.** The batch job does
  not run your controller.
- **Enum chosen for a set the product owner will extend.** Every addition
  is now a migration that cannot be done in one transaction.
- **`DISTINCT ON` with no tie-break past the timestamp.** Non-deterministic
  results, discovered as flapping dashboards.
- **Auditing whole-row snapshots.** Correct, and ten times the storage;
  the diff is what anyone reads.
- **`current_user` as the actor.** In a pooled app it is one value for
  everyone.
- **`SET` instead of `SET LOCAL`.** Identity leaks across requests.
- **Audit table the app can update.** It is a log with extra steps.
- **No `FOR UPDATE` before a transition decision.** Two agents, one move,
  two events.

## Interview answer

*"How would you model an order/ticket/claim workflow?"*

Say that the status column is a cache and the event log is the truth, then
justify it in one sentence: every question anyone asks later — how long
did this take, who approved it, was that move allowed — is answerable from
the log and unanswerable from the column.

Then give the enforcement mechanism, because that is what separates
answers: legal transitions in a table, a composite foreign key from the
event to that table, so an illegal move is a constraint violation rather
than a code review comment. Mention that this makes the state machine
inspectable — a product manager can read `SELECT * FROM
ticket_transitions` — which is the practical reason it survives.

Close with the two operational details that show experience: `SELECT ...
FOR UPDATE` on the entity before deciding, because two agents will click
at once; and `SET LOCAL` rather than `SET` for the actor, because
connection pools.

## Check yourself

1. Give one thing a status lookup table can express that a `CHECK`
   constraint cannot.
2. Why can you not `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` and use the new value in the
   same transaction?
3. Which enum operations are impossible, and what is the workaround?
4. Write "the latest event per ticket" with a deterministic tie-break, and
   say what breaks without one.
5. What does the composite foreign key on `(from_status, to_status)`
   enforce, and what does a NULL `from_status` do to it?
6. Express "at most one open assignment per ticket" as a schema object.
7. What exactly does `to_jsonb(NEW) - to_jsonb(OLD)` return?
8. Why is `current_user` insufficient as an audit actor in a pooled
   application?
9. What is the difference between `SET` and `SET LOCAL`, and which bug
   does the wrong one cause?
10. Why does revoking `UPDATE` not make an audit table append-only?
11. Describe the lost-update scenario for two agents resolving one ticket,
    and the one-line fix.
12. When would you use a statement-level trigger with a transition table
    instead of a row trigger?
13. How do you find tickets whose cached status disagrees with the log?
14. What can the event log tell you that a `status` plus `updated_at`
    cannot?

# The long read — the column that forgets

Consider a support ticket that was resolved, reopened, escalated, and
resolved again. Its `status` column says `resolved`. Its `updated_at`
says Tuesday. Every other fact about its life — that it was reopened at
all, that the reopening was the customer's second complaint, that the
escalation happened four minutes before the SLA expired — is gone, and it
was gone the instant the second `UPDATE` overwrote the first. No error was
raised. The data was not corrupted. It was simply never recorded, because
a status column is a variable and variables do not remember their history.

This is the deepest reason to model workflows as event logs, and it has
nothing to do with auditing regulations. It is that the questions people
ask about a process are almost always questions about *transitions*, and a
schema that stores only states cannot answer them at any price.

## How Postgres implements the pieces

**Triggers are functions attached to the storage path.** A `FOR EACH ROW`
trigger fires inside the same transaction as the statement that caused it,
sees `OLD` and `NEW` as `record` values, and can abort the write by
raising. Because it runs in the transaction, an audit row written by a
trigger commits atomically with the change it describes — you cannot have
one without the other, which is a guarantee an application-level audit
write cannot make.

The cost is per row. A million-row `UPDATE` fires the trigger a million
times, each firing a plpgsql function call with its own snapshot of `OLD`
and `NEW`, and the wall-clock difference between a table with and without
an audit trigger on a bulk load is routinely 3-5x. This is why PG10's
transition tables exist: `CREATE TRIGGER ... AFTER UPDATE ... REFERENCING
OLD TABLE AS old NEW TABLE AS new FOR EACH STATEMENT` gives a statement
trigger set-based access to every affected row, so the audit becomes one
`INSERT ... SELECT` instead of a million calls.

**jsonb makes generic auditing possible.** Before `to_jsonb(record)`, an
audit trigger had to name every column, which meant that every schema
change required a trigger change, which meant that trigger drifted. The
row-to-jsonb conversion plus the `-` operator turns the whole problem into
two expressions that are correct for any table, forever. It is the single
biggest practical improvement to audit trails in the last decade and it
arrived as a side effect of a JSON feature.

The `jsonb - jsonb` operator deletes matching key/value pairs from the
left operand. `to_jsonb(NEW) - to_jsonb(OLD)` therefore keeps exactly
those keys whose values differ, holding the *new* values. The reverse gives
the old ones. Note the asymmetry when a column goes NULL — the key remains
present with a `null` value in both directions, which is correct and
occasionally surprising.

**GUCs as a request context.** Postgres lets you set arbitrary namespaced
settings (`app.user_id`, `app.request_id`) and read them back with
`current_setting`. They cost nothing, they are per-session or
per-transaction, and they are the standard way to carry application
context into a trigger or a row-level security policy. The `SET LOCAL`
distinction is the whole game in a pooled world: `SET` lasts until the
session ends, and a session in a pool is shared by every user in turn.

## History and alternatives

Audit-by-trigger is old, and the alternatives are worth knowing so you can
say why you did not choose them.

**Logical decoding / CDC.** Postgres can stream its write-ahead log to a
consumer (`pgoutput`, Debezium). This captures every change with zero
trigger overhead and no schema changes at all, and it is the right answer
when the audit consumer is another system — a warehouse, a search index,
an event bus. It is the wrong answer when the audit must be transactional
with the change and queryable in the same database, because the stream is
asynchronous and can lag or be lost.

**`pgaudit`.** An extension that logs statements to the server log,
including who ran them. Excellent for "who ran DDL" and compliance
statement logging; useless for "what did this row look like last March",
because it records statements rather than row versions.

**Temporal tables.** The SQL:2011 approach, where the database itself
keeps old row versions with validity periods. Postgres has no built-in
support; extensions and hand-rolled history tables fill the gap, and
V3·E5 builds one. Temporal tables answer "what did the row look like at
time T"; an event log answers "what happened and who did it". They are
complementary, and a system with strict requirements often has both.

## Why the transitions table beats the alternatives

There are four places the rule "a resolved ticket may not go back to open"
can live, and they differ in exactly one property: how many writers obey
it.

**In a code review comment.** Zero writers. This is more common than it
sounds — the rule exists as tribal knowledge, and the first violation is
found by a customer.

**In application code.** One writer per implementation. The API obeys it;
the nightly reconciliation script written by the data team does not,
because it writes with `psql` and a `COPY`. Every system accumulates these
side doors, and the rule was never installed on them.

**In a `CHECK` constraint.** Every writer, and unreadable. The expression
becomes a fifteen-clause boolean over `from_status` and `to_status`, and
changing one transition means a migration and a code review nobody can
usefully perform, because reviewing a boolean expression against a diagram
is a task humans are bad at.

**In a transitions table with a composite foreign key.** Every writer, and
readable. `SELECT * FROM ticket_transitions ORDER BY from_status` *is* the
diagram, in a form a product manager can check. Adding a transition is an
`INSERT`; removing one is a `DELETE` that fails if history depends on it,
which is the constraint telling you something true.

The fourth option also composes in a way the others do not. Attach columns
to the transitions table — `requires_role`, `notifies_customer`,
`sla_hours` — and the workflow engine becomes a join rather than a switch
statement. That is the point at which people stop reaching for a separate
workflow product, and it is available because the state machine was
modelled as data from the beginning.

## Performance, honestly

An audit trigger roughly doubles the write cost of a row: one heap insert
into the audit table, plus its index maintenance, plus the function call.
On an OLTP table doing a few hundred writes a second this is invisible. On
a table doing fifty thousand, it is the dominant cost and you should be
looking at logical decoding instead.

The audit table also grows without limit, and it grows faster than the
table it audits — every update adds a row, and rows are never removed. Two
mitigations, both of which V3·E7 makes concrete: partition it by month so
that retention is `DROP TABLE` rather than `DELETE`, and index it
narrowly — `(ticket_id, at DESC)` serves "history of this entity" and is
usually the only access pattern that exists. Resist indexing the jsonb
column with GIN unless someone actually queries it; that index will be
larger than the data.

The state-machine side has a subtler cost: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` before
each transition serialises all activity on one entity. That is correct and
almost always fine, because contention is per-ticket. It stops being fine
when the entity is a queue that everyone touches, at which point you want
`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and a different design.

## When not to do this

**When there is genuinely one transition.** A row that goes `pending →
done` and never moves again does not need a transitions table, an event
log, or a trigger. It needs a nullable `completed_at`. Building a state
machine for a boolean is the most common overreach in this area.

**When the workflow is still being designed.** A transitions table you
edit every week is worse than a `CHECK` you edit every week, because it
looks authoritative. Wait until the diagram stops moving.

**When the audit consumer is external.** If the only reader of your audit
data is a warehouse, put the effort into CDC and skip the triggers.

**When the entity is high-volume and low-value.** Auditing every row of a
telemetry table is a storage decision disguised as a compliance one. Audit
the things people argue about — money, permissions, state changes with
legal meaning — and let the rest be data.

The line to hold: model the *process* when the process is a real thing
that people ask questions about, and resist modelling it when the answer
to every question is "it happened, once, and then it was done".

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — statuses as rows, not as a string

```sql
tickets(ticket_id bigint PK, customer_ref text, subject text,
        priority text, status text NOT NULL,
        opened_at timestamptz, closed_at timestamptz)   -- 3,000 rows
```

`status` is free text. The data happens to contain only the six real
values, but nothing says so, and a trailing space would create a seventh
forever.

Build the lookup table instead of a `CHECK`, because statuses have
properties that a list of strings cannot carry:

```sql
ticket_statuses (status      text PRIMARY KEY,
                 is_terminal boolean NOT NULL,
                 sort_order  int     NOT NULL)
```

Seed it, in `sort_order` 1..6:

| status | is_terminal | sort_order |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `open` | false | 1 |
| `triaged` | false | 2 |
| `in_progress` | false | 3 |
| `resolved` | false | 4 |
| `closed` | true | 5 |
| `cancelled` | true | 6 |

Then add `CONSTRAINT tickets_status_fk` on `tickets.status` referencing
it, with `ON UPDATE CASCADE` — status names are a natural key, and if
`in_progress` is ever renamed you want the tickets to follow rather than
the rename to be impossible. That is V3·E2's cascade cost, accepted
deliberately because the child count is small and renames are rare.

Finish with a statement that proves the attribute earns its keep: `UPDATE`
every ticket whose status is terminal and whose `closed_at` is NULL, to
set `closed_at = opened_at + interval '1 day'`. Write the "is terminal"
part as a **join to `ticket_statuses`**, not as a hard-coded list —
that is the whole reason the column exists.

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e04_state_machines_audit ex1`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Create, seed, constrain, use — in that order. The foreign key cannot be
added before the parent rows exist, and the final `UPDATE` is what
demonstrates why you built a table rather than a `CHECK`.

## Hint 2

An update driven by a join to the lookup:

```sql
UPDATE tickets t
SET closed_at = t.opened_at + interval '1 day'
FROM ticket_statuses s
WHERE s.status = t.status AND s.is_terminal AND t.closed_at IS NULL;
```

`UPDATE ... FROM` is the Postgres spelling; the joined table goes in
`FROM` and the join condition in `WHERE`.

## Hint 3

Note what the `ON UPDATE CASCADE` is and is not for. It handles a rename
of a status. It does nothing about deleting a status that is still in use
— that is `ON DELETE`, unspecified here, so you get `NO ACTION`, which
refuses. Refusing is right: a status with tickets on it must not vanish,
and being unable to delete it is the constraint telling you to migrate the
tickets first.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what question the lookup table lets you answer that a `CHECK` would
not. "How many tickets are in a non-terminal state?" is a join. "Show
statuses in workflow order" is an `ORDER BY sort_order`. "Which statuses
have no tickets?" is a `LEFT JOIN`. None of those exist if the set of
statuses is a string inside a constraint expression.

## Hint 2

Before adding the foreign key, check the data will accept it — the habit
from V3·E1:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT t.status
FROM tickets t
LEFT JOIN ticket_statuses s ON s.status = t.status
WHERE s.status IS NULL;
```

Zero rows means the constraint will build. Non-zero means you found a
trailing space, and you found it before the migration did.

## Hint 3

Consider the counter-argument honestly. A lookup table costs a join on
every read that wants the attributes, an extra table in every schema
diagram, and a foreign-key check on every ticket write. For a two-value
status on a table with a thousand rows, a `CHECK` is the better
engineering. The lookup wins here because there are six statuses with
properties and a transitions table about to reference them — and it is
that second reason, not the first, that usually decides.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e04_state_machines_audit/ex1 — statuses as a lookup table
CREATE TABLE ticket_statuses (
  status      text PRIMARY KEY,
  is_terminal boolean NOT NULL,
  sort_order  int     NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO ticket_statuses (status, is_terminal, sort_order) VALUES
  ('open',        false, 1),
  ('triaged',     false, 2),
  ('in_progress', false, 3),
  ('resolved',    false, 4),
  ('closed',      true,  5),
  ('cancelled',   true,  6);

ALTER TABLE tickets
  ADD CONSTRAINT tickets_status_fk FOREIGN KEY (status)
  REFERENCES ticket_statuses(status) ON UPDATE CASCADE;

UPDATE tickets t
SET closed_at = t.opened_at + interval '1 day'
FROM ticket_statuses s
WHERE s.status = t.status
  AND s.is_terminal
  AND t.closed_at IS NULL;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — the diagram becomes a constraint

Your ex1 script runs automatically first.

The workflow lives in a slide deck:

```
open ─▶ triaged ─▶ in_progress ─▶ resolved ─▶ closed
resolved ─▶ in_progress                    (reopened)
open, triaged, in_progress ─▶ cancelled
```

`ticket_events` records transitions but enforces nothing, which is why 40
events in the seeded data record moves the workflow forbids.

Make the diagram enforceable:

1. Create `ticket_transitions (from_status text NOT NULL REFERENCES
   ticket_statuses(status), to_status text NOT NULL REFERENCES
   ticket_statuses(status), PRIMARY KEY (from_status, to_status))`.
2. Seed it with **exactly** the nine legal pairs above:
   `open→triaged`, `triaged→in_progress`, `in_progress→resolved`,
   `resolved→closed`, `resolved→in_progress`, `open→cancelled`,
   `triaged→cancelled`, `in_progress→cancelled`, `open→in_progress`
   (the last one is real: a triage-skipping fast path for `high`
   priority).
3. Delete the illegal events — those whose `(from_status, to_status)` pair
   is not in the table **and** whose `from_status` is not NULL. Opening
   events have a NULL `from_status` and are legal by definition.
4. Add `CONSTRAINT ticket_events_transition_fk` on `ticket_events
   (from_status, to_status)` referencing `ticket_transitions`.

Step 4 relies on the default `MATCH SIMPLE`: a NULL `from_status` skips
the check entirely, which is exactly what the opening event needs. V3·E3
warned you about that behaviour; here it is the feature.

Expected: `ticket_transitions` has 9 rows, `ticket_events` loses 40.

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e04_state_machines_audit ex2`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four statements. The one worth thinking about is step 3, where "not in the
table" is an anti-join and the NULL condition has to be written explicitly
because a NULL never equals anything.

## Hint 2

The anti-join delete:

```sql
DELETE FROM ticket_events e
WHERE e.from_status IS NOT NULL
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ticket_transitions t
                  WHERE t.from_status = e.from_status
                    AND t.to_status   = e.to_status);
```

`NOT EXISTS` rather than `NOT IN`, because `NOT IN` against a subquery
that could produce NULL returns no rows at all — the classic trap from
lesson 5.

## Hint 3

Run the delete's `SELECT` form first and look at what you are about to
remove. Forty rows, and reading a few of them tells you what the old
system permitted — `resolved → open` is the common one, which is why the
workflow later grew an explicit `resolved → in_progress` reopen path. The
data is a record of the rules changing, which is worth a minute before you
delete it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reframe: a state machine's transition function is a *relation*, and
relations are what this database stores. Once you see the diagram as nine
rows, the enforcement mechanism is the one you already have — a foreign
key — rather than something new.

## Hint 2

Inspect the damage before repairing it, grouped so the pattern is visible:

```sql
SELECT e.from_status, e.to_status, count(*)
FROM ticket_events e
LEFT JOIN ticket_transitions t
  ON t.from_status = e.from_status AND t.to_status = e.to_status
WHERE e.from_status IS NOT NULL AND t.from_status IS NULL
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 3 DESC;
```

That output is the list of rules your workflow has been violating, ranked.
In a real system it is the first artefact you show the product owner,
because half of those pairs usually turn out to be transitions that
*should* be legal and nobody wrote down.

## Hint 3

Think about deleting versus quarantining. Deleting evidence of past
illegal moves is what this exercise asks and is rarely what you want at
work: better is to copy them to a `ticket_events_rejected` table first, or
to add the foreign key `NOT VALID` and never validate it, keeping history
intact while enforcing the rule going forward. V3·E3 gave you that tool;
this exercise deletes only to keep the gate simple, and the honest version
is one statement longer.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e04_state_machines_audit/ex2 — legal transitions as data, with an FK
CREATE TABLE ticket_transitions (
  from_status text NOT NULL REFERENCES ticket_statuses(status),
  to_status   text NOT NULL REFERENCES ticket_statuses(status),
  PRIMARY KEY (from_status, to_status)
);

INSERT INTO ticket_transitions (from_status, to_status) VALUES
  ('open',        'triaged'),
  ('triaged',     'in_progress'),
  ('in_progress', 'resolved'),
  ('resolved',    'closed'),
  ('resolved',    'in_progress'),
  ('open',        'cancelled'),
  ('triaged',     'cancelled'),
  ('in_progress', 'cancelled'),
  ('open',        'in_progress');

DELETE FROM ticket_events e
WHERE e.from_status IS NOT NULL
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                  FROM ticket_transitions t
                  WHERE t.from_status = e.from_status
                    AND t.to_status   = e.to_status);

ALTER TABLE ticket_events
  ADD CONSTRAINT ticket_events_transition_fk
  FOREIGN KEY (from_status, to_status)
  REFERENCES ticket_transitions (from_status, to_status);

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — an enum, and the three things it will not let you do

`tickets.priority` is `text` holding `'low'`, `'normal'`, `'high'`. This
set is genuinely closed — it has not changed in six years, the ordering is
semantic, and nobody is proposing a fourth. That makes it the one column
in this schema where an enum is the right call.

In one script:

1. `CREATE TYPE ticket_priority AS ENUM ('low', 'normal', 'high');` —
   declaration order is the sort order, permanently.
2. Convert the column:
   `ALTER TABLE tickets ALTER COLUMN priority TYPE ticket_priority
   USING priority::ticket_priority;` This rewrites the table.
3. Prove the ordering is free: return, as the script's final statement,
   one row per priority with columns `priority` and `tickets`, **ordered
   by `priority` ascending** — which now sorts `low, normal, high` rather
   than alphabetically (`high, low, normal`). That reordering is the enum
   earning its place.

Then meet the restriction, in a comment you must actually write: the
product team asks for `'urgent'`. `ALTER TYPE ticket_priority ADD VALUE
'urgent';` works on its own, but the following **fails**:

```sql
BEGIN;
  ALTER TYPE ticket_priority ADD VALUE 'urgent';
  UPDATE tickets SET priority = 'urgent' WHERE subject ILIKE '%outage%';
COMMIT;
-- ERROR: unsafe use of new value "urgent" of enum type ticket_priority
```

The value is not usable until the transaction that added it has
committed. Since most migration tools wrap each migration in a
transaction, adding an enum value and backfilling with it is **two
migrations**. Add `ALTER TYPE ticket_priority ADD VALUE 'urgent';` as the
last statement of your script, on its own, to show the working form.

The gate checks the column's type is `ticket_priority`, that `'urgent'`
exists in the type, that the row counts are unchanged, and that your final
`SELECT` returns the three original priorities in workflow order.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e04_state_machines_audit ex3`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four statements, all short. The conceptual content is in what you cannot
do, not in what you type.

## Hint 2

The conversion needs a `USING` clause because there is no implicit cast
from `text` to an enum:

```sql
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c TYPE my_enum USING c::my_enum;
```

If any row holds a value not in the enum, this fails and names the value —
which is a validation pass for free.

## Hint 3

Order the statements so the `SELECT` runs before the `ADD VALUE`, or your
grouped output gains an empty fourth category depending on how you write
it. Whether `'urgent'` should appear with a zero count is a real reporting
question — a `LEFT JOIN` from the enum's values via
`unnest(enum_range(NULL::ticket_priority))` would include it, and a plain
`GROUP BY` over the table will not.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Decide the enum-versus-lookup question before writing any of it, and be
able to defend the answer for *this* column and the opposite answer for
`status` one exercise earlier. Priority: closed set, semantic order, no
attributes, no transitions — enum. Status: open-ish set, attributes
(`is_terminal`), referenced by a transitions table — lookup. The two
answers differing in one schema is the correct outcome, not an
inconsistency.

## Hint 2

Look at what the type system now gives you:

```sql
SELECT 'high'::ticket_priority > 'low'::ticket_priority;   -- true
SELECT enum_range(NULL::ticket_priority);
SELECT max(priority) FROM tickets;
```

`max()` on an enum works and returns the highest-ordered value, which is
meaningful. `max()` on the old `text` column returned `'normal'`
alphabetically, which was meaningless and looked fine.

## Hint 3

Know the escape hatches, because you will need one eventually. There is no
`DROP VALUE`: to remove one you create a new type, `ALTER TABLE ... TYPE
... USING`, and drop the old — a full table rewrite per column. Renaming
is cheap (`ALTER TYPE ... RENAME VALUE 'x' TO 'y'`, PG10+). Reordering is
the expensive one and the reason to think hard about declaration order:
`ADD VALUE ... BEFORE 'normal'` exists, so at least insertion into the
middle is possible.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the log is the truth; the column is a cache

Your ex1 and ex2 scripts run automatically first.

`tickets.status` and `ticket_events` are two independent records of the
same fact, and nothing keeps them in agreement. Derive the truth from the
log, then find where the cache lies.

Two views, then one query.

**1. `ticket_derived_status`** — one row per ticket that has events:
`ticket_id`, `status` (the latest event's `to_status`), `since` (that
event's `at`), `actor`. The latest event is decided by `at DESC`, ties
broken by `event_id DESC`. That second key is not optional: batch-written
events share a timestamp, and without it the view returns different
answers on different runs, which shows up as a dashboard that disagrees
with itself on refresh.

**2. `ticket_status_drift`** — the tickets where the cached column and the
derived status disagree: `ticket_id`, `cached`, `derived`. Use `IS
DISTINCT FROM` so that a ticket with a NULL on either side is compared
correctly rather than silently dropped.

**3. The final statement** returns one row: `tickets_total`,
`with_events`, `drifted` — the row counts of `tickets`,
`ticket_derived_status`, and `ticket_status_drift` respectively.

There *is* drift in the seeded data, and ex2's deletion of illegal events
created more of it — removing an event changes what "latest" means. That
is a genuinely instructive side effect: any repair of an event log
rewrites the history the cache was derived from.

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e04_state_machines_audit ex4`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

"Latest per group" is `DISTINCT ON` (lesson 49) — one row per
`ticket_id`, ordered so the row you want comes first within each group.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT ON (ticket_id)
       ticket_id, to_status, at
FROM ticket_events
ORDER BY ticket_id, at DESC, event_id DESC;
```

The `ORDER BY` must begin with the `DISTINCT ON` expression; everything
after it decides which row survives.

## Hint 3

For the drift view, join `tickets` to the derived view — and choose the
join type deliberately. An inner join reports only tickets that have
events; a `LEFT JOIN` also surfaces tickets with a status and no events at
all, which is arguably the worst kind of drift. The prompt's row counts
work with either, but the two views answer different questions and you
should know which you built.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

State the invariant you are testing in one sentence before writing SQL:
*a ticket's status column equals the `to_status` of its most recent
event.* Everything in this exercise is that sentence — the derivation, the
comparison, the count. When the invariant is written down, the query
almost types itself, and more importantly you can tell whether the query
tests it.

## Hint 2

Reproduce the non-determinism the tie-break prevents, so you believe in
it:

```sql
SELECT ticket_id, count(*) FROM ticket_events e1
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ticket_events e2
              WHERE e2.ticket_id = e1.ticket_id AND e2.at = e1.at
                AND e2.event_id <> e1.event_id)
GROUP BY ticket_id;
```

Those tickets have simultaneous events. Run a `DISTINCT ON` without the
`event_id` tie-break twice and compare — the planner is free to pick
either row, and on a large table with a parallel scan it will.

## Hint 3

Think about what you would do with the drift list in production. Three
options, in increasing order of maturity: fix the column from the log
(treating the log as truth), fix the log from the column (treating the
column as truth, which means fabricating an event and is usually wrong),
or record the drift and investigate before touching either. The challenge
makes drift impossible going forward by writing both in one trigger; this
exercise is the archaeology you do first.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e04_state_machines_audit/ex4 — derive status from the log, find the lies
CREATE VIEW ticket_derived_status AS
SELECT DISTINCT ON (ticket_id)
       ticket_id,
       to_status AS status,
       at        AS since,
       actor
FROM ticket_events
ORDER BY ticket_id, at DESC, event_id DESC;

CREATE VIEW ticket_status_drift AS
SELECT t.ticket_id,
       t.status AS cached,
       d.status AS derived
FROM tickets t
JOIN ticket_derived_status d ON d.ticket_id = t.ticket_id
WHERE t.status IS DISTINCT FROM d.status;
