SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM tickets)               AS tickets_total,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM ticket_derived_status) AS with_events,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM ticket_status_drift)   AS drifted;

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — one open assignment at a time

Tickets get assigned to agents, and an assignment has a life: it starts,
and later it ends when the ticket is reassigned or closed. The rule is:

> A ticket has **at most one** open assignment at any moment. Any number
> of closed ones may exist, and their history must be kept.

Build it:

```sql
ticket_assignments (
  assign_id   bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  ticket_id   bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES tickets(ticket_id),
  agent       text   NOT NULL,
  assigned_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  released_at timestamptz,
  CONSTRAINT ticket_assignments_span
    CHECK (released_at IS NULL OR released_at > assigned_at))
```

plus a **partial unique index** `ticket_assignments_one_open` on
`(ticket_id) WHERE released_at IS NULL`.

`UNIQUE (ticket_id)` would forbid reassignment entirely, which is the
opposite of the requirement. A counting trigger races: two agents grab the
same ticket, each sees zero open assignments, both insert.

Then exercise it, in this order:

1. Assign ticket 1 to `'ines'` (leave `assigned_at` to its default).
2. Reassign to `'omar'` — which means *first* setting the open row's
   `released_at = now()`, then inserting the new row. Doing it the other
   way round violates the index, which is the index doing its job.
3. Assign ticket 2 to `'ines'` — a second open assignment for the same
   agent on a different ticket, which must succeed, because the rule is
   per ticket and not per agent.

The gate then attempts a second open assignment on ticket 1 and expects a
unique violation naming your index.

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e04_state_machines_audit ex5`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One `CREATE TABLE`, one `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... WHERE`, four DML
statements. The ordering inside step 2 is the part worth being careful
about.

## Hint 2

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX t_one_open ON t (parent_id) WHERE closed_at IS NULL;
```

Rows failing the predicate are not in the index at all, so any number of
released assignments can coexist.

## Hint 3

Step 2 is release-then-insert, and the reason is the index: while the old
row is still open, a second open row for that ticket cannot exist. In a
real application both statements go in one transaction so that a ticket is
never momentarily unassigned as far as any other session can see — and
note that this is *not* a case for deferral, because the intermediate
state (zero open assignments) is perfectly legal.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Recognise the shape, because it recurs everywhere: one current row plus a
history of past rows, distinguished by a NULL end-timestamp. Employment
records, tenancies, price lists, feature flags, subscriptions. Once you
see `WHERE ended_at IS NULL` as "the current one", the partial unique
index is the obvious enforcement and V3·E5's history tables are the
obvious generalisation.

## Hint 2

Prove the race exists in the version you are not building. Open two psql
sessions:

```sql
-- both sessions
BEGIN;
SELECT count(*) FROM ticket_assignments
WHERE ticket_id = 1 AND released_at IS NULL;   -- both see 0
INSERT INTO ticket_assignments (ticket_id, agent) VALUES (1, 'a');
```

With the index, the second session blocks and then fails. Without it, both
commit. That block is the index taking the lock your application forgot
to.

## Hint 3

Consider the alternative model and why it is worse: a single
`tickets.assigned_agent` column, updated in place. It enforces one
assignment trivially and destroys the history — you can never answer "who
had this before?" or "how long was it with omar?". The assignment table
with a NULL `released_at` gives you both properties for the price of one
index, and it is the same argument as the event log versus the status
column, one table down.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — audit the change, not the row

Your ex1 script runs automatically first.

Build a generic audit trail for `tickets` — generic meaning it needs no
column list, so it keeps working when the table gains a column next
quarter.

```sql
ticket_audit (
  audit_id  bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  ticket_id bigint NOT NULL,
  op        text   NOT NULL,
  changed   jsonb  NOT NULL,
  previous  jsonb  NOT NULL,
  at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now())
```

Note there is **no foreign key** to `tickets`. An audit row must survive
its subject being deleted; a foreign key with `CASCADE` would erase the
evidence and one with `RESTRICT` would make deletion impossible.

Write `ticket_audit_fn()` and attach it as `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR
DELETE FOR EACH ROW` trigger `tickets_audit_trg` on `tickets`:

- `INSERT`: `op = 'INSERT'`, `changed = to_jsonb(NEW)`, `previous =
  '{}'::jsonb`.
- `UPDATE`: `op = 'UPDATE'`, `changed = to_jsonb(NEW) - to_jsonb(OLD)`,
  `previous = to_jsonb(OLD) - to_jsonb(NEW)`. The `jsonb - jsonb` operator
  removes pairs present on both sides, so what remains is exactly the
  columns that changed, holding the new values on one side and the old on
  the other. No column list anywhere.
- `DELETE`: `op = 'DELETE'`, `changed = '{}'::jsonb`, `previous =
  to_jsonb(OLD)`.
- `ticket_id` comes from `NEW` except on `DELETE`, where only `OLD`
  exists.

An `AFTER ... FOR EACH ROW` trigger's return value is ignored; return
`NULL`.

Then exercise it: update ticket 1's `priority` to `'high'`, update ticket
2's `subject` to `'escalated'`, and delete ticket 3 — after first deleting
its events, because `ticket_events` references it.

The gate checks three audit rows exist with the right ops, that ticket 1's
`changed` has exactly one key (`priority`), and that the delete's
`previous` contains the whole row.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e04_state_machines_audit ex6`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One table, one function, one trigger, three DML statements. The function
branches on `TG_OP`, which is a text variable Postgres sets to `'INSERT'`,
`'UPDATE'` or `'DELETE'`.

## Hint 2

The skeleton:

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION f() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF TG_OP = 'DELETE' THEN
    INSERT INTO aud (id, op, previous) VALUES (OLD.id, TG_OP, to_jsonb(OLD));
  ELSE
    INSERT INTO aud (id, op, changed)  VALUES (NEW.id, TG_OP, to_jsonb(NEW));
  END IF;
  RETURN NULL;
END $$;
```

Referencing `NEW` inside a `DELETE` firing raises at runtime, so the
branch is not optional.

## Hint 3

Test the diff operator on its own before trusting it inside a trigger:

```sql
SELECT '{"a":1,"b":2}'::jsonb - '{"a":1,"b":9}'::jsonb;   -- {"b": 2}
```

Only `b` differs, and the result carries the *left* operand's value. Which
side you put where therefore decides whether you captured the new value or
the old one, and getting it backwards produces an audit trail that reads
correctly and says the opposite of the truth.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what a reader of this table needs a year from now. Not "row 42 was
updated" — that is a log line. They need: which fields moved, what they
moved from, what they moved to, and when. The two jsonb columns are
exactly that, and the reason to store both rather than only the new values
is that "what did it say before" is the question that gets asked.

## Hint 2

After running it, read your own audit rows and check they are legible:

```sql
SELECT audit_id, ticket_id, op, changed, previous FROM ticket_audit
ORDER BY audit_id;
```

If `changed` on the priority update contains six keys, your operands are
the wrong way round or you stored `to_jsonb(NEW)` wholesale. If it
contains zero keys, an `UPDATE` fired that changed nothing — which is
worth auditing too, or worth suppressing with `WHEN (OLD IS DISTINCT FROM
NEW)` on the trigger.

## Hint 3

Two refinements to know about. `CREATE TRIGGER ... FOR EACH ROW WHEN (OLD
IS DISTINCT FROM NEW)` skips no-op updates entirely, which matters on
tables where ORMs write every column every time. And for bulk updates, a
statement-level trigger with `REFERENCING OLD TABLE AS o NEW TABLE AS n`
lets you audit a million rows with one `INSERT ... SELECT` instead of a
million function calls — the same audit, one to two orders of magnitude
cheaper, and the reason to know it exists before you meet the bulk update.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — who did it, through a connection pool

Your ex1 and ex6 scripts run automatically first, so the audit trigger
exists and its rows have no actor.

`current_user` is the database role your connection authenticated as. In
any pooled application that is one role — `app` — for every request from
every human, so recording it answers "which service" and never "which
person". The application knows the human; it has to pass that down.

The mechanism is a custom setting:

```sql
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL app.user_id = 'agent:ines';
UPDATE tickets SET status = 'triaged' WHERE ticket_id = 5;
COMMIT;
```

and inside the trigger, `current_setting('app.user_id', true)`. The second
argument is `missing_ok`: with it, an unset value returns NULL; without
it, an unaudited code path raises and the write fails.

In one script:

1. `ALTER TABLE ticket_audit ADD COLUMN actor text NOT NULL DEFAULT
   'unknown'` — the default matters, because the trigger has been running
   without an actor and the existing rows need a value.
2. `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION ticket_audit_fn()` so that every branch
   also writes `actor`, computed once at the top as
   `coalesce(current_setting('app.user_id', true), session_user)`.
   Replacing the function is enough; the trigger points at it by name and
   needs no change.
3. Demonstrate both paths. In one transaction, `SET LOCAL app.user_id =
   'agent:ines'` and update ticket 5's status to `'triaged'`. Then,
   **outside** any explicit transaction and with no setting, update ticket
   6's status to `'triaged'` — its audit row must fall back to
   `session_user`.

The gate checks ticket 5's audit row has actor `'agent:ines'`, that ticket
6's does not, and — the important one — that after the first transaction
commits, a *subsequent* statement's audit row is **not** attributed to
`'agent:ines'`. That is what `LOCAL` guarantees and what plain `SET` would
break.

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e04_state_machines_audit ex7`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One `ALTER TABLE`, one `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION`, and two updates
wrapped differently. No trigger changes: a trigger references its function
by name, so replacing the function replaces the behaviour.

## Hint 2

Declare the actor once rather than repeating the expression in three
branches:

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION f() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  who text := coalesce(current_setting('app.user_id', true), session_user);
BEGIN
  ...
END $$;
```

The `DECLARE` block runs on every invocation, so the value is per-row and
current.

## Hint 3

The custom setting's name must contain a dot. `SET LOCAL user_id = ...`
fails — Postgres only accepts unrecognised parameters when they are
namespaced, `app.user_id` style, which is how it distinguishes your
variables from typos of its own. Which prefix you choose is convention;
`app.` is the common one and consistency across a codebase matters more
than the choice.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Understand the failure this prevents by imagining it. A pool of 20
connections; a request sets `app.user_id` without `LOCAL` and finishes;
the connection returns to the pool; the next request — a different person
— gets that connection and does not set the value. Every change they make
is now attributed to the previous user. The audit trail is not merely
incomplete, it is *wrong*, which is worse, because people will act on it.

## Hint 2

Demonstrate the leak in one session:

```sql
SET app.user_id = 'leaky';        -- no LOCAL
BEGIN; SELECT current_setting('app.user_id'); COMMIT;
SELECT current_setting('app.user_id');   -- still 'leaky'
```

Now the same with `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction, and read it after the
commit — unset. Thirty seconds, and you will never write the wrong one.

## Hint 3

Decide the `coalesce` policy deliberately. Falling back to `session_user`
means an unaudited code path produces a weak but truthful attribution and
the write succeeds. Omitting the fallback — using `current_setting('app.
user_id')` with no `missing_ok` — means such a path *fails*, loudly,
which is what you want in a system where every change must be attributable
to a person. The strict version is better for financial and access-control
tables; the lenient one is better for everything else, because a failed
write is an outage. Pick per table, not per codebase.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — an audit table that refuses to be edited

Your ex1, ex6 and ex7 scripts run automatically first.

`ticket_audit` currently records everything and protects none of it.
Anybody who can write to the database can rewrite history, which makes it
a log rather than an audit trail — and the difference is exactly the
property a compliance reviewer will ask about.

Two defences, because neither is sufficient alone.

**Privileges** stop the application. `setup.sql` created a role
`app_writer` which currently has full DML on the audit table. Revoke
`UPDATE` and `DELETE` on `ticket_audit` from `app_writer` and from
`PUBLIC`, leaving `INSERT` and `SELECT`.

**A trigger** stops the table's owner. Privilege checks do not apply to an
object's owner, so the migration role — the one your deploy runs as — can
still rewrite audit rows despite any `REVOKE`. Create
`audit_immutable()` raising an exception, and attach it as `BEFORE UPDATE
OR DELETE ON ticket_audit FOR EACH ROW` trigger `ticket_audit_immutable`.
Use `RAISE EXCEPTION 'ticket_audit is append-only (attempted %)', TG_OP;`
so the message names the operation.

Then prove it: the script's last statement must be a `SELECT` returning
one row with `can_update` and `can_delete` — both `boolean`, both `false`
— computed with `has_table_privilege('app_writer', 'ticket_audit',
'UPDATE')` and the same for `DELETE`.

The gate additionally attempts `UPDATE ticket_audit SET actor = 'x'` as
the owner and expects your trigger's exception, and attempts an `INSERT`
and expects it to succeed — an append-only table that cannot be appended
to is a different bug.

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e04_state_machines_audit ex8`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two `REVOKE`s (or one with two targets), one function, one trigger, one
`SELECT`. The conceptual point is that privileges and triggers defend
against different attackers.

## Hint 2

```sql
REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON ticket_audit FROM app_writer, PUBLIC;

CREATE FUNCTION f() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  RAISE EXCEPTION 'append-only (attempted %)', TG_OP;
END $$;
```

A `BEFORE` trigger that raises aborts the statement; there is no need to
return anything, because control never reaches a `RETURN`.

## Hint 3

`BEFORE ... FOR EACH ROW` is the right timing here, but note it means the
exception fires on the first offending row rather than on the statement.
A `BEFORE ... FOR EACH STATEMENT` trigger would refuse the statement
outright even when it would have matched zero rows — arguably better,
since `DELETE FROM ticket_audit WHERE false` should probably also be
refused as a matter of intent. Either is defensible; know which you built.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think in terms of who you are defending against, and be honest about the
limits. Application bug or compromised app role: privileges stop it.
Deploy role or a DBA in a hurry: the trigger stops it. Superuser, or
anyone who first runs `DROP TRIGGER`: nothing in the database stops them,
and the goal was never to make tampering impossible — it is to make it
require a deliberate, separately visible act.

## Hint 2

Verify the privilege change rather than assuming the `REVOKE` matched:

```sql
SELECT grantee, privilege_type
FROM information_schema.table_privileges
WHERE table_name = 'ticket_audit'
ORDER BY grantee, privilege_type;
```

Watch for privileges granted via `PUBLIC` or via role membership, which a
`REVOKE ... FROM app_writer` alone does not remove. That is the reason the
prompt asks you to revoke from `PUBLIC` too.

## Hint 3

Consider the complete version, so you know what this exercise leaves out.
Real append-only storage also wants: no `TRUNCATE` (a separate privilege
and a trigger event of its own, `BEFORE TRUNCATE ... FOR EACH STATEMENT`),
partitioning so retention is `DROP TABLE` rather than `DELETE` (V3·E7),
and ideally a periodic export to storage the database cannot reach at all.
The database can make tampering loud; only an external copy makes it
detectable after the fact.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the transition, enforced and recorded, once

Your ex1, ex2 and ex4 scripts run automatically first, so you have the
status lookup, the transitions table, and the derived-status view.

Right now a status change is three separate acts of discipline: update the
column, insert a matching event, and don't do anything the workflow
forbids. Three chances to forget. Replace all three with one function that
cannot be bypassed by anyone using it.

Build `move_ticket(p_ticket_id bigint, p_to_status text, p_actor text)
RETURNS void`, in `plpgsql`, which:

1. Takes a row lock: `SELECT status INTO v_from FROM tickets WHERE
   ticket_id = p_ticket_id FOR UPDATE`. Without this, two agents resolving
   the same ticket both read `in_progress`, both write `resolved`, and you
   get two events for one move — the lost-update problem, in the place it
   does the most damage. With it, the second call waits and then sees the
   state its decision depends on.
2. Raises `'no such ticket %', p_ticket_id` if `NOT FOUND`.
3. Raises `'illegal transition % -> %', v_from, p_to_status` unless that
   pair exists in `ticket_transitions`. The foreign key on `ticket_events`
   would catch it too, but a purpose-written message beats a constraint
   violation for something users trigger routinely — and the check
   *before* any write means the ticket row is never touched on a rejected
   move.
4. Inserts the event (`from_status = v_from`, `to_status = p_to_status`,
   `actor = p_actor`, `at = now()`).
5. Updates `tickets.status`, and sets `closed_at = now()` when the new
   status is terminal (join `ticket_statuses`), leaving it alone
   otherwise.

Steps 4 and 5 are atomic with each other because they are in one
transaction — which is the entire reason the cache can be trusted from now
on, and why ex4's drift view should return nothing for tickets moved this
way.

Then call it three times on ticket 10, which starts at `'open'`:
`'triaged'` by `'agent:ines'`, `'in_progress'` by `'agent:omar'`,
`'resolved'` by `'agent:omar'`.

The gate: checks ticket 10 ends `'resolved'` with three new events and no
drift; calls `move_ticket(10, 'open', 'x')` and expects the illegal-
transition exception with the ticket row unchanged; and calls
`move_ticket(999999, 'triaged', 'x')` expecting the no-such-ticket
exception.

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e04_state_machines_audit challenge`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One function, five steps, in the order given. Each step is two or three
lines; the value is entirely in the sequencing — lock, validate, write,
write — and in what each step prevents.

## Hint 2

The lock-and-check opening:

```sql
SELECT status INTO v_from FROM tickets
WHERE ticket_id = p_ticket_id FOR UPDATE;
IF NOT FOUND THEN
  RAISE EXCEPTION 'no such ticket %', p_ticket_id;
END IF;
```

`NOT FOUND` is a plpgsql special variable set by the preceding `SELECT
INTO`, and `FOR UPDATE` holds the row lock until the function's
transaction ends — not until the function returns.

## Hint 3

For the terminal check, a scalar subquery reads better than a join inside
an `UPDATE`:

```sql
UPDATE tickets SET status = p_to_status,
       closed_at = CASE WHEN (SELECT is_terminal FROM ticket_statuses
                              WHERE status = p_to_status)
                        THEN now() ELSE closed_at END
WHERE ticket_id = p_ticket_id;
```

Note `ELSE closed_at` rather than `ELSE NULL` — the difference between
leaving a value alone and erasing it, and one of the most common bugs in
`CASE`-driven updates.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build it by asking what each guard is for, because a reader of the
function should be able to tell. The lock is for concurrency. The
`NOT FOUND` check is for a bad id. The transition check is for a bad
request. The single transaction is for the cache. Four different failure
modes, four lines, and a function that is genuinely hard to misuse — which
is the actual deliverable.

## Hint 2

See the lock work. Two sessions:

```sql
-- session 1
BEGIN; SELECT move_ticket(11, 'triaged', 'a');   -- do not commit
-- session 2
BEGIN; SELECT move_ticket(11, 'cancelled', 'b'); -- blocks
```

Session 2 waits. When session 1 commits, session 2 proceeds and — this is
the part worth seeing — re-reads `status`, finds `'triaged'`, and
validates `triaged → cancelled` rather than the `open → cancelled` it
would have validated a moment earlier. The lock does not merely serialise;
it makes each caller's decision based on the state that will actually
apply.

## Hint 3

Two extensions worth naming. First, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` turns
the wait into an immediate error, which is better for an interactive UI
that would rather say "someone else is editing this" than hang. Second,
this function is the natural place to require an actor — dropping
`p_actor` and reading `current_setting('app.user_id')` instead would make
attribution structural rather than a parameter a caller can lie about.
Combining that with ex7's audit trigger gives you two independent records
of who did what, which is not redundant: one is the workflow's account and
one is the storage engine's.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — the question a status column cannot answer

Your ex1, ex2 and ex4 scripts run automatically first.

The support manager wants to know where time goes: *how long does a ticket
spend in each state?* `tickets.status` cannot answer it at any price, and
`updated_at` cannot either. The event log can, and the technique is the
one lesson 95 drilled — each event's duration is the gap to the next event
for the same ticket.

Return, per status, across all tickets:

- `status` — the state being measured
- `entries` (bigint) — how many times any ticket entered this state
- `avg_hours` (numeric) — the average time spent in it, rounded to 2,
  counting only **completed** spells: a state a ticket is still sitting in
  has no end and must be excluded, not treated as ending now
- `total_hours` (numeric) — the sum of those completed spells, rounded to
  2

The end of a spell is the `at` of the *next* event for that ticket,
ordered by `at`, ties by `event_id` — the same deterministic ordering ex4
needed. `lead()` over a partition by `ticket_id` gives it to you in one
pass. Convert an interval to hours with
`extract(epoch FROM (next_at - at)) / 3600.0`.

**Ordered by `total_hours` descending, then `status` ascending.**

Statuses that no ticket ever entered must not appear; statuses entered
only by tickets currently sitting in them will appear with `entries` > 0
and NULL averages, which is correct and worth noticing — it is the
difference between "we have no data" and "the answer is zero".

Edit `review1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e04_state_machines_audit review1`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two stages. First, per event, find when the ticket left that state — a
window function over the ticket's events. Then aggregate those durations
by `to_status`.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT ticket_id, to_status, at,
       lead(at) OVER (PARTITION BY ticket_id ORDER BY at, event_id) AS next_at
FROM ticket_events;
```

`lead()` returns NULL for the last event of each ticket, which is exactly
the "still in this state" case you must exclude.

## Hint 3

The exclusion happens for free: `avg()` and `sum()` skip NULLs, so a
duration computed from a NULL `next_at` is simply not counted. `count(*)`
does *not* skip them, which is why `entries` counts every entry while the
averages count only completed spells — the asymmetry the prompt describes
is a consequence of aggregate NULL semantics rather than something you
have to code around.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Sanity-check the shape on one ticket before aggregating anything:

```sql
SELECT ticket_id, from_status, to_status, at,
       lead(at) OVER (PARTITION BY ticket_id ORDER BY at, event_id) AS until
FROM ticket_events WHERE ticket_id = 1 ORDER BY at;
```

Read the rows as a story: entered `open` at T1, left at T2 for `triaged`,
left that at T3. Each row's *duration* belongs to its `to_status`, not its
`from_status` — an off-by-one-column that produces plausible, wrong
numbers and is the single most common mistake in this query.

## Hint 2

Decide the open-spell policy explicitly, because it changes the answer and
both choices are defensible. Excluding them (what the prompt asks)
measures "how long did completed spells take" and is right for SLA
reporting. Treating them as ending at `now()` measures "how much time has
been spent so far" and is right for a live queue dashboard. Mixing them —
excluding some and not others — is how a metric becomes untrustworthy.
State which you built, in a comment.

## Hint 3

Extend the thought to the shape of the whole sector. Every question the
manager asks next — median rather than mean, per-agent, per-priority,
"tickets that bounced back from resolved more than once" — is a variation
on this one query, and every one of them is unanswerable from a status
column. That is the return on modelling the process rather than the state,
and it arrives long after the design decision, which is why the decision
is usually made wrongly.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e04_state_machines_audit/review1 — time spent per state, from the log
WITH spells AS (
  SELECT ticket_id,
         to_status,
         at,
         lead(at) OVER (PARTITION BY ticket_id
                        ORDER BY at, event_id) AS next_at
  FROM ticket_events
)
SELECT to_status AS status,
       count(*)  AS entries,
       round(avg(extract(epoch FROM (next_at - at)) / 3600.0)::numeric, 2)
         AS avg_hours,
       round(sum(extract(epoch FROM (next_at - at)) / 3600.0)::numeric, 2)
         AS total_hours
FROM spells
GROUP BY to_status
ORDER BY total_hours DESC NULLS LAST, status;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3e04_state_machines_audit/review1 — same numbers via a self-join lateral
WITH spells AS (
  SELECT e.ticket_id, e.to_status, e.at, n.at AS next_at
  FROM ticket_events e
  LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT e2.at
    FROM ticket_events e2
    WHERE e2.ticket_id = e.ticket_id
      AND (e2.at, e2.event_id) > (e.at, e.event_id)
    ORDER BY e2.at, e2.event_id
    LIMIT 1) n ON true
)
SELECT to_status AS status,
       count(*)  AS entries,
       round(avg(extract(epoch FROM (next_at - at)) / 3600.0)::numeric, 2)
         AS avg_hours,
       round(sum(extract(epoch FROM (next_at - at)) / 3600.0)::numeric, 2)
         AS total_hours
FROM spells
GROUP BY to_status
ORDER BY total_hours DESC NULLS LAST, status;

lessons.title: V3·E5 — Soft deletes, history tables and temporal queries
lessons.summary: An HR schema where nothing is ever really deleted and every fact has a validity period. The cost of deleted_at on uniqueness and referential integrity, SCD type 2 with daterange and an exclusion constraint, as-of queries, point-in-time joins, coverage gaps, a bitemporal second axis, and what retention looks like.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·E5 — Soft deletes, history tables and temporal queries

`DELETE` is the only operation in SQL that destroys information, and most
businesses cannot afford it. An employee record removed on request is
still needed by payroll for seven years. A price row deleted from the
catalogue is still the price somebody paid last March. So teams stop
deleting, and the schema acquires two features that look small and change
everything: a `deleted_at` column, and tables where every row carries the
period during which it was true.

Both are correct responses to a real requirement. Both cost more than
their advocates admit, and the costs are the subject of this sector.
V3·E1's snapshot argument is the foundation — *the price at the time of
the order is a different fact from the current price* — and here you
generalise it: every fact has a period of validity, and a schema that
stores only the current value has silently asserted that the period is
"forever".

## The schema

`setup.sql` builds a small HR system, already carrying four years of
history and one soft-delete column:

```sql
CREATE TABLE departments (
  dept_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  code    text NOT NULL,
  name    text NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE staff_members (
  staff_id   bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email      text NOT NULL,
  full_name  text NOT NULL,
  hired_on   date NOT NULL,
  deleted_at timestamptz);        -- NULL means live

CREATE TABLE staff_history (      -- SCD type 2
  hist_id    bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  staff_id   bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES staff_members(staff_id),
  dept_id    bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES departments(dept_id),
  title      text NOT NULL,
  salary     numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
  valid_from date NOT NULL,
  valid_to   date);               -- NULL means "still current"

CREATE TABLE payments (
  payment_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  staff_id   bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES staff_members(staff_id),
  paid_on    date NOT NULL,
  amount     numeric(10,2) NOT NULL);
```

800 staff, 3,100 history rows, 19,000 payments. Some staff are soft
deleted. Some history rows overlap, because nothing stops them. Some staff
have gaps in their history, because nothing requires coverage.

## What a soft delete actually costs

**Every query needs the predicate, and one will forget.** `SELECT * FROM
staff_members` is now wrong everywhere it appears. The mitigation is not
discipline; it is a view — `staff_live` — that the application selects
from, or row-level security (V3·E8) that applies the predicate
structurally. A view built with `WITH (security_barrier)` additionally
stops the planner from pushing a user-supplied function below the
predicate, which matters the moment the view is a security boundary rather
than a convenience.

**Uniqueness must become conditional.** `UNIQUE (email)` now forbids
re-hiring someone whose old record was soft-deleted, because the deleted
row is still occupying the value. The rule you actually want is "unique
among live rows", which is a partial unique index — V3·E3's mechanism,
arriving here as a necessity rather than a refinement.

**Foreign keys still see deleted parents.** A `REFERENCES` constraint
knows nothing about `deleted_at`, so a payment can reference a
soft-deleted employee and the database considers it perfectly valid. Your
referential integrity is now partly fictional, and detecting the fiction
is a query you have to write and run — ex3.

**Indexes grow with the dead.** Every index on `staff_members` still
contains the deleted rows. Partial indexes (`WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`)
keep the working set small, and are usually the difference between a soft
delete that costs nothing and one that quietly degrades every lookup.

## History tables: SCD type 2

The other half. Rather than overwriting an employee's title, you close the
current row and open a new one:

```
staff_id  title       salary   valid_from   valid_to
   42     Analyst      55000   2022-01-01   2023-07-01
   42     Sr Analyst   68000   2023-07-01   NULL
```

Two conventions decide everything downstream. **Half-open intervals**:
`valid_to` is exclusive, so consecutive rows share a boundary date and
`valid_from <= d < valid_to` is the containment test with no off-by-one.
**NULL means open-ended**, which is convenient for humans and awkward for
SQL — every comparison needs `coalesce(valid_to, 'infinity')` — which is
why ex5 replaces the pair of columns with a generated `daterange` and lets
the type system carry the convention.

Once the range exists, two things become possible that were not. An
**exclusion constraint** makes overlapping history for one employee
unrepresentable: `EXCLUDE USING gist (staff_id WITH =, valid_range WITH
&&)`. And **as-of queries** become containment tests — `WHERE valid_range
@> date '2024-06-30'` — which are index-supported by the same GiST index
the constraint built.

## The queries history exists for

An **as-of query** reconstructs the world at a moment: everyone's title
and salary on 30 June 2024. A **point-in-time join** does it per row: each
payment matched to the salary that was in effect on its own `paid_on`,
which is the query payroll reconciliation is made of and the one people
get wrong by joining to the current row. **Coverage gaps** — periods where
an employee has no history row at all — are the data-quality question
nobody asks until an audit.

And then the honest paragraph, ex-challenge: history tables have a second
time axis. *Valid time* is when the fact was true in the world. *Transaction
time* is when your database learned it. A backdated promotion entered in
August but effective from June differs on both axes, and a query asking
"what did we believe on 1 July?" cannot be answered without recording
both. That is bitemporal modelling; it doubles the complexity of every
query, and the correct default is to skip it until somebody asks a
question that needs it — at which point you cannot retrofit the answer,
because the information was never captured.

## Retention

"Keep everything" is not a policy, it is the absence of one. History
tables grow without bound, and the only thing that reliably shrinks them
is a rule someone wrote down. review1 builds the archive-and-move version;
V3·E7 shows you the version where retention is `DROP TABLE` and takes
milliseconds.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - v3e05_soft_deletes_history

Two mechanisms, one idea: a row is true during a period, and the period is
part of the data.

## Notes

**A soft delete is a state, not a deletion.** `deleted_at IS NOT NULL` is
a status column with one value, and everything V3·E4 said about status
columns applies: it records where the row is now and not how it got there
or who did it. If the answer to "who deleted this and why" matters, you
want an audit trail as well, not instead.

**Uniqueness among live rows is a partial unique index.** `CREATE UNIQUE
INDEX ... ON staff_members (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`. The
`lower()` is a separate decision worth making explicitly — email
comparison is case-insensitive in practice and case-sensitive in Postgres
— and an expression index costs nothing extra here.

**Foreign keys do not know about `deleted_at`.** This is the cost nobody
warns you about. `payments.staff_id REFERENCES staff_members` is satisfied
by a soft-deleted employee, so referential integrity now guarantees
something weaker than it appears to. There is no clean fix: a `CHECK`
cannot query another table, and a trigger that verifies liveness on every
insert is expensive and still racy against a concurrent delete. The
practical answers are (a) accept it and monitor with a detection query,
(b) make deletion a workflow that first reparents or closes children, or
(c) do not soft-delete rows that are referenced — archive them instead.

**Partial indexes keep the live set fast.** An index over 800 rows of
which 200 are deleted is not interesting. An index over 8 million rows of
which 6 million are deleted is a different table. `WHERE deleted_at IS
NULL` on every index that serves live-row queries is the standard
mitigation, and it also makes the index smaller than the table's row
count, which is a pleasant surprise the first time.

**`security_barrier` is about the planner, not about permissions.** A
normal view can have its predicate reordered: if you write `SELECT * FROM
staff_live WHERE leaky(full_name)`, the planner may evaluate `leaky()`
before `deleted_at IS NULL`, and a function that raises with its argument
in the message has just leaked deleted rows. `WITH (security_barrier =
true)` forbids that reordering. The cost is fewer optimisations, sometimes
substantially fewer; use it when the view is a boundary, not when it is a
shorthand.

**Half-open intervals, always.** `[valid_from, valid_to)` means
consecutive rows share a boundary and no date belongs to two rows. The
alternative — inclusive `valid_to` — requires every consecutive pair to
differ by one day, which is wrong for timestamps and merely annoying for
dates. `daterange(valid_from, valid_to, '[)')` is the convention made
explicit and checkable.

**A generated range column is the right home for the convention.**
`valid_range daterange GENERATED ALWAYS AS (daterange(valid_from,
coalesce(valid_to, 'infinity'), '[)')) STORED`. Now `@>` tests
containment, `&&` tests overlap, GiST indexes both, and the exclusion
constraint can exist. The `coalesce` to `'infinity'` is what removes the
`NULL`-means-open special case from every downstream query.

**Overlap prevention is an exclusion constraint, not a trigger.** `EXCLUDE
USING gist (staff_id WITH =, valid_range WITH &&)` — V3·E3's mechanism,
and the canonical use for it. A trigger version races; two concurrent
inserts each find no overlap and both commit.

**As-of is containment; point-in-time join is containment per row.**
`WHERE valid_range @> date '2024-06-30'` for the first. For the second,
`LEFT JOIN LATERAL (... WHERE h.valid_range @> p.paid_on ...) ON true`,
or an inner join on the same predicate — the lateral form generalises
better when you want "the most recent row at or before" rather than
"the row containing".

**Gaps are `range_agg` or `lag`.** `range_agg(valid_range)` (PG14+)
produces a `datemultirange`, and comparing it to the employment span tells
you whether coverage is complete. The `lag()` form — this row's
`valid_from` versus the previous row's `valid_to` — is more portable and
shows you where the gap is rather than that one exists.

**Bitemporal doubles everything.** Valid time and transaction time are
independent axes; a bitemporal row has four dates and every query needs a
predicate on both. It is the right model for anything where "what did we
know then" is a question — insurance, tax, regulatory reporting — and
over-engineering everywhere else.

## ex1

The re-hire collision, and the partial unique index that permits it. Note
that plain `UNIQUE` would make soft deletion and re-hiring mutually
exclusive.

## ex2

The view as the enforcement mechanism, plus the partial indexes that make
the live subset cheap.

## ex3

The referential lie. This query belongs in your monitoring, not in a
lesson.

## ex4

Finding the overlaps you already have, before constraining against them —
the V3·E1 habit, applied to ranges.

## ex5

The generated range column and the exclusion constraint. Repair first,
constrain second; the order is not optional.

## ex6

As-of, as containment. One `@>` replaces a `BETWEEN` with a `coalesce` in
it.

## ex7

The point-in-time join, which is where "just join to the current row"
stops being an approximation and starts being a payroll error.

## ex8

Coverage gaps. The answer is a data-quality report, and the interesting
part is deciding what counts as a gap.

## challenge

The second time axis, and a question that needs it.

## review1

Retention: an archive table, a move, and the numbers that justify the
policy.

## Further reading

- [Range Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/rangetypes.html) — constructors, bound notation, `@>`, `&&`, and multiranges.
- [Range Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-range.html) — `range_agg`, `range_merge`, and the multirange functions.
- [`CREATE VIEW`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createview.html) — `security_barrier` and updatable-view rules.
- [Constraints — Exclusion](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html#DDL-CONSTRAINTS-EXCLUSION) — the overlap constraint.
- [Partial Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-partial.html) — keeping the live subset small.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·E5 — Soft deletes and history (archive)

Everything that changes when a row can be dead, and everything that
changes when a row is only true for a while.

## Soft deletes: the full checklist

Adding `deleted_at timestamptz` is one line. Making it correct is seven.

```sql
-- 1. uniqueness among the living
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX staff_live_email_key
  ON staff_members (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

-- 2. a view that cannot be forgotten
CREATE VIEW staff_live WITH (security_barrier = true) AS
  SELECT * FROM staff_members WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

-- 3. partial indexes for the live working set
CREATE INDEX staff_live_hired_idx
  ON staff_members (hired_on) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

-- 4. a detection query for the referential lie
SELECT p.payment_id, p.staff_id
FROM payments p JOIN staff_members s USING (staff_id)
WHERE s.deleted_at IS NOT NULL;

-- 5. a deletion procedure, not an UPDATE scattered in the codebase
-- 6. an audit row saying who deleted and why (V3·E4)
-- 7. a retention rule that eventually removes the rows for real
```

Items 4 through 7 are the ones teams skip, and they are the ones that
matter after year two. In particular: a soft delete with no retention rule
is a table that grows forever holding data you promised to erase, which in
several jurisdictions is the opposite of compliance.

**When not to soft-delete at all.** If the row is referenced by children
and deletion is genuinely rare, moving it to an archive table is cleaner:
the live table stays honest, the foreign keys stay meaningful, and the
archive can be queried when needed. Soft deletes earn their place when
deletion is common, reversible, and the row must remain joinable.

## SCD type 2, done properly

```sql
ALTER TABLE staff_history
  ADD COLUMN valid_range daterange
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS
    (daterange(valid_from, coalesce(valid_to, 'infinity'), '[)')) STORED;

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

ALTER TABLE staff_history
  ADD CONSTRAINT staff_history_no_overlap
  EXCLUDE USING gist (staff_id WITH =, valid_range WITH &&);
```

Three things happen at once. Overlapping history for one employee becomes
impossible. `valid_range @> some_date` becomes an indexed containment
test. And the `NULL`-means-current convention disappears from every query,
because `'infinity'` is a real value the range type understands.

Closing a row and opening the next is then a two-statement transaction:

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE staff_history SET valid_to = DATE '2024-07-01'
WHERE staff_id = 42 AND valid_to IS NULL;

INSERT INTO staff_history (staff_id, dept_id, title, salary, valid_from)
VALUES (42, 3, 'Staff Engineer', 91000, DATE '2024-07-01');
COMMIT;
```

Order matters: insert first and the exclusion constraint rejects you,
because for an instant two rows claim `[2024-07-01, infinity)`. That
rejection is the constraint working, and it is also why some teams make
the constraint deferrable — V3·E3's swap problem in a new costume.

## The three temporal queries

**As-of** — the world at a moment:

```sql
SELECT s.staff_id, s.full_name, h.title, h.salary
FROM staff_members s
JOIN staff_history h ON h.staff_id = s.staff_id
WHERE h.valid_range @> DATE '2024-06-30';
```

**Point-in-time join** — each row matched to what was true for *it*:

```sql
SELECT p.payment_id, p.paid_on, p.amount, h.title, h.salary
FROM payments p
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT title, salary FROM staff_history h
  WHERE h.staff_id = p.staff_id AND h.valid_range @> p.paid_on
  LIMIT 1) h ON true;
```

Joining `payments` to "the current history row" instead is the error this
query exists to prevent: it reports last March's payment against this
year's salary, and the totals look plausible.

**Coverage gaps** — periods with no row:

```sql
SELECT staff_id,
       lag(valid_to) OVER w AS gap_start,
       valid_from            AS gap_end
FROM staff_history
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY staff_id ORDER BY valid_from)
-- rows where lag(valid_to) < valid_from are gaps
```

or, set-wise, `range_agg(valid_range)` compared against the employment
span.

## Bitemporal, in one page

Two independent axes:

- **valid time** — when the fact was true in the world
- **transaction time** — when this database was told

A promotion effective 1 June, entered on 20 August, has `valid_from =
2024-06-01` and `recorded_at = 2024-08-20`. The question "what did payroll
believe on 1 July?" needs both: rows whose valid range contains 1 July
*and* whose known range contained 1 July. Without `recorded_at` the
question is unanswerable, and it cannot be reconstructed later.

The cost is that every query grows a second predicate and every correction
becomes an insert rather than an update — you never modify a bitemporal
row, you supersede it. Adopt it when someone is going to ask what you knew
and when; otherwise the single valid-time axis is the right default.

## Common mistakes

- **`UNIQUE (email)` alongside `deleted_at`.** Re-hiring is now
  impossible.
- **Forgetting the predicate.** One report counts deleted staff; the
  numbers disagree and nobody knows which is right.
- **Assuming foreign keys respect `deleted_at`.** They do not.
- **Inclusive `valid_to`.** Every consecutive pair now needs a one-day
  gap, and timestamps make it unfixable.
- **`NULL` valid_to compared with `<`.** `valid_to > d` is NULL for the
  current row, so the current row silently vanishes from your results.
- **Overlapping history with no constraint.** Two rows contain the same
  date; the as-of query returns two rows per person and the report
  double-counts.
- **Inserting the new history row before closing the old one.** The
  exclusion constraint rejects it, correctly.
- **Joining payments to the current history row.** Payroll reconciliation
  is wrong for everyone who ever got a raise.
- **No retention policy.** The history table becomes the largest object in
  the database and holds data you agreed to erase.

## Interview answer

*"How do you handle deletes and history?"*

Separate the two questions, because candidates who conflate them get lost.
For deletes: soft delete is a state, so treat it like one — partial unique
indexes for the live set, a view or RLS so the predicate cannot be
forgotten, partial indexes so the dead rows do not slow the living, and a
retention rule that eventually removes them for real. Say explicitly that
foreign keys do not respect `deleted_at`, because that is the detail
interviewers use to tell whether you have run this in production.

For history: SCD type 2 with half-open intervals, expressed as a range
type so that overlap prevention is an exclusion constraint rather than
trigger code. Then name the two queries it exists for — as-of and
point-in-time join — and mention that joining a payment to the *current*
salary row rather than the one in effect is the classic silent error.

If you have room, add the bitemporal distinction and immediately say you
would not build it by default. Knowing when not to use a technique reads
as more experience than knowing the technique.

## Check yourself

1. Why does `UNIQUE (email)` break re-hiring under soft deletes, and what
   replaces it?
2. What does `WITH (security_barrier = true)` prevent, and what does it
   cost?
3. Does a foreign key stop a payment referencing a soft-deleted employee?
4. Give two reasons partial indexes matter more as the deleted fraction
   grows.
5. Why are half-open intervals the right convention for validity periods?
6. Write the generated column that turns `valid_from`/`valid_to` into a
   `daterange` including the open-ended case.
7. What does `EXCLUDE USING gist (staff_id WITH =, valid_range WITH &&)`
   forbid, and why is a trigger not equivalent?
8. In what order must you close the old history row and insert the new
   one, and what happens if you reverse it?
9. Write the as-of predicate for 2024-06-30 in both the range and the
   two-column spellings.
10. Why is joining a payment to the current history row wrong, and what
    does it look like when it is wrong?
11. How do you find periods where an employee has no history row at all?
12. Distinguish valid time from transaction time with a concrete example.
13. Why can bitemporal history not be retrofitted?
14. Name two retention strategies for a history table and the cost of
    each.
lessons.fullReading:
# The long read — every fact has a period

The relational model says a row asserts a fact. What it does not say is
*when* the fact is true, and the omission is the source of an entire class
of bug that no constraint catches, because nothing is inconsistent — the
data is simply answering a question about now when the question was about
then.

A row in a table with no temporal columns carries an implicit assertion:
this is true, currently, and we do not know or care when it started. That
is often fine. A country's name, a product's SKU, a user's account id.
It stops being fine the moment somebody asks a question with a date in it,
and the tell is that you cannot answer without an apology.

## What soft deletes really are

The name is misleading. `deleted_at` does not delete anything; it adds a
state, and the state changes what every query means. Consider what happens
to the three guarantees a table normally offers.

**Uniqueness** becomes conditional, and the condition is not enforceable
by a constraint — only by a partial index, which is not a constraint and
therefore cannot be referenced by a foreign key. That last consequence is
subtle and occasionally decisive: if a child table needs to reference "the
live employee with this email", it cannot, because `REFERENCES` requires a
real unique constraint over the whole table.

**Referential integrity** becomes partial. Postgres will faithfully
enforce that `payments.staff_id` matches some row of `staff_members`. It
has no opinion about whether that row is dead. Your schema now guarantees
"references an employee record" where you believed it guaranteed
"references an employee", and the gap between those is where the bugs
live. There is no version of this that Postgres can fix, because
`deleted_at` is application semantics wearing a column.

**Query correctness** becomes a discipline. Every `FROM staff_members`
needs `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`, forever, in every report, in every
migration script, in every ad-hoc query somebody runs during an incident.
The only structural fixes are a view (which people bypass) or row-level
security (which they cannot). This is one of the strongest practical
arguments for RLS in a system that soft-deletes, and V3·E8 makes it
concrete.

The performance story is more benign than reputation suggests, provided
you use partial indexes. A B-tree with a `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`
predicate contains only live rows, so lookups against the live set cost
what they would if the dead rows had really been removed. The heap still
carries them, which costs sequential scans and `VACUUM` time (lesson 44)
but nothing else. The failure mode is a team that adds `deleted_at` and
none of the partial indexes, and then measures a gradual slowdown they
attribute to growth.

## How ranges work underneath

A `daterange` is a composite value: two bounds and a flags byte recording
inclusivity and emptiness. `'infinity'` is a real `date` value, not a
NULL, which is exactly why moving the open-ended convention into the range
removes the special case — comparisons against infinity behave arithmetically
rather than under three-valued logic.

The operators that matter are `@>` (contains), `&&` (overlaps), `-|-`
(adjacent) and `<@` (contained by). All are supported by GiST indexes,
which store bounding boxes and support containment search in logarithmic
time. That is what makes both the exclusion constraint and the as-of query
efficient using one index — a rare case where a correctness feature and a
performance feature are the same object.

Exclusion constraints (Postgres 9.0) are implemented as an index scan for
conflicting rows plus a lock, executed as a deferred-capable constraint
trigger. `EXCLUDE USING gist (staff_id WITH =, valid_range WITH &&)` needs
`btree_gist` because GiST has no native operator class for `bigint`
equality; the extension supplies one, and the resulting index is a GiST
over a composite key. It is slightly larger and slower than the B-tree you
would otherwise have, and it is doing a job no B-tree can.

Multiranges arrived in Postgres 14, and with them `range_agg`, which
aggregates a set of ranges into a normalised multirange — merging
adjacent and overlapping pieces. That is the tool for coverage questions:
`range_agg(valid_range)` for one employee produces either a single
contiguous range (complete coverage) or several (gaps), and comparing it
to the employment span answers the question directly.

## History and the SCD vocabulary

The "slowly changing dimension" types come from data warehousing —
Kimball's terminology, 1990s. Type 1 overwrites (no history). Type 2 adds
a row per version with validity dates (what this sector builds). Type 3
adds a "previous value" column (history of depth one, occasionally
exactly right). Types 4 and 6 combine a current table with a history
table, which is worth knowing because it is often the best operational
answer: the hot table stays small and single-versioned, the history table
grows, and queries choose.

SQL:2011 standardised temporal tables — `PERIOD FOR`, `AS OF SYSTEM
TIME`, application-time period tables. Postgres has implemented none of
it, and the community's answer has been range types plus exclusion
constraints, which is more flexible and less convenient. Extensions
(`temporal_tables`, `periods`) fill parts of the gap. Knowing the standard
exists is useful mainly for reading other databases' documentation without
confusion.

## Performance notes

History tables are append-mostly and grow linearly with change volume, not
with entity count — which surprises people, because a table of 800
employees can hold half a million history rows if titles and salaries
change often. Index them for the two access patterns that exist:
`(staff_id, valid_from)` for one entity's timeline, and the GiST range
index for as-of queries across everyone. A GIN or B-tree on `valid_from`
alone is rarely useful.

The as-of query across all entities is the expensive one: it touches every
entity's history and filters by containment. If it runs constantly — a
dashboard showing "the org chart as of X" — materialise it. If it runs
monthly, let it scan.

Point-in-time joins deserve attention because they are quietly quadratic
when written badly. A `LATERAL` with `LIMIT 1` per driving row is
n·log(m); a join on `p.paid_on BETWEEN h.valid_from AND h.valid_to` with
no index on the range is n·m. On 19,000 payments and 3,100 history rows
that difference is a coffee break.

## When not to do any of this

**When deletion is genuinely permanent and rare.** A row nobody will ask
about again should be deleted, and an archive table serves the "just in
case" instinct better than a flag on the live table.

**When the history is already elsewhere.** If every change is published to
an event log or a warehouse, a second history table in the OLTP database
is duplicated effort with a second chance to be wrong.

**When only the current value is ever queried.** A table of user
preferences does not need SCD type 2. Adding it means every read grows a
predicate to serve a question nobody asks.

**When the entity is high-churn and low-value.** Session records, cache
entries, rate-limit counters. Version history for these is storage spent
on nothing.

**Bitemporal, by default.** Two axes double the predicates in every query
and the cognitive load on every reader. Adopt it when someone will ask
what you knew and when — and note the asymmetry that makes this decision
hard: you cannot add the second axis retroactively, so the cost of
guessing wrong is not symmetric. The compromise most teams reach is to
record `recorded_at` on history rows from day one, which is cheap and
preserves the option, without building the full bitemporal query
discipline until it is needed.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — the re-hire that a unique constraint forbids

```sql
staff_members(staff_id bigint PK, email text NOT NULL,
              full_name text NOT NULL, hired_on date NOT NULL,
              deleted_at timestamptz)      -- 800 rows, 140 soft-deleted
```

There is no uniqueness on `email` at all yet. Somebody proposes `UNIQUE
(email)`. That constraint would be wrong in both directions: it fails to
build (two soft-deleted rows already share an address with a live one),
and if it did build it would make re-hiring impossible — a returning
employee's old, deleted row permanently occupies their address.

The rule you actually want is *unique among the living*.

In one script:

1. Create partial unique index `staff_live_email_key` on
   `staff_members (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`. The `lower()`
   is deliberate: email comparison is case-insensitive in every system
   that matters and case-sensitive in Postgres, so the index makes the
   intended rule explicit.
2. Re-hire someone: insert a new row for the email of the soft-deleted
   staff member with `staff_id = 3` — same `email`, `full_name` `'Nadia
   Kovač'`, `hired_on` `'2026-01-05'`, `deleted_at` NULL. This must
   succeed, and it is the operation a plain unique constraint would have
   made impossible.
3. Return, as the final statement, one row: `live` (count of rows with
   `deleted_at IS NULL`), `deleted` (count of the rest), and
   `index_rows` = the number of rows the partial index actually contains,
   which equals `live`.

The gate then attempts a second live row with the same email and expects a
unique violation naming `staff_live_email_key`, and attempts a second
*deleted* row with that email and expects it to succeed.

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e05_soft_deletes_history ex1`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The requirement has an "among the rows where" in it, so it is a partial
index. The expression `lower(email)` makes it an expression index as well;
both are ordinary features that happen to be combined here.

## Hint 2

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX t_live_key ON t (lower(code)) WHERE archived_at IS NULL;
```

For step 2, the insert needs the existing address, so read it rather than
retyping it:

```sql
INSERT INTO staff_members (email, full_name, hired_on)
SELECT email, 'Nadia Kovač', DATE '2026-01-05'
FROM staff_members WHERE staff_id = 3;
```

## Hint 3

For `index_rows`, you do not need to inspect the index itself — the
partial index contains exactly the rows matching its predicate, so a
`count(*) FILTER (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL)` is the same number and is
honest about being a derivation. If you would rather read the real thing,
`pg_class.reltuples` for the index is an estimate, not a count, and
estimates are the wrong answer to a gate.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Frame it as an argument you will have to win. Someone will say "just add
`UNIQUE (email)`, we can clean the deleted rows". Ask them what happens
when a former employee returns in 2029: either the old row is destroyed
(losing the history you soft-deleted to keep) or the re-hire is refused.
Soft deletes and total uniqueness are structurally incompatible, and the
partial index is not a workaround, it is the correct statement of the
rule.

## Hint 2

Confirm the index's predicate rather than trusting your typing:

```sql
SELECT indexdef FROM pg_indexes WHERE indexname = 'staff_live_email_key';
```

It should end `WHERE (deleted_at IS NULL)`. If the `WHERE` is missing, the
creation itself would have failed on the existing duplicates — so a
successful `CREATE` is already weak evidence, and the definition is the
strong kind.

## Hint 3

Notice the second-order consequence, because it decides schema designs
later. A partial unique index is *not* a unique constraint: it does not
appear in `pg_constraint`, and `REFERENCES staff_members(email)` cannot
use it, because a foreign key requires a constraint over the whole table.
So a child table cannot reference "the live employee with this email" —
only `staff_id`. That limitation is one of the quieter costs of soft
deletion, and it is the reason surrogate keys and soft deletes go together
so naturally.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e05_soft_deletes_history/ex1 — uniqueness among the living
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX staff_live_email_key
  ON staff_members (lower(email))
  WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

INSERT INTO staff_members (email, full_name, hired_on)
SELECT email, 'Nadia Kovač', DATE '2026-01-05'
FROM staff_members
WHERE staff_id = 3;

SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL)     AS live,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL) AS deleted,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL)     AS index_rows
FROM staff_members;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — make the predicate impossible to forget

Your ex1 script runs automatically first.

`SELECT * FROM staff_members` is now wrong in every report, every export
and every ad-hoc query run during an incident. Discipline does not scale;
structure does.

Build three things:

1. **`staff_live`** — a view over `staff_members` selecting `staff_id`,
   `email`, `full_name`, `hired_on` where `deleted_at IS NULL`, created
   `WITH (security_barrier = true)`.

   The barrier is not about permissions. Without it, the planner may
   evaluate a user-supplied `WHERE` condition *before* the view's own
   predicate — so `SELECT * FROM staff_live WHERE leaky(full_name)`, where
   `leaky()` raises an error containing its argument, can disclose the
   names of deleted staff. With the barrier, the view's predicate is
   evaluated first, always. The cost is that some optimisations are
   forbidden, which occasionally matters and is the reason it is not the
   default.

2. **`staff_live_hired_idx`** — a partial index on
   `staff_members (hired_on) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`. With 140 of 800
   rows deleted this is a small win; at 6 million of 8 million it is the
   difference between a working index and a decorative one.

3. **The final statement**: one row, `live_via_view` = `count(*)` from
   `staff_live`, and `all_rows` = `count(*)` from `staff_members`. The
   two differing is the entire point of the view.

The gate checks the view exists with `security_barrier` set (read
`pg_class.reloptions`), that the index is partial, and that `staff_live`
excludes every deleted row.

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e05_soft_deletes_history ex2`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One `CREATE VIEW` with an option list, one `CREATE INDEX` with a `WHERE`,
one `SELECT` with two scalar subqueries. The syntax for view options is
the part you may not have used.

## Hint 2

```sql
CREATE VIEW v WITH (security_barrier = true) AS
SELECT a, b FROM t WHERE tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::int;
```

The `WITH (...)` clause goes between the view name and `AS`.

## Hint 3

Decide whether the view should list columns explicitly or use `SELECT *`,
because it matters more than it looks. `SELECT *` in a view is frozen at
creation time — Postgres expands it immediately — so a column added to the
table later will not appear in the view, and you will spend twenty minutes
confused. Listing columns makes that behaviour explicit instead of
surprising.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the leak, because it is the only reason `security_barrier`
exists and it sounds theoretical until you construct it:

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION leaky(t text) RETURNS boolean
  LANGUAGE plpgsql COST 0.0001 AS $$
BEGIN RAISE NOTICE 'saw %', t; RETURN true; END $$;
```

A cheap function is attractive to the planner, so it gets pushed below the
view's predicate and runs on *every* row including deleted ones — printing
names you built the view to hide. The barrier forbids the reordering.

## Hint 2

Verify the option actually took, since a typo in the option name is
accepted silently in some versions and ignored:

```sql
SELECT relname, reloptions FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'staff_live';
```

You want to see `{security_barrier=true}`. An empty `reloptions` means the
clause did not apply and your view is an ordinary one.

## Hint 3

Know the honest limitation of this approach: a view is a convention that
anyone with table access can bypass, deliberately or by habit. The
structural version is row-level security, where the predicate is attached
to the table itself and no `SELECT` can escape it — V3·E8's subject. The
view is the right answer when the goal is convenience and consistency;
RLS is the right answer when the goal is a boundary you are willing to
defend in an audit.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — the referential integrity you no longer have

`payments.staff_id REFERENCES staff_members(staff_id)` is enforced, and it
guarantees less than everybody believes. A foreign key knows nothing about
`deleted_at`, so a payment may reference a soft-deleted employee and
Postgres considers the row perfectly valid.

This is not fixable with a constraint — a `CHECK` cannot query another
table, and a trigger checking liveness on insert is both expensive and
racy against a concurrent delete. What you can do is *know*, which means
writing the detection query and running it on a schedule.

Return every payment whose employee is soft-deleted:

- `payment_id`
- `staff_id`
- `paid_on`
- `amount`
- `deleted_at` — when the employee was deleted
- `paid_after_delete` (boolean) — true when `paid_on` is on or after
  `deleted_at::date`. This is the column that matters: a payment dated
  *before* the deletion is ordinary history, while a payment dated after
  is money moving to someone the system considers gone, which is either a
  bug or a fraud alert.

**Ordered by `paid_after_delete` descending, then `paid_on` descending,
then `payment_id` ascending.**

Example row: `(8812, 3, '2025-11-30', 4200.00, '2025-06-14 09:12:00+00',
true)`.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e05_soft_deletes_history ex3`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An inner join from `payments` to `staff_members` filtered to the deleted
employees. The only computed column is a boolean comparison between a date
and the date part of a timestamp.

## Hint 2

Comparing a `date` to a `timestamptz` needs one of them cast, and the
direction matters:

```sql
SELECT DATE '2025-11-30' >= '2025-06-14 09:12:00+00'::date;   -- true
```

Casting the timestamp down to a date is the right move here; casting the
date up to a timestamp would drag the session time zone into the
comparison.

## Hint 3

Think about the ordering the prompt asks for and why: the `true` rows
first, most recent first. That is a triage order — the query is meant to
be read top-down by someone deciding what to investigate — and designing
the ordering of a monitoring query as deliberately as its columns is a
habit worth building.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Understand what you are measuring before you write it. The soft delete
turned a hard guarantee ("every payment belongs to an employee") into a
soft one ("every payment belongs to an employee record"). You cannot
restore the hard guarantee, so the engineering response is to convert the
gap into a monitored quantity. That reframing — from "prevent" to
"detect" — is the whole exercise.

## Hint 2

Check the size of the problem before the details:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.deleted_at IS NOT NULL) AS to_deleted,
       count(*) AS total
FROM payments p JOIN staff_members s USING (staff_id);
```

If the ratio is large, soft deletion is being used for something it should
not be — probably as an archive — and the schema fix is to move those rows
out rather than to monitor them forever.

## Hint 3

Consider the three structural alternatives, so you can say why monitoring
was the choice. **Reparent on delete**: deletion becomes a procedure that
first moves or closes children; correct, and it makes deletion slow and
occasionally impossible. **Denormalize the flag**: copy `deleted_at` onto
`payments` and constrain it with a composite foreign key to
`(staff_id, deleted_at)` — genuinely enforceable, and it drags V3·E1's
denormalization ownership problem into the design. **Do not soft-delete
referenced rows**: archive them instead, which keeps the foreign key
meaningful. The third is usually right, and it is unavailable to you here
because the decision was made three years ago.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e05_soft_deletes_history/ex3 — payments pointing at deleted employees
SELECT p.payment_id,
       p.staff_id,
       p.paid_on,
       p.amount,
       s.deleted_at,
       (p.paid_on >= s.deleted_at::date) AS paid_after_delete
FROM payments p
JOIN staff_members s ON s.staff_id = p.staff_id
WHERE s.deleted_at IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY paid_after_delete DESC, p.paid_on DESC, p.payment_id;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3e05_soft_deletes_history/ex3 — same rows via a semi-join on the dead set
WITH dead AS (
  SELECT staff_id, deleted_at
  FROM staff_members
  WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT p.payment_id, p.staff_id, p.paid_on, p.amount, d.deleted_at,
       (p.paid_on >= d.deleted_at::date) AS paid_after_delete
FROM payments p
JOIN dead d USING (staff_id)
ORDER BY paid_after_delete DESC, p.paid_on DESC, p.payment_id;

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the overlaps you already have

```sql
staff_history(hist_id bigint PK, staff_id bigint NOT NULL,
              dept_id bigint NOT NULL, title text NOT NULL,
              salary numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
              valid_from date NOT NULL, valid_to date)   -- 3,100 rows
```

`valid_to` is exclusive; NULL means "still current". Nothing prevents two
rows for one employee from covering the same day, and the seeded data
contains such pairs — which means an as-of query returns two rows for
those people, and any report summing salary double-counts them.

Before constraining against overlaps in ex5, find them. Return one row per
**offending pair**:

- `staff_id`
- `hist_a` — the lower `hist_id` of the pair
- `hist_b` — the higher
- `overlap_days` (int) — the number of days the two spells share

Two spells overlap when the half-open intervals `[valid_from, valid_to)`
intersect, treating a NULL `valid_to` as `'infinity'`. Building each row's
`daterange(valid_from, coalesce(valid_to, 'infinity'), '[)')` inline and
testing with `&&` is far cleaner than four date comparisons — and
`upper(a * b) - lower(a * b)` gives the shared length directly, where `*`
is range intersection.

Report each pair once: join with `a.hist_id < b.hist_id`.

**Ordered by `overlap_days` descending, then `staff_id`, then `hist_a`.**

Note the `'infinity'` case: two open-ended spells for one employee overlap
infinitely, which would make `overlap_days` unrepresentable. The seeded
data has no such pair — verify that rather than assuming it, because if
one existed your query would raise and the gate would tell you nothing
useful.

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e05_soft_deletes_history ex4`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A self-join on `staff_id` with `a.hist_id < b.hist_id` to get each pair
once, and an overlap test in the `WHERE`. The overlap test is where ranges
earn their keep.

## Hint 2

```sql
SELECT daterange(DATE '2024-01-01', DATE '2024-07-01', '[)')
    && daterange(DATE '2024-06-01', DATE '2024-09-01', '[)');   -- true

SELECT daterange(DATE '2024-01-01', DATE '2024-07-01', '[)')
     * daterange(DATE '2024-06-01', DATE '2024-09-01', '[)');
-- [2024-06-01,2024-07-01)
```

`*` is intersection; `upper(r) - lower(r)` on a `daterange` gives an
integer number of days.

## Hint 3

Write the range expression once in a CTE rather than four times in the
join — `SELECT hist_id, staff_id, daterange(...) AS r FROM staff_history`
— and the self-join becomes two columns and one operator. Whether you
also want to keep `title` and `salary` in that CTE depends on whether you
plan to read the output rather than only count it, and reading it is how
you find out what the overlaps actually are.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The habit being drilled is the one from V3·E1 ex1 and V3·E4 ex2: before
adding a constraint, measure the violations. Every time you skip it, you
find out at `ALTER TABLE` time, in a maintenance window, with a rollback
plan you have not written.

## Hint 2

Look at one offending employee's whole timeline, not just the pair:

```sql
SELECT hist_id, title, valid_from, valid_to
FROM staff_history WHERE staff_id = (
  SELECT staff_id FROM staff_history GROUP BY staff_id, valid_from
  HAVING count(*) > 1 LIMIT 1)
ORDER BY valid_from;
```

Reading a real timeline tells you which of the two rows is wrong, which a
pair count never will. Most overlaps in real data are a missing `valid_to`
on the old row — somebody inserted the new spell and forgot to close the
previous one.

## Hint 3

Decide what "overlap" means at the boundary, because it is a genuine
choice. Under half-open intervals, a spell ending 2024-07-01 and one
starting 2024-07-01 do **not** overlap, which is what consecutive spells
require. Under inclusive `valid_to` they would, and every clean handover
in your data would be flagged. If your query reports thousands of
one-day overlaps, this is why — and the fix is the bound notation, not
the query.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e05_soft_deletes_history/ex4 — overlapping history spells, pairwise
WITH spans AS (
  SELECT hist_id, staff_id,
         daterange(valid_from, coalesce(valid_to, 'infinity'), '[)') AS r
  FROM staff_history
)
SELECT a.staff_id,
       a.hist_id AS hist_a,
       b.hist_id AS hist_b,
       (upper(a.r * b.r) - lower(a.r * b.r))::int AS overlap_days
FROM spans a
JOIN spans b ON b.staff_id = a.staff_id
            AND b.hist_id  > a.hist_id
            AND a.r && b.r
ORDER BY overlap_days DESC, a.staff_id, hist_a;

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — make overlapping history unrepresentable

Your ex4 query found the overlapping pairs. Now repair and constrain.

In one script:

1. **Repair.** For every overlapping pair, the older row is the one that
   was never closed. Close it: set `valid_to` to the *later* row's
   `valid_from`, for every row that overlaps a later row of the same
   employee. Concretely — for each `staff_history` row `a`, if some row
   `b` for the same `staff_id` has `b.valid_from > a.valid_from` and the
   two spans overlap, set `a.valid_to = min(b.valid_from)` over all such
   `b`.

2. **Add the range column:**

```sql
ALTER TABLE staff_history
  ADD COLUMN valid_range daterange
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS
    (daterange(valid_from, coalesce(valid_to, 'infinity'), '[)')) STORED;
```

   The `coalesce` to `'infinity'` is what removes the NULL-means-current
   special case from every query downstream. `'infinity'` is a real `date`
   value, so range operators handle it arithmetically rather than under
   three-valued logic.

3. **Constrain:**

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;
ALTER TABLE staff_history
  ADD CONSTRAINT staff_history_no_overlap
  EXCLUDE USING gist (staff_id WITH =, valid_range WITH &&);
```

   The extension is required because you are mixing `=` on a `bigint` with
   `&&` on a range, and plain GiST has no operator class for `bigint`
   equality.

Order is not optional: the constraint will not build while overlaps
remain, which is the constraint proving your repair worked.

The gate checks zero overlaps remain, that the constraint exists, and then
attempts to insert an overlapping spell and expects it to be refused.

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test v3e05_soft_deletes_history ex5`.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One `UPDATE`, one `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN`, one `CREATE EXTENSION`,
one `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT`. The `UPDATE` is the only one with
any thinking in it.

## Hint 2

An update driven by a correlated aggregate:

```sql
UPDATE staff_history a
SET valid_to = (SELECT min(b.valid_from) FROM staff_history b
                WHERE b.staff_id = a.staff_id
                  AND b.valid_from > a.valid_from)
WHERE ...;
```

The `WHERE` on the outer update restricts it to rows that actually overlap
something, so untouched rows keep their `valid_to`.

## Hint 3

Be careful that the repair does not shorten rows that are already correct.
A row whose `valid_to` already equals the next row's `valid_from` is
fine — it does not overlap — so the outer `WHERE` must test for overlap,
not merely for the existence of a later row. Getting this wrong produces a
table with no overlaps and several silently truncated spells, which the
constraint will happily accept.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Question the repair rule before applying it. "The older row was never
closed" is a hypothesis about how the data got this way, and ex4's
important-hints suggested checking it by reading a real timeline. If some
overlaps are instead a *duplicate* spell — same title, same salary,
different `hist_id` — closing the older one leaves a zero-length or
nonsensical range, and the right repair is to delete one. A migration that
applies one rule to two different problems is how data-cleaning scripts
earn their reputation.

## Hint 2

Verify at each step rather than at the end:

```sql
-- after the repair, before the constraint: must return zero rows
WITH spans AS (SELECT hist_id, staff_id,
                      daterange(valid_from,
                                coalesce(valid_to,'infinity'),'[)') AS r
               FROM staff_history)
SELECT count(*) FROM spans a JOIN spans b
  ON b.staff_id = a.staff_id AND b.hist_id > a.hist_id AND a.r && b.r;
```

If that is non-zero the `ALTER TABLE` will fail, and it will fail after
scanning 3,100 rows and building an index it then throws away.

## Hint 3

Notice that you now have one object doing two jobs. The GiST index behind
the exclusion constraint enforces non-overlap *and* accelerates
`valid_range @> some_date`, which is exactly the as-of query ex6 asks for.
That coincidence is unusual and worth naming: correctness features and
performance features rarely arrive in the same object, and when they do it
is a strong argument for the design.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3e05_soft_deletes_history/ex5 — repair overlaps, then forbid them
UPDATE staff_history a
SET valid_to = (SELECT min(b.valid_from)
                FROM staff_history b
                WHERE b.staff_id   = a.staff_id
                  AND b.valid_from > a.valid_from)
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM staff_history b
              WHERE b.staff_id   = a.staff_id
                AND b.valid_from > a.valid_from
                AND daterange(a.valid_from,
                              coalesce(a.valid_to, 'infinity'), '[)')
                 && daterange(b.valid_from,
                              coalesce(b.valid_to, 'infinity'), '[)'));

ALTER TABLE staff_history
  ADD COLUMN valid_range daterange
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS
    (daterange(valid_from, coalesce(valid_to, 'infinity'), '[)')) STORED;

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

ALTER TABLE staff_history
  ADD CONSTRAINT staff_history_no_overlap
  EXCLUDE USING gist (staff_id WITH =, valid_range WITH &&);

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — the world as it was on one day
